sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Random motion and the birth of drift

board_events.text: What is actually moving inside a wire?
Inside a metal, the outermost electron of each atom breaks free of its own nucleus and joins a shared sea of free electrons.
Those free electrons move fast, around ten to the power five metres per second at room temperature, but in completely random directions.
Averaged over the whole wire they go nowhere: as much charge crosses any section leftward as rightward, so the net current is zero.
Connect a cell and an electric field appears inside the wire, pushing every electron with a force of magnitude $eE$ opposite to the field.
The random storm does not stop. A gentle, persistent push is simply superimposed on top of it.

board_events.text: That small average velocity riding on furious random motion is the drift velocity, written $v_d$.

segments.text: Let us begin with a question that sounds simple but is not: what is moving inside a wire when a current flows?
Inside a metal, the outermost electron of each atom is not tied to any one nucleus. It joins a shared sea of free electrons belonging to the whole piece of metal.

<curious>These free electrons are not sitting still.</curious> They move around ten to the power five metres per second at room temperature, but in completely random directions, colliding constantly with the vibrating lattice.
Here is the consequence. Average that motion over the whole wire and the electrons go nowhere. As much charge crosses any cross-section leftward as rightward, so the net current is exactly zero.
Now connect a cell. An electric field is set up inside the metal, pushing every electron with a force of magnitude e times capital E, opposite to the field.
Notice what does not happen. The random storm does not stop. The electrons keep colliding and zig-zagging exactly as before, and a gentle persistent push is simply superimposed on that chaos.

Picture the two situations side by side. Field off, the paths are tangled and the net displacement is zero. Field on, those same tangled paths are each tilted very slightly, so the whole crowd creeps one way.
That small average velocity, riding on top of furious random motion, is what we call the drift velocity, written v subscript d. Everything in this subtopic is built on it.
Ek sawaal se शुरू करते हैं जो सुनने में simple लगता है लेकिन है नहीं: जब current बहता है तो wire के अंदर असल में move क्या कर रहा है?
Metal के अंदर हर atom का outermost electron किसी एक nucleus से बंधा नहीं होता। वो आज़ाद होकर free electrons के एक साझा समुद्र में शामिल हो जाता है।
Ye free electrons शांत बैठे नहीं हैं। Room temperature पर ये लगभग ten to the power five metre per second से चलते हैं, लेकिन बिलकुल random directions में, vibrating lattice से लगातार टकराते हुए।
Iska नतीजा देखिए। उस motion को पूरे wire पर average कीजिए और electrons कहीं जाते ही नहीं। किसी भी cross-section से जितना charge बाईं तरफ़ जाता है उतना ही दाईं तरफ़, इसलिए net current बिलकुल zero है।

<curious>Ab एक cell जोड़िए।</curious> Metal के अंदर electric field बन जाता है, जो हर electron को e into capital E के बराबर force से धक्का देता है, field के उल्टी दिशा में, क्योंकि electron का charge negative है।
Dhyan दीजिए कि क्या नहीं होता। Random storm रुकता नहीं। Electrons पहले की तरह ही टकराते और zig-zag करते रहते हैं, बस उस अफरातफरी के ऊपर एक हल्का लगातार धक्का चढ़ जाता है।
Dono हालात साथ साथ सोचिए। Field off हो तो रास्ते उलझे हैं और net displacement zero है। Field on हो तो वही उलझे रास्ते ज़रा सा झुक जाते हैं, और पूरी भीड़ एक तरफ़ सरकने लगती है।
Wahi छोटी सी average velocity, जो इस तेज़ random motion के ऊपर सवार है, उसे drift velocity कहते हैं, v subscript d। इस पूरे subtopic की नींव यही है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Slow carriers, fast signal

board_events.text: Slow carriers, fast signal
In a typical copper wire carrying a few amperes, the drift speed is around ten to the power minus four metres per second.
That is slower than a snail, a fraction of a millimetre every second.
So why does a tubelight glow the instant you flip the switch, even when the wire is metres long?
Because you are not waiting for one electron to travel from the switch to the bulb.

board_events.text: The field is established along the entire wire at nearly the speed of light, so every electron starts drifting almost simultaneously.
That includes electrons already inside the bulb filament, which begin moving without waiting for anything to arrive from the switch.

segments.text: The next fact about drift velocity is genuinely surprising, and examiners test it constantly.
In a typical copper wire carrying just a few amperes, the drift speed works out to around ten to the power minus four metres per second.
Let that sink in. That is slower than a snail. The electrons advance a fraction of a millimetre in a whole second.
<curious>Which raises an obvious problem.</curious> If electrons crawl that slowly, why does a tubelight glow the instant you flip the switch, even when the wire running to it is metres long?
The resolution is that you are not waiting for one particular electron to travel all the way from the switch to the bulb. That is the wrong mental picture entirely.
Hold onto this analogy instead: a long pipe already completely full of water. Open the tap and water gushes from the far end immediately, even though any single water molecule is moving slowly.

In the wire, the electric field plays the role of that signal. It is established along the entire length at nearly the speed of light, so every electron everywhere starts drifting almost simultaneously.

That includes the electrons already sitting inside the bulb filament. They begin moving straight away, without waiting for anything to arrive from the switch. The signal is fast; the carriers are slow.
Drift velocity के बारे में अगली बात सचमुच चौंकाने वाली है, और examiners इसे लगातार पूछते हैं।
Ek typical copper wire में जो सिर्फ़ कुछ ampere ले जा रही है, drift speed निकलती है लगभग ten to the power minus four metre per second।
Zara सोचिए इसका मतलब। ये घोंघे से भी धीमा है। Electrons पूरे एक second में एक millimetre का छोटा सा हिस्सा ही आगे बढ़ते हैं।
Isse एक साफ़ सवाल खड़ा होता है। अगर electrons इतने धीरे रेंगते हैं, तो switch दबाते ही tubelight उसी पल क्यों जल जाती है, जबकि उस तक जाने वाली wire कई metre लंबी है?
<excited>Jawab ये है कि आप किसी एक electron के switch से bulb तक पहुँचने का इंतज़ार कर ही नहीं रहे।</excited> वो mental picture पूरी तरह ग़लत है।
Iski जगह ये analogy पकड़िए: एक लंबा पाइप जो पहले से पूरा पानी से भरा है। Tap खोलिए और दूर वाले सिरे से पानी तुरंत बहने लगता है, जबकि कोई एक पानी का molecule धीरे ही चलता है।
Wire में electric field उसी signal का काम करता है। ये पूरी लंबाई पर लगभग light की speed से बन जाता है, इसलिए हर जगह के सारे electrons लगभग एक साथ drift करना शुरू कर देते हैं।
Isme bulb के filament के अंदर पहले से बैठे electrons भी शामिल हैं। वो तुरंत चलना शुरू कर देते हैं, switch से कुछ आने का इंतज़ार किए बिना। Signal तेज़ है, carriers धीमे।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Defining current, and why it is a scalar

board_events.text: Current is a scalar, not a vector
Electric current is the rate at which charge flows past a cross-section of the conductor.
We do speak of a direction: conventional current is the direction a positive charge would flow, and so it opposes the actual electron drift.
But current does not add like a vector. At a junction, currents combine by simple algebraic addition along the wires.

board_events.text: No single vector could describe the current along a bent wire, because the current follows the wire wherever it goes.
Direction here is a sign convention along a conductor. Current density, by contrast, genuinely is a vector.

segments.text: Now let us pin down what current actually is, and settle a distinction that trips up an enormous number of students.
Electric current is simply the rate at which charge flows past a cross-section of the conductor.
For a steady flow it is the total charge divided by the time taken, and more generally it is the instantaneous derivative, d q by d t.
Now, we do routinely speak of the direction of a current. Conventional current is the direction in which a positive charge would flow, so in a metal it points opposite to the real electron drift.

<whisper>Here is the exam-favourite point.</whisper> Even though current has a direction, it does not add like a vector. At a wire junction, currents combine by simple algebraic addition along the wires, with signs.
Look at the junction drawn here. Five amperes and three amperes arriving give eight amperes leaving. You add the numbers; you never resolve them into components and apply the parallelogram law.
Think about a bent wire and you will see why. No single vector could describe the current along it, because the current simply follows the wire wherever the wire happens to go.

So direction here is a sign convention along a conductor, not a true vector quantity. Current is a scalar. Current density, which we meet in the formulas, genuinely is a vector, and mixing the two up is one of the commonest errors in this chapter.
Ab साफ़ करते हैं कि current असल में है क्या, और एक ऐसा फ़र्क़ तय करते हैं जिस पर बहुत सारे students फिसलते हैं।
Electric current बस वो rate है जिससे charge conductor के किसी cross-section से होकर बहता है।
Steady flow के लिए ये कुल charge divided by लगा हुआ time है, और आम तौर पर ये instantaneous derivative है, d q by d t।
Ab, हम current की direction की बात तो करते ही हैं। Conventional current वो दिशा है जिसमें positive charge बहेगा, इसलिए metal में ये असली electron drift के उल्टा होता है।
Ye रहा exam का पसंदीदा point। Direction होने के बावजूद current vector की तरह नहीं जुड़ता। Wire के junction पर currents wires के साथ साधारण algebraic addition से जुड़ते हैं, sign के साथ।
<curious>Yahan बना हुआ junction देखिए।</curious> पाँच ampere और तीन ampere आ रहे हैं, तो आठ ampere निकलते हैं। आप numbers जोड़ते हैं; कभी components में तोड़ कर parallelogram law नहीं लगाते।
Ek मुड़ी हुई wire सोचिए और वजह साफ़ हो जाएगी। कोई एक vector उसमें बहते current को बता ही नहीं सकता, क्योंकि current बस wire के पीछे पीछे जाता है, wire जहाँ भी जाए।

To यहाँ direction सिर्फ़ conductor के साथ एक sign convention है, कोई सच्ची vector quantity नहीं। Current scalar है। Current density, जो formulas में मिलेगी, सचमुच vector है, और इन दोनों को मिला देना इस chapter की सबसे आम ग़लतियों में से एक है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: The free-electron model and its limits

board_events.text: The free-electron model, and where it breaks
The whole drift picture rests on the Drude free-electron model.
It treats the electrons as a classical gas that accelerates between collisions and is randomised at every collision.
The model is characterised by a single average relaxation time, written $\tau$, the mean time between collisions.
This works beautifully for ordinary metals at normal temperatures, but it is only an approximation.
It ignores quantum effects, and it breaks down for semiconductors, for electrolytes where ions carry the charge, and for gases.
The relation $I = neAv_d$ separately assumes a single type of carrier with uniform number density across the whole section.
J E E Advanced problems are built by violating exactly one of these assumptions at a time.

segments.text: Before we derive anything with this picture, it is worth being honest about what the picture assumes, because the harder exams attack precisely those assumptions.
The whole drift story rests on what is called the Drude free-electron model.
That model treats the free electrons as a classical gas. Each electron accelerates freely between collisions, and every collision with the lattice randomises its motion completely.
The entire model is characterised by a single number: an average relaxation time, written tau, which is the mean time between one collision and the next.
Now, this works beautifully for ordinary metals at normal temperatures, and every result we derive will come out of it. But remember it is only an approximation, not a law of nature.
It ignores quantum effects entirely, and it breaks down for semiconductors, for electrolytes where ions rather than electrons carry the charge, and for gases.
Separately, the simple relation current equals n e A times drift velocity assumes there is a single type of carrier, with a uniform number density right across the cross-section.

<whisper>Here is the pattern worth knowing.</whisper> J E E Advanced problems in this subtopic are almost always built by violating exactly one of these assumptions at a time: a non-uniform conductor, or more than one kind of carrier.
Is picture से कुछ भी derive करने से पहले ये मानना ज़रूरी है कि ये picture क्या मान कर चलती है, क्योंकि मुश्किल exams ठीक उन्हीं assumptions पर हमला करते हैं।
Poori drift की कहानी जिस चीज़ पर टिकी है उसे Drude free-electron model कहते हैं।
Wo model free electrons को classical gas मानता है। हर electron collisions के बीच आज़ादी से accelerate होता है, और lattice से हर टक्कर उसकी motion पूरी तरह random कर देती है।
Poora model एक ही number से तय होता है: एक average relaxation time, जिसे tau लिखते हैं, यानी एक collision से अगले collision तक का औसत time।
<curious>Ye आम metals के लिए normal temperature पर बहुत बढ़िया काम करता है</curious>, और आगे हम जो derive करेंगे वो सब इसी से निकलेगा। लेकिन याद रखिए ये सिर्फ़ approximation है, प्रकृति का नियम नहीं।
Ye quantum effects को पूरी तरह नज़रअंदाज़ करता है, और semiconductors, electrolytes जहाँ electrons नहीं ions charge ले जाते हैं, और gases के लिए टूट जाता है।
Alag से, वो साधारण relation current equals n e A into drift velocity ये मान कर चलता है कि carrier एक ही तरह का है, और उसकी number density पूरे cross-section पर एक जैसी है।

Ye pattern जानने लायक़ है। इस subtopic में J E E Advanced के सवाल लगभग हमेशा इन्हीं assumptions में से एक को एक बार में तोड़ कर बनाए जाते हैं: कोई non-uniform conductor, या एक से ज़्यादा तरह के carrier।

sections.title: When Ohm's law fails: non-linear and one-way devices

board_events.text: When Ohm's law fails: non-linear and one-way devices
Ohm's law is a useful approximation, not a law of nature like conservation of charge.
It holds cleanly only for metallic conductors at constant temperature and modest fields. Real devices deviate in three textbook ways.
First failure: $V$ is not proportional to $I$, so the graph is a curve and resistance is no longer a single constant.

Second failure: the relation depends on the sign of $V$, so reversing the applied voltage does not simply reverse the current.

segments.text: Ohm's law is so familiar that students treat it as universal. It is not, and C B S E asks for its limitations by name, usually with the graph.
State it plainly: Ohm's law is a useful approximation, not a law of nature in the way conservation of charge is.
It holds cleanly only for metallic conductors at constant temperature and modest fields, and real materials deviate from it in three textbook-classic ways.
The first failure is that voltage is simply not proportional to current. The graph is a curve rather than a straight line, so resistance is no longer a single constant number.
Look at the two traces. The straight line through the origin is an ohmic metal at constant temperature. The curve bending away from it is a filament lamp.
The mechanism is one we have already built. As the current rises the filament heats, the relaxation time falls, the resistivity rises, and so the graph bends away from the straight line.

<curious>The second failure is stranger.</curious> The relation depends on the sign of the applied voltage, so reversing the voltage does not simply reverse the current. The magnitude is different too.
The semiconductor diode is the standard example. Above a small forward threshold it conducts freely, while in reverse bias it passes almost nothing at all until breakdown.
Ohm's law इतना जाना पहचाना है कि students इसे universal मान लेते हैं। ये है नहीं, और C B S E इसकी limitations नाम लेकर पूछता है, अक्सर graph के साथ।
Saaf कह दीजिए: Ohm's law एक काम की approximation है, प्रकृति का नियम नहीं, जैसा conservation of charge है।
Ye सिर्फ़ metallic conductors के लिए, constant temperature और मामूली fields पर साफ़ चलता है, और असली materials इससे तीन classic तरीक़ों से हटते हैं।
Pehli नाकामी ये है कि voltage current के अनुपात में होता ही नहीं। Graph सीधी line की जगह एक curve है, इसलिए resistance अब कोई एक स्थिर number नहीं रहा।
<curious>Dono traces देखिए।</curious> Origin से गुज़रती सीधी line constant temperature पर एक ohmic metal है। उससे हटता हुआ curve एक filament lamp है।
Iska mechanism हम पहले ही बना चुके हैं। Current बढ़ने पर filament गरम होता है, relaxation time गिरता है, resistivity बढ़ती है, और इसीलिए graph सीधी line से हट जाता है।
Doosri नाकामी और अजीब है। Relation लगाए गए voltage के sign पर depend करता है, इसलिए voltage उल्टा करने से current बस उल्टा नहीं होता। उसका magnitude भी अलग होता है।
Semiconductor diode इसका standard उदाहरण है। एक छोटे forward threshold के ऊपर ये आसानी से conduct करता है, जबकि reverse bias में breakdown तक लगभग कुछ भी नहीं गुज़रने देता।

sections.title: Non-unique characteristics and two kinds of resistance

board_events.text: Non-unique characteristics, and two kinds of resistance
Third failure: the relation is non-unique, giving more than one value of $I$ for the same $V$.

        stroke="#c2820a" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>

board_events.caption: A characteristic that bends back on itself, so one voltage maps to several currents, with a down-sloping negative-resistance region.

board_events.text: Materials such as gallium arsenide contain a region where $dV/dI$ is negative: current rises as voltage falls.
A device obeying $V = IR$ with constant $R$ is ohmic. Anything else is non-ohmic: diode, transistor, thermistor, electrolyte, gas discharge, filament.
Static resistance is the slope of the line from the origin; dynamic resistance is the local slope of the curve itself.
For an ohmic resistor the two are equal. For any curved characteristic they differ, and in a negative-resistance region the dynamic value turns negative while the static value stays positive.

segments.text: The third and strangest failure of Ohm's law leads directly into a distinction that J E E loves: two different meanings of the word resistance.
The third failure is that the relation can be non-unique. For some materials, a single value of voltage corresponds to more than one value of current.
Look at how the characteristic bends back on itself. Draw a vertical line at one voltage and it crosses the curve at several different currents.

Materials such as gallium arsenide behave this way, and the down-sloping middle portion is called a negative-resistance region, where d V by d I is negative and current actually rises as voltage falls.

So here is the clean classification. A device obeying V equals I R with a constant R is ohmic. Anything else is non-ohmic: a diode, a transistor, a thermistor, an electrolyte, a gas discharge, a filament.
<curious>Now the distinction worth marks.</curious> For a non-ohmic device we define two resistances. Static resistance is voltage over current. Dynamic resistance is the derivative, d V by d I.
Read them off the graph. Static resistance is the slope of the straight line drawn from the origin to your operating point. Dynamic resistance is the local slope of the curve itself at that point.

For an ordinary ohmic resistor the two are identical, which is why you never had to distinguish them. For any curved characteristic they differ, and in a negative-resistance region the dynamic value turns negative while the static stays firmly positive.
Ohm's law की तीसरी और सबसे अजीब नाकामी सीधे उस फ़र्क़ तक ले जाती है जो J E E को बहुत पसंद है: resistance शब्द के दो अलग मतलब।
Teesri नाकामी ये है कि relation non-unique हो सकता है। कुछ materials में voltage की एक ही value पर current की एक से ज़्यादा values आती हैं।
Dekhiye characteristic अपने ऊपर कैसे मुड़ जाता है। एक voltage पर खड़ी line खींचिए और वो curve को कई अलग currents पर काटेगी।
Gallium arsenide जैसे materials ऐसा ही करते हैं, और बीच का नीचे ढलता हिस्सा negative-resistance region कहलाता है, जहाँ d V by d I negative है और voltage गिरने पर current असल में बढ़ता है।

<excited>To साफ़ classification ये रही।</excited> जो device V equals I R को स्थिर R के साथ मानता है वो ohmic है। बाक़ी सब non-ohmic: diode, transistor, thermistor, electrolyte, gas discharge, filament।
Ab वो फ़र्क़ जिस पर marks मिलते हैं। Non-ohmic device के लिए हम दो resistance define करते हैं। Static resistance है voltage over current। Dynamic resistance है derivative, d V by d I।
Inhe graph पर पढ़िए। Static resistance origin से आपके operating point तक खींची सीधी line का slope है। Dynamic resistance उसी point पर curve के अपने local slope का।

Saadharan ohmic resistor में दोनों एक जैसे होते हैं, इसीलिए पहले कभी फ़र्क़ करना नहीं पड़ा। किसी भी मुड़े हुए characteristic में ये अलग होते हैं, और negative-resistance region में dynamic value negative हो जाती है जबकि static value पक्की positive रहती है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Current, drift velocity and current density

board_events.text: Current, drift velocity and current density
SI unit: the ampere, one coulomb per second. The ampere is an S I base unit, so its dimensional formula is simply $A$.
Here $n$ is the free-electron number density in per cubic metre, $e$ the electronic charge, and $\tau$ the relaxation time.
Current density is a true vector, directed along the conventional current. Its unit is ampere per square metre.
Its dimensional formula is $L^{-2}A$, whereas current itself carries the dimension $A$ alone.

segments.text: Here is the first block of formulas for this subtopic. Everything on this board should be reproducible from memory before you sit the exam.
Current is the rate of flow of charge, d q by d t.

Its S I unit is the ampere, equal to one coulomb per second. The ampere is one of the seven S I base units, which is why its dimensional formula is simply A, with no combination of mass, length or time.
Drift velocity works out to e times the field times tau, divided by the electron mass. Substituting that into the flow of charge gives current as n e A times drift velocity.

In these expressions n is the free-electron number density in per cubic metre, e is the electronic charge of one point six times ten to the power minus nineteen coulomb, and tau is the relaxation time.
Current density is defined as n e times drift velocity. It equals current divided by area, and it also equals conductivity times the electric field.
<curious>Pay attention to this one.</curious> Current density is a true vector, directed along the conventional current, and its unit is the ampere per square metre.

Its dimensional formula is L to the minus two, A, whereas current itself carries the dimension A alone. If a quantity in a question has both a direction in space and units of per area, it is current density and not current.
Ye है इस subtopic के formulas का पहला हिस्सा। Exam में बैठने से पहले इस board की हर चीज़ याद से लिख पाना चाहिए।
Current है charge के बहने की rate, यानी d q by d t।
Iska S I unit ampere है, जो एक coulomb per second के बराबर है। Ampere सात S I base units में से एक है, इसीलिए इसका dimensional formula सिर्फ़ A है, इसमें mass, length या time का कोई combination नहीं।
Drift velocity निकलती है e into field into tau, electron के mass से divide। इसे charge के flow में रखने पर current मिलता है n e A into drift velocity।

<curious>In expressions में n है free-electron number density per cubic metre में</curious>, e है electronic charge यानी one point six into ten power minus nineteen coulomb, और tau है relaxation time।
Current density को define करते हैं n e into drift velocity। ये current divided by area के बराबर है, और conductivity into electric field के भी।
Is बात पर ख़ास ध्यान दीजिए। Current density एक सच्ची vector है, conventional current की दिशा में, और इसका unit ampere per square metre है।

Iska dimensional formula L to the minus two, A है, जबकि current का dimension अकेला A है। अगर सवाल में किसी quantity की space में direction भी हो और unit per area हो, तो वो current density है, current नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Mobility, and Ohm's law in two forms

board_events.text: Mobility, and Ohm's law in two forms
Mobility is the drift speed acquired per unit applied field. Its unit is metre squared per volt second.
Its dimensional formula is $M^{-1}T^{2}A$, and for copper it comes out around four times ten to the power minus three.
The macroscopic form describes a whole object; the microscopic form describes a single point inside the material.
They carry identical physics for a uniform wire, but the microscopic form is the one that survives when the conductor is not uniform.

segments.text: The second formula block introduces mobility and then states Ohm's law in the two forms you are expected to know.
Mobility is defined as the magnitude of the drift velocity divided by the applied field, and substituting the drift velocity expression collapses it to e tau over m.
In words, mobility is the drift speed a carrier acquires per unit of applied field. Its S I unit is metres squared per volt second.
Its dimensional formula is M to the minus one, T squared, A, and for copper the value comes out around four times ten to the power minus three in those units.
Now Ohm's law. The form you met in school is the macroscopic one: voltage equals current times resistance.

<curious>But there is a second, deeper form.</curious> Microscopic Ohm's law says current density equals conductivity times electric field, or equivalently that the field equals resistivity times current density.

The difference matters. The macroscopic form describes a whole object, an entire resistor with a length and a cross-section. The microscopic form describes conditions at a single point inside the material.
For a uniform wire they carry identical physics. But the microscopic form is the one that survives when the conductor is not uniform, which is exactly why advanced problems reach for it.
Formulas का दूसरा हिस्सा mobility से शुरू होता है और फिर Ohm's law को उन दो रूपों में बताता है जो आपसे अपेक्षित हैं।
Mobility को define करते हैं drift velocity के magnitude divided by applied field, और drift velocity की expression रखने पर ये सिमट कर e tau over m बन जाती है।
Shabdon में, mobility वो drift speed है जो एक carrier per unit applied field हासिल करता है। इसका S I unit है metre squared per volt second।
Iska dimensional formula है M to the minus one, T squared, A, और copper के लिए ये value उन्हीं units में लगभग four into ten power minus three आती है।
Ab Ohm's law। जो रूप आपने school में पढ़ा वो macroscopic है: voltage equals current into resistance।
Lekin एक दूसरा, गहरा रूप भी है। Microscopic Ohm's law कहता है current density equals conductivity into electric field, या बराबरी में, field equals resistivity into current density।
<excited>Ye फ़र्क़ मायने रखता है।</excited> Macroscopic रूप पूरी वस्तु को बताता है, एक पूरा resistor जिसकी length और cross-section है। Microscopic रूप material के अंदर एक ही point की हालत बताता है।
Uniform wire के लिए दोनों में physics एक ही है। लेकिन जब conductor uniform न हो तब microscopic रूप ही बचता है, और इसीलिए advanced सवाल उसी को उठाते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Resistance, resistivity and conductivity

board_events.text: Resistance, resistivity and conductivity
Resistance is measured in ohm, with dimensional formula $M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-2}$.
Resistivity is a material property, entirely independent of the size or shape of the specimen. Its unit is the ohm metre.
Conductivity is its reciprocal, in siemens per metre, with dimensional formula $M^{-1}L^{-3}T^{3}A^{2}$.
The temperature coefficient $\alpha$ is positive for metals and negative for semiconductors and insulators.

segments.text: The last definitional block covers resistance, resistivity and conductivity, and sets up the temperature behaviour studied properly in the next subtopic.
Resistance depends on geometry: it is resistivity times length divided by cross-sectional area.
Resistance is measured in ohm, which is one volt per ampere, and its dimensional formula is M, L squared, T to the minus three, A to the minus two.
Resistivity itself we derive in a moment. It equals the reciprocal of conductivity, and from the free-electron model it equals m over n e squared tau.
<whisper>This next point is worth a mark on its own.</whisper> Resistivity is a material property. It is entirely independent of the size or shape of the specimen, and its unit is the ohm metre.
Conductivity is simply its reciprocal, measured in siemens per metre, with dimensional formula M to the minus one, L to the minus three, T cubed, A squared.
Finally, both resistivity and resistance follow the same linear temperature law: the value at a reference temperature multiplied by one plus alpha times the temperature change.
That coefficient alpha is positive for metals, where resistance rises on heating, and negative for semiconductors and insulators, where it falls. We see exactly why in the next subtopic.
Aakhri definitional हिस्सा resistance, resistivity और conductivity को cover करता है, और उस temperature behaviour की नींव रखता है जिसे अगले subtopic में ठीक से पढ़ेंगे।
Resistance geometry पर depend करता है: ये resistivity into length divided by cross-sectional area है।
Resistance ohm में मापा जाता है, जो एक volt per ampere है, और इसका dimensional formula है M, L squared, T to the minus three, A to the minus two।
Resistivity को हम अभी derive करेंगे। ये conductivity के reciprocal के बराबर है, और free-electron model से m over n e squared tau निकलती है।
Ye अगली बात अपने आप में एक mark की है। Resistivity material की property है। ये specimen के size या shape से बिलकुल स्वतंत्र है, और इसका unit ohm metre है।
<excited>Conductivity बस इसका reciprocal है</excited>, siemens per metre में, dimensional formula M to the minus one, L to the minus three, T cubed, A squared के साथ।
Aakhir में, resistivity और resistance दोनों एक ही linear temperature law follow करते हैं: reference temperature की value into one plus alpha into temperature change।
Wo coefficient alpha metals के लिए positive है, जहाँ गरम करने पर resistance बढ़ता है, और semiconductors तथा insulators के लिए negative, जहाँ घटता है। ठीक क्यों, ये अगले subtopic में।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Board derivation, step one: drift velocity

board_events.text: Board derivation, step one: drift velocity from the field
Take a uniform conductor of cross-section $A$, holding free electrons of number density $n$, each of mass $m$ and charge $-e$.
With no field applied, the electron velocities are random and average to zero.
Apply a uniform field and each electron feels a force $-e\vec{E}$, giving it the acceleration shown.
An electron accelerates only until its next collision with the lattice, which randomises its motion completely.
So it can only build up drift over the average time $\tau$, never indefinitely. This is the whole reason $\tau$ appears in the answer.

segments.text: We now build the central board derivation of this subtopic, the one C B S E asks for almost every year. It comes in three linked steps, and this is step one.
Take a uniform conductor of cross-sectional area A, holding free electrons of number density n, each of mass m and charge minus e.
Before applying anything, note the starting condition: with no field, the electron velocities are random and average to exactly zero.
Now apply a uniform field. Newton's second law gives each electron an acceleration equal to minus e times the field, divided by the electron mass.
The minus sign is simply telling us the acceleration is opposite to the field, because the electron carries negative charge.

<curious>Here is the step that does the real work.</curious> An electron accelerates only until its next collision with the lattice, and that collision randomises its motion completely, wiping out whatever velocity the field had given it.
So the electron can only build up drift over the average time between collisions, never indefinitely. That is the whole reason the relaxation time tau appears in the answer at all.
Therefore the average extra velocity it carries, which is the drift velocity, is just the acceleration acting over that average time: minus e E tau over m.
Ab हम इस subtopic की केंद्रीय board derivation बनाते हैं, वही जो C B S E लगभग हर साल पूछता है। ये तीन जुड़े हुए steps में आती है, और ये पहला step है।
Ek uniform conductor लीजिए जिसका cross-sectional area A है, जिसमें free electrons की number density n है, हर एक का mass m और charge minus e।
Kuch भी लगाने से पहले शुरुआती हालत नोट कीजिए: field के बिना electron velocities random हैं और average बिलकुल zero है।
Ab एक uniform field लगाइए। Newton का दूसरा नियम हर electron को acceleration देता है, minus e into field, electron के mass से divide।
Minus sign बस ये बता रहा है कि acceleration field के उल्टा है, क्योंकि electron पर negative charge है।

Ye रहा वो step जो असली काम करता है। Electron सिर्फ़ अपनी अगली lattice collision तक accelerate होता है, और वो collision उसकी motion पूरी तरह random कर देती है, field ने जो velocity दी थी उसे मिटा देती है।
<curious>Isliye electron सिर्फ़ collisions के बीच के औसत time तक ही drift जमा कर सकता है</curious>, हमेशा के लिए नहीं। यही पूरी वजह है कि answer में relaxation time tau आता ही क्यों है।
Isliye वो जो औसत extra velocity लेकर चलता है, यानी drift velocity, बस acceleration into उस औसत time है: minus e E tau over m।

board_events.text: Board derivation, step two: current from drift velocity
Consider a slice of the conductor whose length is $v_d\,dt$, the distance an electron drifts in a small time $dt$.

board_events.text: Every free electron inside this slice crosses the right-hand face within the time $dt$.

board_events.latex: \text{slice volume} = A v_d\,dt \implies \text{electrons} = n A v_d\,dt

segments.text: Step two connects that drift velocity to the current we can actually measure, and the whole argument turns on one clean geometric idea.
Consider a thin slice of the conductor whose length is the drift velocity times a small time interval. That is precisely the distance an electron drifts in that interval.
Picture the slice sitting against the far face of the conductor, with the electrons inside it sweeping rightward across the cross-sectional area.
Now the key physical claim. Every free electron inside that slice will cross the right-hand face within the time interval, and no electron outside the slice can reach it in time.
The volume of the slice is area times drift velocity times the time interval, so the number of electrons inside it is the number density multiplied by that volume.
Each of those electrons carries charge e, so the total charge crossing the face in that interval is n A v d, d t, all multiplied by e.
Dividing by the time interval gives the current directly: current equals n e A times the drift velocity. That is the result the whole step was aiming at.
Dividing once more, this time by the area, gives the current density as n e times drift velocity, and restoring the direction gives the vector form.
Step do उस drift velocity को उस current से जोड़ता है जिसे हम असल में माप सकते हैं, और पूरी दलील एक साफ़ geometric idea पर टिकी है।
Conductor की एक पतली slice सोचिए जिसकी लंबाई drift velocity into एक छोटा time interval है। यही वो दूरी है जो electron उस interval में drift करता है।
Us slice को conductor के दूर वाले face से सटा हुआ सोचिए, जिसके अंदर के electrons cross-sectional area के आर पार दाईं तरफ़ बह रहे हैं।
<curious>Ab असली physical दावा।</curious> उस slice के अंदर का हर free electron उस time interval में दाएँ face को पार कर लेगा, और slice के बाहर का कोई electron उतने समय में वहाँ पहुँच ही नहीं सकता।
Slice का volume है area into drift velocity into time interval, इसलिए उसके अंदर electrons की संख्या number density into वो volume है।
Un में से हर electron charge e लेकर चलता है, इसलिए उस interval में face पार करने वाला कुल charge है n A v d, d t, पूरा e से multiply।
Time interval से divide करने पर current सीधा मिल जाता है: current equals n e A into drift velocity। पूरा step इसी नतीजे की तरफ़ जा रहा था।
Ek बार और divide कीजिए, इस बार area से, तो current density मिलती है n e into drift velocity, और direction लौटाने पर इसका vector रूप।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Board derivation, step three: Ohm's law emerges

board_events.text: Board derivation, step three: Ohm's law emerges
Substitute the drift velocity from step one into the current expression from step two.
In a uniform conductor of length $L$ carrying a potential difference $V$, the field is $E = V/L$.
Ohm's law holds only because $n$, $e$, $m$ and $\tau$ are constants of the material at a fixed temperature.
The instant $\tau$ changes, resistivity changes and the linear law fails. That is precisely why a tungsten filament is non-ohmic.

segments.text: Step three is where the payoff arrives. We have current in terms of drift velocity, and drift velocity in terms of the field, so we simply put them together.
Substitute the drift velocity from step one directly into the current expression from step two.
That gives current as n e squared tau over m, times area, times the field. Notice the drift velocity has vanished and only material constants remain.
Now bring in the geometry. In a uniform conductor of length L carrying a potential difference V across its ends, the field inside is simply V over L.
Substituting and rearranging isolates V on one side, giving voltage equals current multiplied by a bracket containing only material constants and the dimensions of the wire.
Compare that with V equals I R and you can read off the resistance directly. It is resistivity times length over area, with resistivity itself equal to m over n e squared tau.
<whisper>Now the physics this actually reveals.</whisper> Ohm's law holds only because n, e, m and tau are constants of the material at a fixed temperature, which makes resistivity a constant.

The instant tau changes, say because the wire heats up and collisions become more frequent, resistivity changes and the simple linear law fails. That is precisely why a tungsten bulb filament is non-ohmic and its graph curves.
Step teen में असली फ़ायदा मिलता है। हमारे पास drift velocity के रूप में current है, और field के रूप में drift velocity, तो बस दोनों को जोड़ देते हैं।
Step एक की drift velocity को सीधे step दो की current expression में रख दीजिए।
Isse current मिलता है n e squared tau over m, into area, into field। ध्यान दीजिए drift velocity ग़ायब हो गई और सिर्फ़ material के constants बचे।
Ab geometry ले आइए। L लंबाई के uniform conductor में जिसके सिरों पर V का potential difference है, अंदर का field बस V over L है।
Rakh कर rearrange करने पर V एक तरफ़ अलग हो जाता है, और मिलता है voltage equals current into एक bracket जिसमें सिर्फ़ material के constants और wire के dimensions हैं।
<excited>Ise V equals I R से मिलाइए</excited> और resistance सीधा पढ़ लीजिए। ये resistivity into length over area है, और resistivity ख़ुद m over n e squared tau के बराबर।
Ab वो physics जो ये असल में खोलता है। Ohm's law सिर्फ़ इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि n, e, m और tau एक fixed temperature पर material के constants हैं, जिससे resistivity constant बन जाती है।

Jिस पल tau बदला, मान लीजिए wire गरम हुई और collisions ज़्यादा हुए, resistivity बदल जाती है और साधारण linear law टूट जाता है। ठीक इसीलिए tungsten bulb का filament non-ohmic है और उसका graph मुड़ जाता है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Worked example: drift velocity in a copper wire

board_events.text: Worked example, C B S E board level: drift velocity in copper
A copper wire of cross-sectional area one point five square millimetres carries a steady current of three amperes.
Free-electron density of copper is $8.5 \times 10^{28}$ per cubic metre, and the electronic charge is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulomb.
Convert the area first: one point five square millimetres is $1.5 \times 10^{-6}$ square metres.
The electrons crawl forward at well under a millimetre per second, yet the wire carries a sizeable three amperes.

segments.text: The first worked example is at C B S E board level, and it makes the drift velocity idea quantitative.
A copper wire of cross-sectional area one point five square millimetres carries a steady current of three amperes, and we want the drift velocity of its electrons.

You are given the free-electron density of copper as eight point five times ten to the twenty eight per cubic metre, and the electronic charge as one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb.
The relation you need is current equals n e A times drift velocity, so simply rearrange it to make drift velocity the subject.

<whisper>Now the step where marks are lost.</whisper> Convert the area before substituting. One point five square millimetres is one point five times ten to the minus six square metres, and forgetting that factor of ten to the six is the single commonest slip here.
Substituting all four numbers, the denominator multiplies out to two point zero four times ten to the four.
Dividing gives a drift velocity of about one point four seven times ten to the minus four metres per second, which is roughly zero point one five millimetres per second.

Look at how small that is. The electrons crawl forward at well under a millimetre per second, and yet the wire is carrying a perfectly ordinary three amperes. This is the slow-carriers, fast-signal idea made numerical.
Pehla worked example C B S E board level का है, और ये drift velocity के idea को numbers में बदल देता है।
Ek copper wire जिसका cross-sectional area एक point पाँच square millimetre है, तीन ampere का steady current ले जा रही है, और हमें उसके electrons की drift velocity चाहिए।
Aapko दिया है copper की free-electron density आठ point पाँच into ten to the twenty eight per cubic metre, और electronic charge one point six into ten to the minus nineteen coulomb।
Jo relation चाहिए वो है current equals n e A into drift velocity, तो बस उसे rearrange कीजिए ताकि drift velocity subject बन जाए।

Ab वो step जहाँ marks कटते हैं। Substitute करने से पहले area convert कीजिए। एक point पाँच square millimetre है one point five into ten to the minus six square metre, और ten to the six का ये factor भूलना यहाँ की सबसे आम ग़लती है।
<curious>Chaaron numbers रखिए</curious>, तो denominator गुणा होकर two point zero four into ten to the four बन जाता है।
Divide करने पर drift velocity आती है लगभग one point four seven into ten to the minus four metre per second, यानी क़रीब zero point one five millimetre per second।
Dekhiye ये कितनी छोटी है। Electrons एक millimetre per second से भी काफ़ी कम रेंगते हैं, और फिर भी wire में बिलकुल आम तीन ampere बह रहे हैं। यही slow-carriers, fast-signal वाला idea numbers में है।

board_events.text: Worked example, N E E T speed trap: the stretched wire
A uniform wire of resistance $R$ is stretched until its length becomes one point five times the original.

board_events.text: The trap: seeing $R = \rho L/A$, scaling only the length, and answering $1.5R$.
Stretching conserves the volume of metal, so as the length grows the cross-section must shrink in proportion.

board_events.latex: V_0 = AL \implies A = \frac{V_0}{L}, \qquad R = \frac{\rho L}{V_0/L} = \frac{\rho L^2}{V_0}

board_events.text: Resistivity does not change at all: copper is still copper, whatever shape you pull it into.

segments.text: The second worked example is a classic N E E T speed trap, and it punishes exactly one careless assumption.
A uniform wire of resistance R is stretched until its length becomes one point five times the original. We want the new resistance, and whether the resistivity has changed.
Look carefully at what stretching does. The wire gets longer and thinner at the same time, because the amount of metal is fixed.
Here is the trap. Most students see resistance equals rho L over A, scale the length by one point five, and answer one point five R. They forget the area shrank too.
Since stretching conserves the volume of metal, as the length grows the cross-section must shrink in exact proportion.
So rewrite the resistance using area equals volume over length. The two lengths combine, and resistance comes out proportional to length squared at constant volume.
<excited>That gives the answer immediately.</excited> Square the length ratio: one point five squared is two point two five, so the new resistance is two point two five R.
And the second half of the question: resistivity does not change at all. Copper is still copper whatever shape you pull it into. Only resistance, which depends on geometry, has changed.
Doosra worked example एक classic N E E T speed trap है, और ये ठीक एक लापरवाह assumption की सज़ा देता है।
R resistance वाली एक uniform wire को तब तक खींचा जाता है जब तक उसकी length original की one point five गुना न हो जाए। हमें नई resistance चाहिए, और ये भी कि resistivity बदली या नहीं।
Dhyan से देखिए खींचने से होता क्या है। Wire एक साथ लंबी भी होती है और पतली भी, क्योंकि धातु की मात्रा तय है।

<chuckle>Ye रहा trap।</chuckle> ज़्यादातर students resistance equals rho L over A देखते हैं, length को one point five से बढ़ाते हैं, और one point five R लिख देते हैं। वो भूल जाते हैं कि area भी सिकुड़ा।
Kyunki खींचने पर धातु का volume स्थिर रहता है, इसलिए length बढ़ने के साथ cross-section ठीक उसी अनुपात में घटना ही चाहिए।
To resistance को दोबारा लिखिए, area equals volume over length रखकर। दोनों lengths मिल जाती हैं, और constant volume पर resistance length के square के अनुपात में निकलती है।
Isse answer तुरंत मिल जाता है। Length ratio का square लीजिए: one point five का square है two point two five, इसलिए नई resistance two point two five R है।
Aur सवाल का दूसरा हिस्सा: resistivity बिलकुल नहीं बदलती। Copper को आप किसी भी shape में खींच लें, वो copper ही रहता है। सिर्फ़ resistance बदली, जो geometry पर depend करती है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Worked example: relaxation time and mobility

board_events.text: Worked example, J E E Main level: relaxation time and mobility
For copper the resistivity is $1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ ohm metre and the free-electron density is $8.5 \times 10^{28}$ per cubic metre.
Use electron mass $9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kilogram and charge $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulomb.
Both answers pass the order-of-magnitude check for a metal at room temperature.

segments.text: The third worked example is at J E E Main level, and it links the microscopic form of Ohm's law with the definition of mobility.
For copper you are given the resistivity as one point seven times ten to the minus eight ohm metre, and the free-electron density as eight point five times ten to the twenty eight per cubic metre.
You also need the electron mass, nine point one times ten to the minus thirty one kilogram, and the electronic charge.
Start from the microscopic result: resistivity equals m over n e squared tau. Rearranging makes the relaxation time the subject.
Build the denominator in stages rather than all at once. First square the charge and multiply by the number density, giving two point one seven six times ten to the minus nine.

Multiply that by the resistivity to get three point seven times ten to the minus seventeen, and dividing the electron mass by it gives a relaxation time of about two point five times ten to the minus fourteen seconds.
Mobility then follows immediately from e tau over m, coming out at about four point three times ten to the minus three metres squared per volt second.

<curious>Always finish with the smell test.</curious> A relaxation time near ten to the minus fourteen seconds is exactly the textbook order of magnitude for a metal at room temperature, and a copper mobility of a few times ten to the minus three is what is actually measured.
Teesra worked example J E E Main level का है, और ये Ohm's law के microscopic रूप को mobility की definition से जोड़ता है।
Copper के लिए आपको दिया है resistivity one point seven into ten to the minus eight ohm metre, और free-electron density eight point five into ten to the twenty eight per cubic metre।
Aapko electron का mass भी चाहिए, nine point one into ten to the minus thirty one kilogram, और electronic charge।
Microscopic नतीजे से शुरू कीजिए: resistivity equals m over n e squared tau। Rearrange करने पर relaxation time subject बन जाता है।
<curious>Denominator को एक साथ नहीं, चरणों में बनाइए।</curious> पहले charge का square करके number density से गुणा कीजिए, तो मिलता है two point one seven six into ten to the minus nine।

Use resistivity से गुणा कीजिए तो three point seven into ten to the minus seventeen मिलता है, और electron के mass को इससे divide करने पर relaxation time लगभग two point five into ten to the minus fourteen second आता है।
Mobility फिर सीधे e tau over m से निकल आती है, लगभग four point three into ten to the minus three metre squared per volt second।

Hamesha smell test से ख़त्म कीजिए। Ten to the minus fourteen second के आसपास relaxation time room temperature पर metal के लिए बिलकुल textbook order of magnitude है, और copper की mobility कुछ into ten to the minus three ही मापी जाती है।

board_events.text: Part one: in the steady state no charge piles up anywhere, so the same current crosses every section.
Electrons drift fastest at the narrow end, exactly like river water speeding up through a gorge.

segments.text: The final worked example is at J E E Advanced level, and it violates exactly one of the assumptions we listed earlier: the conductor is no longer uniform.
A solid conductor is shaped like a truncated cone, its radius growing linearly from a to b over a length L, with a steady current entering the small face.
Draw it first, and mark a thin disc element of thickness d x at distance x from the narrow end, where the radius has grown to r of x.

Part one asks you to argue that the current is the same through every cross-section. In the steady state no charge piles up inside, so whatever enters per second must leave per second, and that holds for every slice.
For part two, the radius varies linearly with distance, so the area at any point is pi times that radius squared.
Since the current is fixed while the area varies, the drift velocity must vary inversely as the area, which means inversely as the radius squared.

<curious>So the electrons drift fastest at the narrow end</curious> and slowest at the wide end. Current density crowds where the conductor is thin, exactly like river water speeding up through a narrow gorge.

For part three, treat the cone as a stack of thin discs in series and integrate. Substituting the radius as the variable, the integral evaluates cleanly, and the bracket simplifies to give total resistance rho L over pi a b.
Aakhri worked example J E E Advanced level का है, और ये ठीक उन assumptions में से एक तोड़ता है जो हमने पहले गिनाई थीं: conductor अब uniform नहीं है।
Ek ठोस conductor truncated cone की shape का है। इसकी radius बाएँ face पर a से बढ़कर दाएँ face पर b हो जाती है, L लंबाई में, और steady current छोटे face से अंदर आता है।
Kuch भी करने से पहले इसे बनाइए, और संकरे सिरे से x दूरी पर d x मोटाई का एक पतला disc element mark कीजिए, जहाँ radius बढ़कर r of x हो चुकी है।

Pehla हिस्सा कहता है दलील दीजिए कि हर cross-section से current एक ही है। Steady state में अंदर कहीं charge जमा नहीं होता, इसलिए per second जितना अंदर आता है उतना ही बाहर जाना चाहिए, और ये बीच की हर slice पर लागू है।
Doosre हिस्से के लिए, radius दूरी के साथ linearly बदलती है, इसलिए किसी भी point पर area है pi into उस radius का square।
<curious>Current तय है जबकि area बदल रहा है</curious>, इसलिए drift velocity area के उल्टे अनुपात में बदलेगी, यानी radius के square के उल्टे अनुपात में।

To electrons संकरे सिरे पर सबसे तेज़ drift करते हैं और चौड़े सिरे पर सबसे धीमे। Current density वहाँ भीड़ बनाती है जहाँ conductor पतला है, ठीक वैसे जैसे नदी का पानी संकरी घाटी से गुज़रते हुए तेज़ हो जाता है।

Teesre हिस्से के लिए cone को series में रखे पतले discs का ढेर मानकर integrate कीजिए। Radius को variable बनाकर रखने पर integral साफ़ हल हो जाता है, और bracket simplify होकर कुल resistance rho L over pi a b दे देता है।

sections.subtopic: Electric Current, Ohm's Law & Drift Velocity
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for current and drift velocity

board_events.text: Pitfalls that cost marks, and the pro-tips that save time
Mixing up current and current density. Current is a scalar in amperes; current density is a vector in ampere per square metre.
If a quantity in a question has a stated direction in space and units of per area, it is $\vec{J}$ and not $I$.
Confusing the slow drift with the fast signal. Never quote $v_d$ when asked why a light turns on instantly.
Treating resistivity as size-dependent. Stretching, recasting or cutting a wire changes $R$, never $\rho$.
Forgetting the unit conversion in $J$. Ampere per square millimetre to ampere per square metre is a factor of ten to the six.

board_events.latex: \text{Stretch rule: } R \propto L^2 \text{ at constant volume}

board_events.text: Order-of-magnitude check before you commit: $v_d$ near ten to the minus four metres per second, $\tau$ near ten to the minus fourteen seconds.

segments.text: Let us close with the four mistakes that cost marks and the two shortcuts that save time.
The first mistake is mixing up current and current density. Current is a scalar measured in amperes; current density is a vector measured in amperes per square metre.
The test is simple. If a quantity has a direction in space and units of per area, it is current density and not current.

The second is confusing the slow drift with the fast signal. The near-instant glow of a bulb is the field propagating at nearly light speed, so never quote drift velocity when asked why a light turns on instantly.
The third is treating resistivity as size-dependent. Stretching, recasting or cutting a wire changes the resistance, never the resistivity.

The fourth is forgetting the unit conversion in current density. Amperes per square millimetre to amperes per square metre is a factor of ten to the six, the commonest arithmetic slip on these numericals.

<excited>Now the pro-tips.</excited> For any stretching or recasting problem at constant volume, skip the area bookkeeping and use resistance proportional to length squared. Halve the length for a quarter of the resistance; double it for four times.

And before committing to any drift velocity or relaxation time answer, do an order-of-magnitude check. Drift velocity near ten to the minus four metres per second, relaxation time near ten to the minus fourteen seconds. If your answer is wildly off those, you have slipped a power of ten.
Is subtopic को उन चार ग़लतियों के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो पक्के तौर पर marks काटती हैं, और उन दो shortcuts के साथ जो पक्के तौर पर time बचाते हैं।
Pehli ग़लती है current और current density को मिला देना। Current scalar है, ampere में; current density vector है, ampere per square metre में।
Exam में test आसान है। अगर किसी quantity की space में direction बताई हो और unit per area हो, तो वो current density है, current नहीं।

Doosri है धीमे drift को तेज़ signal से गड्डमड्ड करना। Drift speed carrier की motion समझाती है, लेकिन bulb का लगभग तुरंत जलना field के लगभग light speed से फैलने की वजह से है। ये पूछे जाने पर कभी drift velocity मत बोलिए।
Teesri है resistivity को size पर निर्भर मान लेना। Resistivity material का constant है। Wire को खींचना, दोबारा ढालना या काटना resistance बदलता है, resistivity कभी नहीं।
Chauthi है current density में unit conversion भूलना। Ampere per square millimetre से ampere per square metre में ten to the six का factor है, और इन numericals में यही सबसे आम arithmetic की चूक है।

Ab pro-tips। Constant volume पर खींचने या दोबारा ढालने वाली किसी भी problem में area का हिसाब छोड़िए और resistance proportional to length squared इस्तेमाल कीजिए। Length आधी कीजिए तो resistance चौथाई; दोगुनी कीजिए तो चार गुना।

<excited>Aur किसी भी drift velocity या relaxation time के answer पर टिकने से पहले order-of-magnitude check कीजिए।</excited> Drift velocity ten to the minus four metre per second के आसपास, relaxation time ten to the minus fourteen second के आसपास। इनसे बहुत दूर हो तो कहीं ten की power फिसली है।

sections.title: Why copper conducts and rubber blocks

board_events.text: Why copper conducts and rubber blocks
A copper wire carries current almost effortlessly, while the rubber wrapped around it blocks it completely. Both are made of atoms.
The difference is how many charge carriers are free to move, and how easily they move once freed.
Resistivity falls when there are many free electrons, a large $n$, and when they travel a long time between collisions, a large $\tau$.

Picture three roads at rush hour: a wide expressway packed with moving vehicles, a quiet town road that fills as the day warms, and a road walled off entirely.

segments.text: This subtopic asks a question the last one set up but never answered: why do different materials resist current so differently?
A copper wire carries current almost effortlessly, while the rubber sheath wrapped around it blocks the current completely. Both are made of atoms, so something else must be responsible.
The difference comes down to two things: how many charge carriers are free to move at all, and how easily those carriers move once they are free.
Recall the resistivity we derived from the free-electron model. It is the electron mass over the number density, the charge squared, and the relaxation time.

Read that formula as a recipe. Resistivity falls when there are many free electrons, meaning a large n, and it falls again when those electrons travel a long time between collisions, meaning a large tau.
<excited>Materials differ so wildly in both that the spread is astonishing.</excited> Look at the scale: resistivities span roughly twenty-four orders of magnitude.
Silver sits near ten to the minus eight ohm metre at one end. A good insulator sits above ten to the sixteen at the other. No other common physical property varies over anything like that range.

The picture to carry is three roads at rush hour. A metal is a wide open expressway packed with moving vehicles. A semiconductor is a quiet town road that fills up as the day warms. An insulator is a road walled off entirely.
Ye subtopic वो सवाल पूछता है जो पिछले ने खड़ा किया था लेकिन जवाब नहीं दिया: अलग अलग materials current को इतने अलग तरीक़े से क्यों रोकते हैं?
<curious>Copper wire current को लगभग बिना मेहनत ले जाती है</curious>, जबकि उसके ऊपर लिपटा rubber current को पूरी तरह रोक देता है। दोनों atoms से बने हैं, तो ज़िम्मेदार कुछ और है।
Farq दो चीज़ों पर आकर टिकता है: कितने charge carriers चलने के लिए आज़ाद हैं, और आज़ाद होने के बाद वो कितनी आसानी से चलते हैं।
Wo resistivity याद कीजिए जो हमने free-electron model से निकाली थी। ये electron का mass, number density, charge के square और relaxation time के हिसाब से बनती है।
Us formula को एक नुस्ख़े की तरह पढ़िए। Resistivity तब घटती है जब free electrons बहुत हों, यानी बड़ा n, और तब और घटती है जब वो electrons collisions के बीच लंबा time चलें, यानी बड़ा tau।
Materials इन दोनों में इतने अलग होते हैं कि फैलाव चौंका देता है। Scale देखिए: resistivity लगभग चौबीस orders of magnitude तक फैली हुई है।
Ek सिरे पर silver है, ten to the minus eight ohm metre के आसपास। दूसरे सिरे पर अच्छा insulator, ten to the sixteen से ऊपर। कोई और आम physical property इतनी range में नहीं बदलती।

Yaad रखने वाली तस्वीर है rush hour की तीन सड़कें। Metal एक चौड़ी खुली expressway है जो चलती गाड़ियों से भरी है। Semiconductor एक शांत town road है जो दिन गरम होते ही भरने लगती है। Insulator एक सड़क है जो पूरी तरह दीवारों से बंद है।

sections.title: Why metals and semiconductors respond oppositely

board_events.text: Metals and semiconductors respond oppositely to heat
Start again from $\rho = m/ne^2\tau$ and ask which factor temperature actually touches.
In a metal $n$ is fixed, because all the valence electrons are already free. Only $\tau$ can respond.
Heating makes the lattice ions vibrate harder, so collisions become more frequent, $\tau$ falls, and resistivity rises.
In a semiconductor, heating breaks covalent bonds and liberates carriers, so $n$ climbs exponentially.
Although $\tau$ falls there too, the exponential growth of $n$ overwhelms it, so resistivity falls with temperature.

segments.text: Here is the single most tested idea in this subtopic, and it is worth deriving rather than memorising, because the reasoning is only two steps long.
Start again from resistivity equals m over n e squared tau, and ask a precise question: which factor in that expression does temperature actually touch?
In a metal, n is essentially fixed. All the valence electrons are already free, and heating does not liberate meaningfully more of them. So only tau can respond.
And it does. Heating makes the lattice ions vibrate harder, so collisions become more frequent, the relaxation time falls, and with n fixed the resistivity must rise.
<curious>In a semiconductor the situation inverts.</curious> Heating breaks covalent bonds and liberates far more carriers, so the number density climbs exponentially.
The relaxation time falls in the semiconductor too, exactly as it does in the metal. But the exponential growth of n completely overwhelms that effect, so the resistivity falls as temperature rises.
Plot the two side by side. The metal rises roughly linearly and flattens near absolute zero to a small residual value. The semiconductor falls steeply, and the fall is exponential rather than linear.

Between these two sit the alloys. Manganin and constantan have resistivity that is moderately high and almost completely unaffected by temperature, which is exactly what you want in a standard resistance or a potentiometer wire.
Ye है इस subtopic का सबसे ज़्यादा पूछा जाने वाला idea, और इसे रटने की जगह derive करना बेहतर है, क्योंकि दलील सिर्फ़ दो क़दम लंबी है।
Phir से शुरू कीजिए resistivity equals m over n e squared tau से, और एक साफ़ सवाल पूछिए: उस expression में temperature असल में किस factor को छूता है?
Metal में n लगभग तय है। सारे valence electrons पहले से आज़ाद हैं, और गरम करने से उनमें कोई ख़ास इज़ाफ़ा नहीं होता। इसलिए सिर्फ़ tau ही जवाब दे सकता है।
Aur वो देता है। गरम करने पर lattice ions ज़्यादा ज़ोर से vibrate करते हैं, collisions बढ़ जाते हैं, relaxation time गिरता है, और n तय होने से resistivity को बढ़ना ही पड़ता है।
Semiconductor में हालत उलट जाती है। गरम करने से covalent bonds टूटते हैं और कहीं ज़्यादा carriers आज़ाद हो जाते हैं, इसलिए number density exponentially चढ़ती है।
<curious>Semiconductor में relaxation time भी गिरता है</curious>, बिलकुल metal की तरह। लेकिन n की exponential बढ़त उस असर पर पूरी तरह भारी पड़ती है, इसलिए temperature बढ़ने पर resistivity गिरती है।
Dono को साथ साथ plot कीजिए। Metal लगभग linearly चढ़ता है और absolute zero के पास एक छोटी residual value पर सपाट हो जाता है। Semiconductor तेज़ी से गिरता है, और वो गिरावट linear नहीं exponential है।
In दोनों के बीच alloys बैठते हैं। Manganin और constantan की resistivity ठीक ठाक ऊँची है और temperature से लगभग बिलकुल अछूती, और यही चीज़ एक standard resistance या potentiometer wire में चाहिए।

sections.title: Superconductivity, thermistors and the limits of the law

board_events.text: Where the linear law runs out
The linear law is only a first-order approximation, valid over moderate temperature ranges.
Over large ranges the curves bend. Metals flatten near absolute zero to a small residual value rather than reaching exactly zero.
Some metals do something the linear law cannot describe at all: below a critical temperature their resistivity drops abruptly to exactly zero.
This is superconductivity. Below $T_c$ electrons pair up and move through the lattice without scattering, so current flows with no energy loss.
The classification into conductor, semiconductor and insulator is itself temperature-dependent, so a poor conductor when cold can behave very differently when hot.
The practical payoff of all this is the thermistor, usually a semiconductor oxide engineered to have a large temperature coefficient.
A negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor drops steeply in resistance as it warms, turning a resistor into a sensitive thermometer.

segments.text: Before the formulas, it is worth marking clearly where the neat linear temperature law stops working, because two of those places are themselves exam topics.
State the limitation plainly. The linear law is only a first-order approximation, and it is valid over moderate temperature ranges rather than universally.
Over large ranges the curves visibly bend. Metals flatten out near absolute zero to a small residual value, rather than continuing down to exactly zero as a straight line would predict.
And some metals do something the linear law cannot describe at all. Below a certain critical temperature their resistivity drops abruptly, discontinuously, to exactly zero.

<curious>That is superconductivity.</curious> Below the critical temperature the electrons pair up and move through the lattice without scattering at all, so the relaxation time effectively becomes infinite and current flows with no energy loss whatsoever.

There is a subtler limitation too. The classification into conductor, semiconductor and insulator is itself temperature-dependent, so a material that is a poor conductor when cold can behave very differently once it is hot.
Now the practical payoff of the whole temperature story: the thermistor. It is usually a semiconductor oxide, deliberately engineered to have a large temperature coefficient of resistance.

A negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor drops steeply in resistance as it warms, which is just semiconductor behaviour put to work. A small temperature change gives a big, easily measured resistance change, turning a resistor into a sensitive thermometer.
Formulas से पहले ये साफ़ करना ज़रूरी है कि वो सुथरा linear temperature law कहाँ काम करना बंद कर देता है, क्योंकि उनमें से दो जगहें ख़ुद exam के topics हैं।
Limitation साफ़ कह दीजिए। Linear law सिर्फ़ एक first-order approximation है, और ये मामूली temperature ranges में चलता है, हर जगह नहीं।
Badi ranges पर curves साफ़ मुड़ जाते हैं। Metals absolute zero के पास एक छोटी residual value पर सपाट हो जाते हैं, बजाय इसके कि सीधी line की तरह बिलकुल zero तक उतरें।
Aur कुछ metals वो करते हैं जिसे linear law बता ही नहीं सकता। एक ख़ास critical temperature के नीचे उनकी resistivity अचानक, बिना निरंतरता के, बिलकुल zero हो जाती है।

Wahi superconductivity है। Critical temperature के नीचे electrons जोड़ी बना लेते हैं और lattice से बिना scatter हुए गुज़रते हैं, इसलिए relaxation time व्यावहारिक रूप से अनंत हो जाता है और current बिना किसी energy loss के बहता है।

<curious>Ek और सूक्ष्म limitation भी है।</curious> Conductor, semiconductor और insulator का बँटवारा ख़ुद temperature पर निर्भर है, इसलिए जो material ठंडा होने पर कमज़ोर conductor है वो गरम होने पर बहुत अलग बर्ताव कर सकता है।
Ab पूरी temperature की कहानी का व्यावहारिक फल: thermistor। ये आम तौर पर एक semiconductor oxide होता है, जिसे जान बूझकर बड़े temperature coefficient के साथ बनाया जाता है।

Negative-temperature-coefficient वाले thermistor की resistance गरम होते ही तेज़ी से गिरती है, जो बस semiconductor का बर्ताव काम पर लगाया गया है। छोटा सा temperature बदलाव बड़ा, आसानी से मापा जाने वाला resistance बदलाव देता है, और resistor एक संवेदनशील thermometer बन जाता है।

sections.title: The temperature law and the coefficient alpha

board_events.text: The temperature law and the coefficient alpha
$\rho_0$ and $R_0$ are the values at the reference temperature $T_0$. The one inside the bracket keeps the original value.
Alpha is the fractional change in resistance per degree of temperature rise. Its unit is per kelvin, dimension $K^{-1}$.
For metals alpha is positive, typically around four times ten to the minus three per kelvin.
For semiconductors and insulators alpha is negative. For alloys such as manganin, constantan and nichrome it is very nearly zero.

segments.text: Now the formulas. There are only two, but the sign conventions and the units around them carry most of the marks.
Both resistivity and resistance follow the same linear law: the value at a reference temperature, multiplied by one plus alpha times the temperature change.

Rho nought and R nought are the values at the reference temperature T nought. <whisper>That one inside the bracket is what keeps the original value in the answer, and dropping it is the commonest error on these numericals.</whisper>
Rearranging the law makes alpha the subject, giving it directly in terms of two resistance readings and the temperature difference between them.

In words, alpha is the fractional change in resistance per degree of temperature rise. Its S I unit is per kelvin, and since a change in degrees celsius equals a change in kelvin, per degree celsius works identically.
For metals alpha is positive, typically around four times ten to the minus three per kelvin. Heating a metal raises its resistance, exactly as the collision picture predicted.

For semiconductors and insulators alpha is negative, because heating liberates carriers. And for alloys such as manganin, constantan and nichrome it is very nearly zero, which is what makes them standards.

One last form worth memorising. Divide through by R nought and you get the ratio of new resistance to old as simply one plus alpha delta T. Working with that ratio keeps most temperature problems to a single line.
Ab formulas। सिर्फ़ दो हैं, लेकिन उनके आसपास के sign conventions और units ही ज़्यादातर marks ले जाते हैं।
Resistivity और resistance दोनों एक ही linear law मानते हैं: reference temperature की value, into one plus alpha into temperature change।
Rho nought और R nought reference temperature T nought पर की values हैं। Bracket के अंदर वो एक ही चीज़ answer में original value बचाकर रखती है, और उसे छोड़ देना इन numericals की सबसे आम ग़लती है।
Law को rearrange करने पर alpha subject बन जाता है, और सीधे दो resistance readings तथा उनके बीच के temperature फ़र्क़ के रूप में मिल जाता है।

<curious>Shabdon में, alpha है per degree temperature बढ़ने पर resistance का fractional change।</curious> इसका S I unit per kelvin है, और चूँकि degree celsius का बदलाव kelvin के बदलाव के बराबर होता है, per degree celsius भी वैसा ही चलता है।
Metals के लिए alpha positive है, आम तौर पर लगभग four into ten to the minus three per kelvin। Metal को गरम कीजिए तो resistance बढ़ती है, ठीक जैसा collision वाली तस्वीर ने बताया था।
Semiconductors और insulators के लिए alpha negative है, क्योंकि गरमी carriers आज़ाद करती है। और manganin, constantan तथा nichrome जैसे alloys के लिए ये लगभग zero है, और यही उन्हें standard बनाता है।

Ek आख़िरी रूप याद रखने लायक़। R nought से divide कीजिए और नई resistance का पुरानी से ratio बस one plus alpha delta T मिल जाता है। उसी ratio से काम करने पर ज़्यादातर temperature problems एक line में निपट जाती हैं।

board_events.text: Resistivity ranges and the resistor colour code
Conductors sit between ten to the minus eight and ten to the minus six ohm metre.
Semiconductors span ten to the minus five up to about one hundred, and are strongly temperature dependent. Insulators run from ten to the eight up to ten to the sixteen.

Gold is plus or minus five percent, silver plus or minus ten percent, and no fourth band at all means plus or minus twenty percent.
Orient the resistor with the tolerance band on the right before reading, then take the digits left to right. The mnemonic runs B B ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife.

segments.text: The second formula block gives you the numbers to recognise a material by, and then the code used to label real components.
Conductors, meaning the metals, sit between ten to the minus eight and ten to the minus six ohm metre.

Semiconductors span ten to the minus five up to about one hundred, and are strongly temperature dependent, so quoting a single figure for one is always approximate. Insulators run from ten to the eight up to ten to the sixteen.
Now the colour code. Carbon film resistors are far too small to print a number on, so their value is carried as four coloured rings.
The first two bands form a two-digit number, the third band multiplies it by a power of ten, and the result is quoted with a tolerance.
Reading them in order: band one is the first digit, band two the second digit, band three the power of ten, and band four the tolerance.
For the tolerance band, gold means plus or minus five percent, silver means plus or minus ten percent, and no fourth band at all means plus or minus twenty percent.

<excited>Two habits make this reliable.</excited> Always orient the resistor with the tolerance band on the right before reading, then take the digits left to right. And for the digit colours, use the old mnemonic: B B ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife.
Doosra formula हिस्सा आपको वो numbers देता है जिनसे material पहचाना जाता है, और फिर वो code जिससे असली components पर label लगता है।
Conductors, यानी metals, ten to the minus eight और ten to the minus six ohm metre के बीच बैठते हैं।

Semiconductors ten to the minus five से लेकर लगभग सौ तक फैले हैं, और temperature पर बहुत निर्भर हैं, इसलिए किसी एक के लिए एक ही figure बताना हमेशा अनुमान ही होगा। Insulators ten to the eight से ten to the sixteen तक चलते हैं।
Ab colour code। Carbon film resistors इतने छोटे होते हैं कि उन पर number छापा ही नहीं जा सकता, इसलिए उनकी value चार रंगीन छल्लों में रखी जाती है।
Pehli दो bands एक दो अंकों का number बनाती हैं, तीसरी band उसे ten की power से गुणा करती है, और नतीजा एक tolerance के साथ बताया जाता है।
<curious>Inhe क्रम से पढ़िए</curious>: band एक पहला digit, band दो दूसरा digit, band तीन ten की power, और band चार tolerance।
Tolerance band में gold का मतलब plus minus पाँच percent, silver का plus minus दस percent, और चौथी band बिलकुल न हो तो plus minus बीस percent।

Do आदतें इसे भरोसेमंद बना देती हैं। पढ़ने से पहले हमेशा resistor को ऐसे रखिए कि tolerance band दाईं तरफ़ हो, फिर बाएँ से दाएँ digits लीजिए। और digit के रंगों के लिए पुराना mnemonic इस्तेमाल कीजिए: B B ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife।

board_events.text: Worked example, C B S E board level: reading the colour code
A carbon resistor has four bands in order: brown, black, red, gold. Find its resistance and tolerance.
