board_events.text: Brown is one, black is zero, red as a multiplier means ten squared, and gold means plus or minus five percent.
So the true value of this particular component lies somewhere between nine hundred fifty ohms and one thousand fifty ohms.
Read the bands with the tolerance band on the right, or the digits and the multiplier swap and the answer inverts.

segments.text: The first worked example for this subtopic is at C B S E board level, and it is pure code reading.
A carbon resistor carries four bands, in order: brown, black, red, and gold. We want its resistance and its tolerance.
Orient it first. Put the tolerance band, the gold one, on the right, and then read the remaining three from the left.
Now decode. Brown is one, so that is the first digit. Black is zero, the second digit. Red in the multiplier position means ten squared. And gold means plus or minus five percent.
Assembling those: the first two bands give the two-digit number ten, and multiplying by ten squared gives one thousand ohms, which is one kilo-ohm.
So the stated value is one kilo-ohm with a tolerance of plus or minus five percent.

Read the tolerance properly, because it is part of the answer. Five percent of one thousand is fifty, so the true value of this particular component lies somewhere between nine hundred fifty and one thousand fifty ohms.

<whisper>And the warning that goes with every colour code question.</whisper> Read the bands with the tolerance band on the right. Read from the wrong end and the digits swap with the multiplier, and your answer inverts completely.
Is subtopic का पहला worked example C B S E board level का है, और ये सिर्फ़ code पढ़ना है।
Ek carbon resistor पर चार bands हैं, क्रम में: brown, black, red और gold। हमें उसकी resistance और tolerance चाहिए।
Pehle उसे सही रखिए। Tolerance band, यानी gold वाली, दाईं तरफ़ कीजिए, और फिर बाक़ी तीन को बाएँ से पढ़िए।
Ab decode कीजिए। Brown है एक, यानी पहला digit। Black है zero, दूसरा digit। Multiplier की जगह red का मतलब ten squared। और gold का मतलब plus minus पाँच percent।
Inhe जोड़िए: पहली दो bands से दो अंकों का number दस बनता है, और ten squared से गुणा करने पर एक हज़ार ohm मिलता है, यानी एक kilo-ohm।
<curious>To बताई गई value है एक kilo-ohm, plus minus पाँच percent tolerance के साथ।</curious>
Tolerance को ठीक से पढ़िए, क्योंकि वो answer का हिस्सा है। एक हज़ार का पाँच percent है पचास, इसलिए इस ख़ास component की असली value नौ सौ पचास और एक हज़ार पचास ohm के बीच कहीं है।
Aur वो चेतावनी जो हर colour code वाले सवाल के साथ आती है। Bands को tolerance band दाईं तरफ़ रखकर पढ़िए। ग़लत सिरे से पढ़ा तो digits multiplier से बदल जाते हैं, और आपका answer पूरी तरह उलट जाता है।

sections.title: Worked example: resistance of a heated wire

board_events.text: Worked example, N E E T speed trap: a heated metal wire
A metallic wire has resistance one hundred ohm at zero degrees celsius. Its temperature coefficient is $4.0\times10^{-3}$ per degree celsius.
Find its resistance at fifty degrees celsius.
The trap: computing $R_0\,\alpha\,\Delta T$ and reporting twenty ohm, which is only the increase.
Direction check: a metal that is heated must end up above its original resistance. Anything below one hundred ohm here is a slip.

segments.text: The second worked example is a N E E T speed trap, and it punishes one specific act of carelessness.
A metallic wire has resistance one hundred ohm at zero degrees celsius, and its temperature coefficient is four point zero times ten to the minus three per degree celsius.
You are asked for its resistance at fifty degrees celsius, so the temperature change is fifty degrees.
<chuckle>Here is the trap.</chuckle> Students multiply one hundred by alpha by fifty, get twenty, and write twenty ohm. But twenty ohm is only the increase, not the new resistance.
The formula tells you why. It is R nought multiplied by the whole bracket, one plus alpha delta T. That one inside the bracket is exactly what carries the original resistance through.
Substituting: alpha times fifty is zero point two zero, so the bracket becomes one plus zero point two zero.
One hundred multiplied by one point two zero gives one hundred twenty ohm, and that is the answer.

Finish with a direction check, which takes two seconds and catches this whole family of errors. A metal that is heated must end up above its original resistance. If you ever get a value below one hundred ohm here, you have slipped somewhere.
Doosra worked example एक N E E T speed trap है, और ये लापरवाही की एक ख़ास हरकत की सज़ा देता है।
Ek metallic wire की resistance zero degree celsius पर सौ ohm है, और इसका temperature coefficient four point zero into ten to the minus three per degree celsius है।
Aapse पचास degree celsius पर resistance पूछी गई है, इसलिए temperature का बदलाव पचास degree है।
Ye रहा trap। Students सौ को alpha से और पचास से गुणा करते हैं, बीस पाते हैं, और बीस ohm लिख देते हैं। लेकिन बीस ohm सिर्फ़ बढ़ोतरी है, नई resistance नहीं।
<curious>Formula ख़ुद वजह बताता है।</curious> ये R nought into पूरा bracket है, one plus alpha delta T। Bracket के अंदर वो एक ही चीज़ original resistance को आगे ले जाती है।
Rakh कर देखिए: alpha into पचास है zero point two zero, इसलिए bracket बनता है one plus zero point two zero।
Sau into one point two zero देता है एक सौ बीस ohm, और यही answer है।

Direction check से ख़त्म कीजिए, जिसमें दो second लगते हैं और जो इस पूरे परिवार की ग़लतियाँ पकड़ लेता है। गरम किया गया metal अपनी original resistance से ऊपर ही जाना चाहिए। यहाँ कभी सौ ohm से नीचे value आए तो कहीं चूक हुई है।

sections.title: Worked example: finding alpha from two readings

board_events.text: Worked example, J E E Main level: finding alpha from two readings
A coil of wire has resistance fifty ohm at twenty degrees celsius and sixty ohm at one hundred twenty degrees celsius.
Find its temperature coefficient of resistance, referred to twenty degrees celsius.
Take $R_0 = 50$ ohm at $T_0 = 20$ degrees celsius, so the temperature change is one hundred degrees.
A positive value of order ten to the minus three is exactly what a metal should give, which is a good consistency check.

segments.text: The third worked example is at J E E Main level and runs the temperature law backwards: you are given two resistances and asked for alpha.
A coil of wire has resistance fifty ohm at twenty degrees celsius, and sixty ohm at one hundred twenty degrees celsius.
You are asked for its temperature coefficient of resistance, referred to twenty degrees celsius. That phrase matters, because it fixes which reading is the reference.
Write down the law in its standard form, with the reference values on the right.
Since the coefficient is referred to twenty degrees, take R nought as fifty ohm at T nought equal to twenty, which makes the temperature change one hundred degrees.
Substituting gives sixty equals fifty times the bracket. Divide both sides by fifty rather than expanding, and the bracket is isolated in one step.
Sixty over fifty is one point two, so one point two minus one is one hundred alpha, giving alpha equal to two point zero times ten to the minus three per degree celsius.

<curious>Now check the answer for plausibility.</curious> It came out positive, and of order ten to the minus three, which is exactly what a metal should give. A negative answer here would have told you something was wrong.
Teesra worked example J E E Main level का है और temperature law को उल्टा चलाता है: आपको दो resistances दी हैं और alpha पूछा गया है।
Ek coil की resistance बीस degree celsius पर पचास ohm है, और एक सौ बीस degree celsius पर साठ ohm।
Aapse बीस degree celsius के हिसाब से temperature coefficient पूछा गया है। ये वाक्यांश मायने रखता है, क्योंकि यही तय करता है कि कौन सी reading reference है।
Law को उसके standard रूप में लिखिए, reference values दाईं तरफ़ रखकर।
<curious>Kyunki coefficient बीस degree के हिसाब से है</curious>, R nought को पचास ohm लीजिए T nought बीस पर, जिससे temperature का बदलाव सौ degree बनता है।
Rakhne पर मिलता है साठ equals पचास into bracket। Expand करने की जगह दोनों तरफ़ पचास से divide कीजिए, तो bracket एक ही क़दम में अलग हो जाता है।
Saath over पचास है one point two, इसलिए one point two minus one बराबर सौ alpha, जिससे alpha निकलता है two point zero into ten to the minus three per degree celsius।
Ab answer की समझदारी जाँचिए। ये positive आया है, और ten to the minus three के order का, जो metal के लिए बिलकुल ठीक है। यहाँ negative answer आपको बता देता कि कुछ ग़लत है।

sections.title: Worked example: a temperature-proof resistor pair

board_events.text: Worked example, J E E Advanced: a temperature-proof pair
A metal resistor with $\alpha_1 = +4.0\times10^{-3}$ per kelvin is joined in series with a carbon resistor of $\alpha_2 = -5.0\times10^{-4}$.
Find the ratio $R_1 : R_2$ for which the combined resistance is independent of temperature.
For the total to be temperature-independent, the rise in the metal must exactly cancel the fall in the carbon.
So a metal paired with carbon in the ratio one to eight gives a resistance that barely drifts with temperature.
This is the principle behind temperature-compensated precision resistors, alongside using alloys with near-zero alpha.

segments.text: The last worked example is at J E E Advanced level, and it uses the sign of alpha as an engineering tool rather than just a fact to memorise.

A metal resistor with alpha one equal to plus four point zero times ten to the minus three per kelvin is joined in series with a carbon resistor whose alpha two is minus five point zero times ten to the minus four.
You are asked for the ratio of the two resistances that makes the combined resistance independent of temperature.
Think about what that requires physically. In series the total is just the sum, so for it to be temperature-independent, the rise in the metal on heating must exactly cancel the fall in the carbon.

To first order each resistance changes by its own value times its own alpha times the temperature change, so setting the total change to zero gives the sum of the two alpha-resistance products equal to zero.
Rearranging gives the ratio directly. The two minus signs cancel, and dividing five times ten to the minus four by four times ten to the minus three gives one eighth.
So a metal paired with carbon in the ratio one to eight gives a combined resistance that barely drifts with temperature at all.

<excited>And that is not a contrived exercise.</excited> It is exactly the principle behind temperature-compensated precision resistors, used alongside the other approach of simply choosing an alloy whose alpha is already near zero.
Aakhri worked example J E E Advanced level का है, और ये alpha के sign को सिर्फ़ रटने की बात न मानकर एक engineering के औज़ार की तरह इस्तेमाल करता है।

Ek metal resistor जिसका alpha एक plus four point zero into ten to the minus three per kelvin है, series में एक carbon resistor से जुड़ा है जिसका alpha दो minus five point zero into ten to the minus four है।
Aapse उन दो resistances का ratio पूछा गया है जिससे मिली हुई resistance temperature से स्वतंत्र हो जाए।
Sochiye इसके लिए physically क्या चाहिए। Series में total बस जोड़ है, इसलिए उसे temperature से स्वतंत्र होने के लिए metal की बढ़त को carbon की गिरावट ठीक ठीक काटनी होगी।

<curious>First order में हर resistance अपनी value into अपना alpha into temperature बदलाव जितनी बदलती है</curious>, इसलिए कुल बदलाव को zero रखने पर दोनों alpha-resistance products का जोड़ zero हो जाता है।
Rearrange करने पर ratio सीधा मिल जाता है। दोनों minus signs कट जाते हैं, और five into ten to the minus four को four into ten to the minus three से divide करने पर एक बटा आठ आता है।
To metal को carbon के साथ एक is to आठ के अनुपात में जोड़िए, और मिली हुई resistance temperature के साथ लगभग बिलकुल नहीं खिसकती।

Aur ये कोई बनावटी exercise नहीं है। यही temperature-compensated precision resistors के पीछे का सिद्धांत है, उस दूसरे तरीक़े के साथ जिसमें बस ऐसा alloy चुन लिया जाता है जिसका alpha पहले से zero के पास हो।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for resistivity and temperature

board_events.text: Pitfalls that cost marks, and the pro-tips that save time
Dropping the one in the temperature formula. $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$ and that one keeps the original resistance.
Assigning the wrong sign of alpha. Metals positive, semiconductors and insulators negative. Mixing these flips the whole answer.
Reading the colour code from the wrong end. Put the tolerance band on the right first, or digits and multiplier swap.
Confusing resistivity with resistance. Heating changes both through alpha, but only resistance also depends on length and area.
Work with that ratio and most temperature problems collapse to one line, with no need to track absolute values until the end.
For colour codes, remember only the B B ROY mnemonic and that the third band is simply how many zeros to append.

segments.text: Let us close Subtopic two with the four mistakes that reliably cost marks, and the two shortcuts that save time under exam pressure.

The first is dropping the one in the temperature formula. Resistance at temperature T equals R nought times the bracket one plus alpha delta T, and that one is what keeps the original resistance in the answer.
Forget it and you report only the change, which is exactly the trap in the heated wire example.

The second is assigning the wrong sign of alpha. Metals are positive, semiconductors and insulators are negative. Mixing these up does not give a slightly wrong answer, it flips the direction of the whole result.
The third is reading the colour code from the wrong end. Always place the tolerance band on the right first, or the digits and the multiplier swap places silently.

The fourth is confusing resistivity with resistance. Heating changes both through alpha, but resistivity is the intrinsic material property, while resistance also depends on the length and the cross-section.

<excited>Now the pro-tips.</excited> For temperature problems, work with the ratio of new resistance to old, which is just one plus alpha delta T. Most problems then collapse to a single line, with no need to track absolute values until the very end.
And for colour codes, you only need to remember two things: the B B ROY mnemonic for the digit colours, and that the third band is simply how many zeros to append to the two-digit number.
Subtopic दो को उन चार ग़लतियों के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो पक्के तौर पर marks काटती हैं, और उन दो shortcuts के साथ जो exam के दबाव में time बचाते हैं।
Pehli है temperature formula में वो एक छोड़ देना। T पर resistance बराबर है R nought into bracket one plus alpha delta T, और वो एक ही answer में original resistance बचाकर रखता है।
Use भूलिए और आप सिर्फ़ बदलाव लिख देंगे, जो ठीक वही trap है जो अभी heated wire वाले example में था।
Doosri है alpha का ग़लत sign लगाना। Metals positive हैं, semiconductors और insulators negative। इन्हें मिला देने से answer थोड़ा ग़लत नहीं होता, पूरे नतीजे की दिशा ही पलट जाती है।

Teesri है colour code को ग़लत सिरे से पढ़ना। Tolerance band को, जो gold या silver होती है और अक्सर थोड़ा हटकर लगी होती है, हमेशा पहले दाईं तरफ़ रखिए। वरना digits और multiplier चुपचाप जगह बदल लेते हैं।

<curious>Chauthi है resistivity और resistance को मिला देना।</curious> गरमी दोनों को alpha के ज़रिए बदलती है, लेकिन resistivity material की अंदरूनी property है, जबकि resistance length और cross-section पर भी निर्भर है।

Ab pro-tips। Temperature की problems में नई resistance का पुरानी से ratio इस्तेमाल कीजिए, जो बस one plus alpha delta T है। ज़्यादातर problems फिर एक line में सिमट जाती हैं, और आख़िर तक absolute values track करने की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती।
Aur colour codes के लिए सिर्फ़ दो चीज़ें याद रखनी हैं: digit के रंगों के लिए B B ROY वाला mnemonic, और ये कि तीसरी band बस बताती है कि दो अंकों वाले number के पीछे कितने zero लगाने हैं।

sections.title: The two patterns every network is built from

board_events.text: The two patterns every network is built from
Real circuits are rarely a single resistor. They are tangles of many, and almost every tangle is these two patterns nested inside each other.
Series is resistors lined up one after another, like toll booths on an expressway. Every car must pass through every booth in turn.
So the same current flows through each resistor, and the total delay is the sum of the individual delays.

board_events.text: Parallel is resistors side by side between the same two points, like several queues at a ticket counter.
Now each path sees the same voltage across its ends, but the current divides, with more of it taking the lower-resistance path.
Series adds, parallel eases. That single intuition tells you the direction of every answer before you compute anything.

segments.text: The whole art of circuit analysis begins here, with just two ways resistors can sit together.
Real circuits are rarely a single resistor. They are tangles of many, and almost every tangle turns out to be these two patterns nested inside each other.
Series means resistors lined up one after another, like toll booths on a highway. Every car, meaning the current, must pass through every booth in turn.
That has a direct consequence. The same current flows through each resistor, and the total delay is the sum of the individual delays, so more booths in a row means more total resistance.
Hold both pictures side by side. Series is layers of cloth over a torch, each dimming it further. Parallel is opening more doors out of a crowded hall, each making it easier for people to leave.
Parallel means resistors sitting side by side between the same two points, like several queues at a railway ticket counter.

<curious>Now the crowd splits.</curious> Each path sees the same voltage across its ends, because both ends touch the same two nodes, but the current divides, with more of it taking the easier lower-resistance path.
So the summary to carry into every problem is this: series adds, parallel eases. That single intuition tells you the direction of every answer before you compute a single number.
Circuit analysis की पूरी कला यहीं से शुरू होती है, सिर्फ़ दो तरीक़ों से जिनसे resistors साथ बैठ सकते हैं।
Asli circuits में अकेला resistor कम ही होता है। वो कई का जाल होते हैं, और लगभग हर जाल इन्हीं दो patterns का एक दूसरे के अंदर रखा हुआ रूप निकलता है।
Series का मतलब है resistors एक के बाद एक line में, जैसे highway पर toll booths। हर गाड़ी, यानी current, को हर booth से बारी बारी गुज़रना पड़ता है।
<curious>Iska सीधा नतीजा है।</curious> हर resistor से एक ही current बहता है, और कुल देरी अलग अलग देरियों का जोड़ है, इसलिए line में जितने ज़्यादा booths, उतनी ज़्यादा कुल resistance।
Dono तस्वीरें साथ रखिए। Series torch पर कपड़े की परतें हैं, हर परत उसे और मद्धम करती है। Parallel भरे हुए hall से और दरवाज़े खोलना है, हर दरवाज़ा लोगों का निकलना आसान करता है।
Parallel का मतलब है resistors एक ही दो points के बीच साथ साथ, जैसे railway ticket counter पर कई queues।

Ab भीड़ बँट जाती है। हर रास्ते के सिरों पर एक ही voltage होता है, क्योंकि दोनों सिरे उन्हीं दो nodes को छूते हैं, लेकिन current बँट जाता है, और ज़्यादा हिस्सा आसान यानी कम resistance वाले रास्ते से जाता है।
To हर problem में साथ ले जाने वाला सार यही है: series जोड़ता है, parallel आसान बनाता है। यही एक intuition आपको एक भी number निकालने से पहले हर answer की दिशा बता देती है।

sections.title: Why parallel is always less than the least

board_events.text: Why parallel is always less than the least
Adding another parallel path gives the current more room to flow, so the total resistance drops.
A parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor in it. Not the average, but below the minimum.
For $n$ identical resistors of value $R$, series gives $nR$ and parallel gives $R/n$.
So the ratio of the largest to the smallest obtainable equivalent is exactly $n$ squared, which is a free check on any such answer.
Predict before computing: any series result must exceed the largest resistor, and any parallel result must fall below the smallest.
If your arithmetic ever violates either, stop and find the error rather than writing the number down.

segments.text: One consequence of the parallel rule is worth isolating, because it catches more arithmetic errors than any other single check in this chapter.
Adding another parallel path gives the current more room to flow. The total resistance therefore drops, and it drops every time you add a branch.
State the result sharply. A parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor in it. Not somewhere near the average, but strictly below the minimum.
There is a clean special case worth memorising. For n identical resistors each of value R, the series combination gives n R and the parallel combination gives R over n.
Dividing one by the other, the R cancels and the two factors of n multiply, so the ratio is exactly n squared.

<excited>That is a free check.</excited> Whenever a question asks for the maximum and minimum equivalent resistance from n identical resistors, the extremes must be in the ratio n squared, and if they are not you have made a mistake somewhere.
More generally, get into the habit of predicting before computing. Any series result must exceed the largest resistor in the group, and any parallel result must fall below the smallest.
If your arithmetic ever violates either of those, stop and find the error rather than writing the number down. It costs ten seconds and saves whole questions.
Parallel के नियम का एक नतीजा अलग से बताने लायक़ है, क्योंकि ये इस chapter के किसी भी दूसरे check से ज़्यादा arithmetic की ग़लतियाँ पकड़ता है।
Ek और parallel रास्ता जोड़ने से current को बहने की और जगह मिल जाती है। इसलिए कुल resistance गिरती है, और हर बार branch जोड़ने पर गिरती है।
Natija तीखे शब्दों में कहिए। Parallel combination हमेशा उसमें मौजूद सबसे छोटे resistor से भी छोटी होती है। Average के आसपास नहीं, बल्कि minimum से भी नीचे।
<curious>Ek साफ़ special case याद रखने लायक़ है।</curious> R value वाले n barabar resistors के लिए series देता है n R, और parallel देता है R over n।
Ek को दूसरे से divide कीजिए, R कट जाता है और n के दोनों factors गुणा हो जाते हैं, इसलिए ratio बिलकुल n squared निकलता है।
Ye एक मुफ़्त check है। जब भी सवाल n barabar resistors से maximum और minimum equivalent resistance पूछे, दोनों सिरे n squared के अनुपात में होने ही चाहिए, और अगर नहीं हैं तो कहीं ग़लती हुई है।
Aam तौर पर, calculate करने से पहले अंदाज़ा लगाने की आदत डालिए। कोई भी series नतीजा group के सबसे बड़े resistor से ऊपर होगा, और कोई भी parallel नतीजा सबसे छोटे से नीचे।
Agar आपकी arithmetic इनमें से किसी को तोड़े, तो number लिखने की जगह रुककर ग़लती ढूँढिए। इसमें दस second लगते हैं और पूरे सवाल बच जाते हैं।

sections.title: When the series and parallel rules do not apply

board_events.text: When these rules do not apply
The series and parallel rules assume ideal resistors with no internal electromotive force and negligible wire resistance, in the steady state.
They apply only to resistors genuinely in series, meaning the same current with no junction between them.
Or genuinely in parallel, meaning both ends share the same two nodes.
A common error is calling resistors parallel just because they look side by side on paper. They must share both end nodes.
Check the actual connections in the circuit, not the convenience of the drawing. Redraw the network if the layout is misleading.
Networks that are neither pure series nor pure parallel, such as an unbalanced bridge, cannot be reduced this way at all.
Those need Kirchhoff's laws, which we build in a later subtopic. Recognising that a network is irreducible is itself a skill.

segments.text: Before the formulas, be clear about when these two rules actually apply, because misapplying them is a far commoner error than getting the arithmetic wrong.
The rules assume ideal resistors carrying no internal electromotive force, with negligible wire resistance, in the steady state.
They apply directly only to resistors that are genuinely in series, which means carrying the same current with no junction sitting between them.
Or genuinely in parallel, which means both ends of each resistor touch the same two nodes as every other branch.

<whisper>Here is the error to watch for.</whisper> Students call resistors parallel just because they happen to be drawn side by side on the page. That is not the test. They must share both end nodes.

So check the actual connections in the circuit rather than the convenience of the drawing, and redraw the network yourself if the printed layout is misleading. A redraw takes a minute and prevents a wrong reduction.

Finally, some networks are neither pure series nor pure parallel anywhere. The classic case is an unbalanced bridge, where a resistor bridges two midpoints, and such a network cannot be reduced this way at all.
Those need Kirchhoff's laws, which we build in a later subtopic. Recognising that a network is irreducible, rather than forcing a reduction that does not exist, is itself an exam skill.
Formulas से पहले साफ़ कर लीजिए कि ये दोनों नियम असल में कब लागू होते हैं, क्योंकि इन्हें ग़लत जगह लगाना arithmetic की ग़लती से कहीं ज़्यादा आम है।
Ye नियम मानकर चलते हैं कि resistors ideal हैं, उनमें कोई अंदरूनी electromotive force नहीं, wire की resistance नगण्य है, और हालत steady state है।
Ye सीधे सिर्फ़ उन resistors पर लगते हैं जो सचमुच series में हैं, यानी जिनमें एक ही current है और जिनके बीच कोई junction नहीं।
Ya फिर जो सचमुच parallel में हैं, यानी जिनके दोनों सिरे बाक़ी हर branch की तरह उन्हीं दो nodes को छूते हैं।
Ye रही वो ग़लती जिससे बचना है। Students resistors को सिर्फ़ इसलिए parallel कह देते हैं क्योंकि वो page पर साथ साथ बने हैं। ये test नहीं है। दोनों end nodes साझा होने चाहिए।

<curious>To circuit के असली connections जाँचिए</curious>, drawing की सुविधा नहीं, और अगर छपा हुआ layout भ्रम पैदा कर रहा हो तो network ख़ुद दोबारा बनाइए। दोबारा बनाने में एक minute लगता है और एक ग़लत reduction रुक जाती है।

Aakhir में, कुछ networks कहीं भी न शुद्ध series होते हैं न शुद्ध parallel। Classic मामला है unbalanced bridge, जहाँ एक resistor दो midpoints को जोड़ता है, और ऐसा network इस तरीक़े से reduce हो ही नहीं सकता।
Unke लिए Kirchhoff के नियम चाहिए, जो हम आगे के subtopic में बनाएँगे। ये पहचान लेना कि network reduce नहीं हो सकता, बजाय ऐसी reduction ज़बरदस्ती करने के जो है ही नहीं, ख़ुद एक exam skill है।

sections.title: The series and parallel formulas

board_events.text: The series and parallel formulas

board_events.latex: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n, \qquad V = V_1 + V_2 + \cdots

board_events.text: In series the current is common to every resistor, and the applied voltage is the sum of the individual drops.
In parallel the voltage is common to every branch, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents.
For exactly two resistors in parallel this product-over-sum form is the fastest route, and it is the case that appears most often.
Take the reciprocal at the end. The sum gives you one over $R_p$, never $R_p$ itself.

segments.text: Here are the two formulas the whole subtopic rests on, together with the conditions that make each one true.
In series, resistances simply add, and the applied voltage equals the sum of the individual drops across the resistors.
The reason both statements hold is the same: the current is common to every resistor in a series chain, because there is nowhere for charge to leave or enter between them.
In parallel, it is the reciprocals that add, and the total current from the source equals the sum of the branch currents.
Again the two statements share a reason: the voltage is common to every branch, because both ends of every branch touch the same pair of nodes.
For the special case of exactly two resistors in parallel, the reciprocal sum simplifies to the product divided by the sum.
That product-over-sum form is the fastest route in practice, and two resistors in parallel is by far the commonest case you will actually meet in a problem.

<whisper>One warning that costs marks every year.</whisper> Take the reciprocal at the end. The sum on the right-hand side gives you one over R p, and reporting that as the answer is the single commonest slip in this subtopic.
Ye रहे वो दो formulas जिन पर पूरा subtopic टिका है, उन शर्तों के साथ जो हर एक को सही बनाती हैं।
Series में resistances सीधे जुड़ जाती हैं, और लगाया गया voltage resistors पर के अलग अलग drops के जोड़ के बराबर होता है।
Dono बातें एक ही वजह से सही हैं: series की कड़ी में हर resistor से एक ही current बहता है, क्योंकि उनके बीच charge के निकलने या आने की कोई जगह नहीं।
Parallel में reciprocals जुड़ते हैं, और source से आने वाला कुल current हर branch के currents के जोड़ के बराबर होता है।
<curious>Yahan भी दोनों बातों की वजह एक ही है</curious>: हर branch पर एक ही voltage होता है, क्योंकि हर branch के दोनों सिरे उन्हीं दो nodes को छूते हैं।
Theek दो resistors parallel में हों तो reciprocal वाला जोड़ सिमट कर product divided by sum बन जाता है।
Wo product-over-sum रूप व्यवहार में सबसे तेज़ रास्ता है, और parallel में दो resistors ही वो मामला है जो problems में सबसे ज़्यादा मिलता है।
Ek चेतावनी जो हर साल marks काटती है। आख़िर में reciprocal लीजिए। दाईं तरफ़ का जोड़ आपको one over R p देता है, और उसी को answer लिख देना इस subtopic की सबसे आम चूक है।

sections.title: Voltage divider, current divider, and n equal resistors

board_events.text: Voltage divider, current divider, and n equal resistors

board_events.latex: V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad V_2 = V\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}

board_events.text: In a series pair each resistor takes a share of the total voltage in proportion to its own resistance.

board_events.latex: I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad I_2 = I\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}

board_events.text: In the current divider the opposite resistor appears on top. More current takes the smaller resistor.
That asymmetry is deliberate, not a misprint. Putting the same resistor on top is one of the most frequent errors in this subtopic.
All quantities are in S I units: resistance in ohm, with dimensional formula $M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-2}$, voltage in volt, current in ampere.

segments.text: The second formula block gives you the two divider rules, which let you find a single branch quantity without solving the whole circuit again.
The voltage divider applies to two resistors in series across a supply. Each one takes a share of the total voltage.
Read the structure. Each resistor's share is proportional to its own resistance, which is intuitive: the bigger resistor drops more of the voltage.
The current divider is the mirror rule for two resistors in parallel carrying a total current between them.
<curious>But look carefully at what sits on top.</curious> In the current divider the opposite resistor appears in the numerator, because more current naturally takes the smaller resistor.

That asymmetry is deliberate and not a misprint. Putting the same resistor on top, by analogy with the voltage divider, is one of the most frequent errors in this subtopic, and it inverts your answer completely.
For n identical resistors, series gives n R, parallel gives R over n, and the ratio of the two is n squared, which we met as a checking device a moment ago.
All of these are in S I units throughout: resistance in ohm, with dimensional formula M L squared T to the minus three A to the minus two, voltage in volt, and current in ampere.
Doosra formula हिस्सा दो divider rules देता है, जिनसे आप पूरा circuit दोबारा हल किए बिना किसी एक branch की quantity निकाल सकते हैं।
Voltage divider supply के आर पार series में लगे दो resistors पर लगता है। हर एक कुल voltage का एक हिस्सा लेता है।
Iski बनावट पढ़िए। हर resistor का हिस्सा उसकी अपनी resistance के अनुपात में है, जो सहज भी है: बड़ा resistor ज़्यादा voltage गिराता है।
Current divider इसका आईना नियम है, parallel में लगे उन दो resistors के लिए जिनके बीच कुल current बँटता है।
Lekin ध्यान से देखिए कि ऊपर क्या बैठा है। Current divider में दूसरा resistor numerator में आता है, क्योंकि ज़्यादा current क़ुदरती तौर पर छोटे resistor से जाता है।

<curious>Ye असमानता जान बूझकर है</curious>, कोई छपाई की ग़लती नहीं। Voltage divider की नक़ल करके वही resistor ऊपर रख देना इस subtopic की सबसे आम ग़लतियों में से है, और ये आपका answer पूरी तरह उलट देता है।
n barabar resistors के लिए series देता है n R, parallel देता है R over n, और दोनों का ratio n squared है, जो अभी थोड़ी देर पहले हमें एक जाँच के औज़ार की तरह मिला था।
Ye सब पूरे तौर पर S I units में हैं: resistance ohm में, dimensional formula M L squared T to the minus three A to the minus two, voltage volt में, और current ampere में।

board_events.text: The current is common because there is no junction between series resistors, so charge conservation forces it.

board_events.latex: V_1 = IR_1, \qquad V_2 = IR_2, \qquad V_3 = IR_3

board_events.text: The single equivalent resistor would draw the same current from the same voltage, so it must satisfy $V = IR_s$.

segments.text: This is the first of the two derivations C B S E asks for by name, and it takes four lines once the setup is clear.
Take three resistors joined end to end across a source of voltage V, carrying a common current I through all three in turn.
Draw it as a single line: source, then the three resistors one after another, with the voltage drops marked across each one.
State why the current is common, because that is the step worth a mark. There is no junction between series resistors, so charge conservation forces identical current through each.
Now apply Ohm's law to each resistor separately. The drop across the first is I R one, across the second is I R two, and across the third is I R three.
By the loop rule, the source voltage equals the sum of the three drops, and since the current is the same in all three, it factorises straight out.
<curious>Now the defining move.</curious> The single equivalent resistor is the one that would draw the same current from the same voltage, so it must satisfy voltage equals current times R s.
Comparing the two expressions gives the equivalent series resistance as the plain sum of the individual resistances, which is the result we were after.
Ye उन दो derivations में से पहली है जो C B S E नाम लेकर पूछता है, और setup साफ़ होने के बाद ये चार lines में हो जाती है।
Teen resistors लीजिए जो V voltage के source के आर पार end to end जुड़े हैं, और तीनों से बारी बारी एक ही current I बहता है।
Ise एक सीधी line में बनाइए: source, फिर तीनों resistors एक के बाद एक, और हर एक पर voltage drop चिह्नित।
Current common क्यों है, ये कहिए, क्योंकि इसी step पर एक mark है। Series resistors के बीच कोई junction नहीं होता, इसलिए charge conservation हर एक में एक ही current मजबूर कर देता है।
<curious>Ab हर resistor पर अलग से Ohm's law लगाइए।</curious> पहले पर drop है I R एक, दूसरे पर I R दो, और तीसरे पर I R तीन।
Loop rule से source का voltage तीनों drops के जोड़ के बराबर है, और तीनों में current एक ही होने से वो सीधे बाहर निकल आता है।
Ab वो क़दम जो definition तय करता है। एक equivalent resistor वो है जो उसी voltage से उतना ही current खींचे, इसलिए उसे voltage equals current into R s मानना ही होगा।
Dono expressions मिलाइए और equivalent series resistance मिल जाती है, अलग अलग resistances का सीधा जोड़, जो हमें चाहिए ही था।

board_events.caption: Three resistors as parallel branches between two nodes, with the total current splitting between them.

board_events.text: The voltage is common because both ends of every branch touch the same pair of nodes, which sit at fixed potentials.

segments.text: This is the second board derivation, and the current divider rule falls out of it as a bonus in the last line.
Take three resistors all connected between the same two nodes, call them A and B, so that every one of them has the same potential difference across it.
Draw them as three parallel branches, with the total current arriving at the first node and splitting between them.
State why the voltage is common, since this is the mirror of the series argument. Both ends of every branch touch the same pair of nodes, and those nodes sit at fixed potentials.
Now apply Ohm's law to each branch. The current in the first is voltage over R one, in the second voltage over R two, and in the third voltage over R three.
By the junction rule, the total current from the source is the sum of the three, and the common voltage factors straight out of that sum.
The equivalent resistor satisfies current equals voltage over R p, so dividing through by the voltage gives the reciprocal sum, which is the result.

<excited>And here is the bonus.</excited> For just two branches, substitute the product-over-sum equivalent back in and the current in branch one comes out as the total current times R two over the sum. The larger the other resistor, the more current stays in branch one.
Ye दूसरी board derivation है, और current divider rule आख़िरी line में मुफ़्त में निकल आता है।
Teen resistors लीजिए जो सब एक ही दो nodes के बीच जुड़े हैं, उन्हें A और B कहिए, ताकि हर एक पर एक ही potential difference हो।
Inhe तीन parallel branches की तरह बनाइए, जहाँ कुल current पहले node पर आता है और उनमें बँट जाता है।
Voltage common क्यों है ये कहिए, क्योंकि ये series वाली दलील का आईना है। हर branch के दोनों सिरे उन्हीं दो nodes को छूते हैं, और वो nodes तय potentials पर हैं।
Ab हर branch पर Ohm's law लगाइए। पहली में current है voltage over R एक, दूसरी में voltage over R दो, तीसरी में voltage over R तीन।
<curious>Junction rule से source का कुल current इन तीनों का जोड़ है</curious>, और साझा voltage उस जोड़ से सीधे बाहर आ जाता है।
Equivalent resistor मानता है current equals voltage over R p, इसलिए voltage से divide करने पर reciprocal वाला जोड़ मिल जाता है, यही नतीजा है।

Aur ये रहा मुफ़्त का फ़ायदा। सिर्फ़ दो branches के लिए product-over-sum वाली equivalent वापस रखिए, तो पहली branch का current निकलता है कुल current into R दो over जोड़। दूसरा resistor जितना बड़ा, उतना ज़्यादा current पहली branch में रुकता है।

sections.title: Worked example: three resistors, series and parallel

board_events.text: Worked example, C B S E board level: three resistors two ways
Resistors of two ohm, three ohm and six ohm are available. Find the equivalent resistance in series, and then in parallel.
Series is immediate: the resistances simply add, giving eleven ohm.
Take the reciprocal now. One over $R_p$ equals one, so $R_p$ equals one ohm.
Check the direction: eleven ohm exceeds the largest resistor, and one ohm falls below the smallest. Both results behave as they must.

segments.text: The first worked example is at C B S E board level and exercises both formulas on the same three resistors.
You are given resistors of two ohm, three ohm and six ohm, and asked for the equivalent resistance first with all three in series, then with all three in parallel.
Series is immediate. The resistances simply add, giving eleven ohm.
There is nothing subtle in that step, and the marks are in the parallel half of the question.
For parallel, take the reciprocals and add them over a common denominator of six. Three plus two plus one gives six over six, which is one.
<whisper>Now do the step students forget.</whisper> That one is the value of one over R p, not R p. Take the reciprocal.
One over R p equals one, so R p equals one ohm, and that is the answer to the second half.

Finish with the direction check we established earlier. Eleven ohm exceeds the largest resistor in the group, and one ohm falls below the smallest, which is two ohm. Both results behave exactly as they must.
Pehla worked example C B S E board level का है और एक ही तीन resistors पर दोनों formulas का अभ्यास कराता है।
Aapko दो ohm, तीन ohm और छह ohm के resistors दिए हैं, और equivalent resistance पूछी है, पहले तीनों series में, फिर तीनों parallel में।
Series तुरंत हो जाता है। Resistances सीधे जुड़ जाती हैं, और ग्यारह ohm मिलता है।
Us step में कुछ सूक्ष्म नहीं है, और marks सवाल के parallel वाले आधे हिस्से में हैं।
Parallel के लिए reciprocals लीजिए और छह के साझा denominator पर जोड़िए। तीन plus दो plus एक देता है छह बटा छह, यानी एक।
Ab वो step कीजिए जो students भूल जाते हैं। वो एक, one over R p की value है, R p की नहीं। Reciprocal लीजिए।
<curious>One over R p बराबर एक</curious>, इसलिए R p बराबर एक ohm, और यही दूसरे हिस्से का answer है।

Us direction check से ख़त्म कीजिए जो हमने पहले तय किया था। ग्यारह ohm group के सबसे बड़े resistor से ऊपर है, और एक ohm सबसे छोटे यानी दो ohm से नीचे। दोनों नतीजे ठीक वैसे ही बर्ताव कर रहे हैं जैसा उन्हें करना चाहिए।

sections.title: Worked example: maximum and minimum from four resistors

board_events.text: Worked example, N E E T speed trap: maximum and minimum
Four identical resistors, each of twelve ohm, are given. Find the maximum and minimum equivalent resistance obtainable using all four.
The trap: hunting through clever mixed arrangements and missing that the extremes are always the pure cases.
The maximum comes from all four in series, and the minimum from all four in parallel. No mixed arrangement beats either.
The ratio comes out as $n$ squared, exactly as it must, which confirms both answers in one line.

segments.text: The second worked example is a N E E T speed trap, and it is really a test of whether you waste time.
Four identical resistors, each of twelve ohm, are given, and you are asked for the maximum and minimum equivalent resistance obtainable using all four.
<chuckle>Here is where the time goes.</chuckle> Students start hunting through clever mixed arrangements, two in series paralleled with two in series, and so on, looking for an extreme.
But the extremes are always the pure cases. The maximum comes from all four in series and the minimum from all four in parallel, and no mixed arrangement beats either of them.
All four in series gives four times twelve, which is forty eight ohm.
All four in parallel gives twelve over four, which is three ohm.
Now use the check we built. Divide the maximum by the minimum: forty eight over three is sixteen.
Sixteen is four squared, which is n squared for four resistors, exactly as the general result demands. That single line confirms both answers, and the whole question should take under thirty seconds.
Doosra worked example N E E T का speed trap है, और असल में ये जाँचता है कि आप time बर्बाद करते हैं या नहीं।
Chaar barabar resistors दिए हैं, हर एक बारह ohm का, और चारों का इस्तेमाल करके maximum और minimum equivalent resistance पूछी गई है।
Ye रही वो जगह जहाँ time जाता है। Students चालाक mixed arrangements ढूँढने लगते हैं, दो series में जो दो series वालों के parallel में हों, वग़ैरह, किसी सिरे की तलाश में।
<chuckle>Lekin सिरे हमेशा शुद्ध मामले ही होते हैं।</chuckle> Maximum आता है चारों series में और minimum चारों parallel में, और कोई mixed arrangement इनमें से किसी को नहीं हरा सकता।
Chaaron series में देते हैं चार into बारह, यानी अड़तालीस ohm।
Chaaron parallel में देते हैं बारह बटा चार, यानी तीन ohm।
Ab वो check इस्तेमाल कीजिए जो हमने बनाया था। Maximum को minimum से divide कीजिए: अड़तालीस बटा तीन बराबर सोलह।
Solah है चार का square, यानी चार resistors के लिए n squared, ठीक जैसा आम नतीजा माँगता है। वो एक line दोनों answers की पुष्टि कर देती है, और पूरा सवाल तीस second से कम में निपटना चाहिए।

board_events.text: The full three amperes flows through the series two ohm, then splits across the parallel pair.
Check: the six ohm branch carries one ampere, and two plus one returns the three amperes we started with.

segments.text: The third worked example is at J E E Main level, and it combines a network reduction with the current divider rule.

A twelve volt battery of negligible internal resistance drives a two ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of six ohm and three ohm. Find the total current, and the current through the three ohm branch.
Work in stages, and never try to do the whole thing at once. First collapse the parallel pair, then handle what remains as a plain series chain.
Product over sum for the parallel pair gives eighteen over nine, which is two ohm.
The network is now just two ohm in series with two ohm, so the total is four ohm and the battery drives three amperes.

<curious>Now go back into the network for part two.</curious> The full three amperes flows through the series two ohm, because there is nowhere else for it to go, and then it splits across the parallel pair.
Apply the current divider with the opposite resistor on top. The three ohm branch gets three amperes times six over nine, which is two amperes.

Always check by conservation. The six ohm branch must carry the remaining one ampere, and two plus one returns the three amperes we started with. You can also verify through the voltage: six volts across the pair gives two and one amperes.
Teesra worked example J E E Main level का है, और ये network reduction को current divider rule के साथ जोड़ता है।

Ek बारह volt की battery, जिसकी internal resistance नगण्य है, दो ohm के resistor को छह ohm और तीन ohm के parallel combination के साथ series में चला रही है। कुल current चाहिए, और तीन ohm branch का current।
<curious>Charnon में काम कीजिए</curious>, पूरा एक साथ करने की कोशिश कभी मत कीजिए। पहले parallel जोड़ी को समेटिए, फिर जो बचे उसे सीधी series की कड़ी की तरह निपटाइए।
Parallel जोड़ी के लिए product over sum देता है अठारह बटा नौ, यानी दो ohm।
Network अब बस दो ohm series में दो ohm है, इसलिए कुल चार ohm है और battery तीन ampere चलाती है।
Ab दूसरे हिस्से के लिए network में वापस जाइए। पूरे तीन ampere series वाले दो ohm से गुज़रते हैं, क्योंकि उनके पास और कोई रास्ता है ही नहीं, और फिर वो parallel जोड़ी में बँट जाते हैं।
Current divider लगाइए, दूसरा resistor ऊपर रखकर। तीन ohm branch को मिलता है तीन ampere into छह बटा नौ, यानी दो ampere।

Hamesha conservation से जाँचिए। छह ohm branch को बचा हुआ एक ampere लेना ही होगा, और दो plus एक वापस वही तीन ampere देते हैं जिनसे शुरू किया था। Voltage से भी जाँच सकते हैं: जोड़ी पर छह volt देता है दो और एक ampere।

board_events.text: The self-similarity trick: because the ladder is infinite, removing the first rung leaves an identical infinite ladder of resistance $X$ again.

board_events.latex: X(R + X) = R(R + X) + RX \implies X^2 - RX - R^2 = 0

board_events.text: The negative root is discarded because resistance cannot be negative. The answer is the golden ratio times $R$.

segments.text: The final worked example for this subtopic is at J E E Advanced level, and it cannot be solved by grinding through resistors one at a time.
An infinite ladder network is built from identical resistors R. Each rung places one R in series along the top and one R as a shunt down to the bottom rail, and this repeats forever.
Look at the structure before writing anything. The pattern never terminates, so there is no far end to start reducing from.

<curious>Here is the trick that unlocks it.</curious> Because the ladder is infinite, removing the very first rung leaves behind a network that is identical to the original, with the same equivalent resistance X.
So the whole network equals one series R, followed by a shunt R sitting in parallel with the rest of the ladder, which is X again. Write that as an equation.
Multiply through by R plus X to clear the fraction, expand both sides, and the R X terms partially cancel to leave a clean quadratic in X.
Solving with the quadratic formula gives R plus root five R, all over two, which is approximately one point six one eight R.
Discard the negative root, since resistance cannot be negative. And notice what the answer is: the golden ratio times R, a small piece of mathematical beauty hiding inside a resistor network.
Is subtopic का आख़िरी worked example J E E Advanced level का है, और इसे एक एक resistor घिसकर हल नहीं किया जा सकता।
Ek infinite ladder network barabar resistors R से बना है। हर rung एक R ऊपर series में रखता है और एक R नीचे की rail तक shunt की तरह, और ये हमेशा के लिए दोहराता है।
Kuch लिखने से पहले बनावट देखिए। Pattern कभी ख़त्म नहीं होता, इसलिए reduce करना शुरू करने के लिए कोई दूर का सिरा है ही नहीं।
Ye रही वो तरकीब जो इसे खोलती है। Ladder infinite है, इसलिए सबसे पहला rung हटाने पर पीछे बिलकुल वैसा ही network बचता है, उसी equivalent resistance X के साथ।
<excited>To पूरा network बराबर है एक series R, उसके बाद एक shunt R जो बाक़ी ladder के parallel में है</excited>, और वो बाक़ी ladder फिर से X ही है। इसे एक equation की तरह लिखिए।
R plus X से गुणा करके fraction हटाइए, दोनों तरफ़ खोलिए, और R X वाले terms आंशिक रूप से कटकर X में एक साफ़ quadratic छोड़ जाते हैं।
Quadratic formula से हल करने पर मिलता है R plus root five R, पूरा दो से divide, यानी लगभग one point six one eight R।
Negative root छोड़ दीजिए, क्योंकि resistance negative नहीं हो सकती। और देखिए answer है क्या: golden ratio into R, गणित की एक छोटी सी ख़ूबसूरती जो एक resistor network के अंदर छिपी बैठी है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for combining resistors

board_events.text: Pitfalls that cost marks, and the pro-tips that save time
Forgetting to invert in parallel. The reciprocal sum gives one over $R_p$, never $R_p$ itself.
Calling side-by-side resistors parallel. They are parallel only if they share both end nodes, whatever the drawing suggests.
Putting the same resistor on top in the current divider. The branch current uses the other resistor in the numerator.
Trying to reduce across a bridging resistor. A network with a bridge between two midpoints usually needs the balance check or Kirchhoff instead.
Before computing, predict: any series result must exceed the largest resistor, and any parallel result must fall below the smallest.

board_events.latex: R_p = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} \quad \text{for two}, \qquad nR \text{ and } \frac{R}{n} \quad \text{for } n \text{ equal}

board_events.text: Finish every network problem with a current-conservation check, confirming the branch currents add back to the total.

segments.text: Let us close this subtopic with the four errors that reliably cost marks and the habits that prevent them.
The first, by a wide margin, is forgetting to invert at the end in parallel. The reciprocal sum gives you one over R p, and reporting that as the answer is the commonest slip in the whole subtopic.
The second is calling two resistors parallel because they happen to be drawn side by side. They are parallel only if they share both end nodes, whatever the layout of the diagram suggests.
The third is putting the same resistor on top in the current divider. The branch current uses the other resistor in the numerator, and getting this backwards inverts your answer completely.

The fourth is trying to reduce across a bridging resistor. If a network has a resistor bridging two midpoints, it is usually not reducible by series and parallel at all, and you need the balance check or Kirchhoff.
<excited>Now the habits.</excited> Before computing anything, predict the direction. Any series result must exceed the largest resistor, and any parallel result must fall below the smallest.
For speed, use product over sum whenever there are exactly two resistors in parallel, and for many equal resistors go straight to n R and R over n rather than summing reciprocals.
And finish every network problem with a current-conservation check, confirming that the branch currents add back up to the total. It catches almost every arithmetic error you are likely to make.
Is subtopic को उन चार ग़लतियों के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो पक्के तौर पर marks काटती हैं, और उन आदतों के साथ जो उन्हें रोकती हैं।
Pehli, और काफ़ी अंतर से, है parallel में आख़िर में invert करना भूल जाना। Reciprocal वाला जोड़ आपको one over R p देता है, और उसी को answer लिख देना पूरे subtopic की सबसे आम चूक है।
Doosri है दो resistors को सिर्फ़ इसलिए parallel कह देना क्योंकि वो साथ साथ बने हैं। वो तभी parallel हैं जब दोनों end nodes साझा हों, diagram का layout चाहे कुछ भी सुझाए।
Teesri है current divider में वही resistor ऊपर रख देना। Branch का current दूसरे resistor को numerator में लेता है, और इसे उल्टा करने से answer पूरी तरह पलट जाता है।

<curious>Chauthi है bridging resistor के आर पार reduce करने की कोशिश।</curious> अगर network में कोई resistor दो midpoints को जोड़ रहा है, तो वो आम तौर पर series parallel से reduce होता ही नहीं, और वहाँ balance check या Kirchhoff चाहिए।
Ab आदतें। कुछ भी calculate करने से पहले दिशा का अंदाज़ा लगाइए। कोई भी series नतीजा सबसे बड़े resistor से ऊपर होगा, और कोई भी parallel नतीजा सबसे छोटे से नीचे।
Speed के लिए, जब भी parallel में ठीक दो resistors हों तो product over sum इस्तेमाल कीजिए, और कई barabar resistors के लिए reciprocals जोड़ने की जगह सीधे n R और R over n पर जाइए।
Aur हर network problem को current-conservation check से ख़त्म कीजिए, ये पक्का करते हुए कि branch currents वापस जुड़कर total बन रहे हैं। ये लगभग हर arithmetic ग़लती पकड़ लेता है जो आप कर सकते हैं।

sections.title: Where the energy actually goes

board_events.text: Where the energy actually goes
Every time current flows through a resistor, the moving electrons crash into the lattice and lose energy.
That lost energy reappears as heat. This is why a charger warms, a heater glows, and a fuse melts.
The cell does work to push charge around the circuit; the resistor converts that work into heat, and sometimes light.

board_events.latex: W = qV, \qquad q = It \implies W = VIt

board_events.text: Picture a toll on a hill road: the toll per car is the voltage, the traffic rate is the current, and the money per second is their product.
Collect for a couple of hours and you have the total energy, which is what your electricity bill actually charges you for.

segments.text: This subtopic is where resistance stops being an obstacle to calculate around and starts doing something useful.
Every time current flows through a resistor, the moving electrons keep crashing into the lattice and losing energy on every collision.
That lost energy does not vanish. It reappears as heat, which is why a phone charger warms up, why a heater glows, and why a fuse melts when asked to carry too much.
The bookkeeping is simple. The cell does work to push charge around the circuit, and the resistor converts that work into heat, and sometimes into light as well.

Now put numbers on it. By the very definition of potential difference, pushing a charge q through a potential difference V takes work q V, and writing the charge as current times time gives work equal to V I t.
Dividing by the time gives the rate of doing work, which is the power, and it comes out as simply voltage times current.

<curious>Picture an electric heater as a paid toll on a hill road.</curious> The toll per car is the voltage, meaning energy handed over per coulomb. The traffic rate is the current, meaning coulombs per second. The money collected per second is naturally their product.
Collect for a couple of hours and you have the total energy, and that total is exactly what your electricity bill charges you for.
Ye subtopic वो जगह है जहाँ resistance सिर्फ़ एक रुकावट नहीं रहती जिसका हिसाब लगाना है, बल्कि कुछ काम की चीज़ करने लगती है।
Jab भी resistor से current बहता है, चलते हुए electrons lattice से टकराते रहते हैं और हर टक्कर पर energy खोते हैं।
Wo खोई हुई energy ग़ायब नहीं होती। वो heat बनकर लौट आती है, इसीलिए phone charger गरम होता है, heater चमकता है, और fuse तब पिघल जाता है जब उससे ज़्यादा current माँगा जाए।
Hisaab सीधा है। Cell circuit में charge को धकेलने का काम करता है, और resistor उस काम को heat में बदल देता है, और कभी कभी रोशनी में भी।
Ab इस पर numbers रखिए। Potential difference की परिभाषा से ही, charge q को V potential difference के आर पार धकेलने में q V काम लगता है, और charge को current into time लिखने पर काम बनता है V I t।
<curious>Time से divide कीजिए</curious> तो काम करने की rate मिलती है, यानी power, और वो निकलती है बस voltage into current।

Electric heater को पहाड़ी सड़क के toll की तरह सोचिए। Per car toll है voltage, यानी per coulomb दी गई energy। Traffic की rate है current, यानी coulomb per second। Per second जमा हुआ पैसा क़ुदरती तौर पर दोनों का गुणा है।
Do घंटे जमा कीजिए और आपके पास कुल energy है, और वही कुल आपके बिजली के bill में आपसे वसूला जाता है।

sections.title: The three faces of power and how to choose one

board_events.text: The three faces of power, and how to choose one
Using Ohm's law, the same power wears three faces. Which one you use depends entirely on what is held constant.
In series the current is shared, so $P = I^2R$ rules and the bigger resistor dissipates more.
In parallel the voltage is shared, so $P = V^2/R$ rules and the smaller resistor dissipates more.

segments.text: Power has three algebraically equivalent forms, and choosing the wrong one is the single biggest source of lost marks in this subtopic.
Using Ohm's law to substitute for voltage or for current, the same power wears three faces: voltage times current, current squared times resistance, and voltage squared over resistance.
They are all equally true, so being correct is not the issue. Which one is useful depends entirely on what is being held constant in the circuit you are looking at.
In a series circuit the current is shared, identical through every element. So current squared times resistance is the ruling form, and the bigger resistor dissipates more power.
In a parallel circuit the voltage is shared instead. So voltage squared over resistance rules, and now the smaller resistor dissipates more.
<curious>Look at the same two bulbs wired both ways.</curious> In series the forty watt bulb, which has the higher resistance, glows brighter. In parallel the hundred watt bulb wins instead.
That single switch explains the famous puzzle of why a low-wattage bulb outshines a high-wattage bulb when the two are wired in series, which looks impossible until you ask which quantity is shared.
So build the habit now. Ask first what is shared, current or voltage, and the correct formula picks itself instantly, with no guessing.

Ohm's law से voltage या current रखकर, वही power तीन चेहरे ले लेती है: voltage into current, current squared into resistance, और voltage squared over resistance।
<curious>Ye तीनों बराबर सही हैं</curious>, इसलिए सही होना मुद्दा है ही नहीं। कौन सा काम का है ये पूरी तरह इस पर है कि आपके सामने वाले circuit में क्या स्थिर रखा गया है।

Parallel circuit में इसकी जगह voltage साझा होता है। इसलिए voltage squared over resistance राज करता है, और अब छोटा resistor ज़्यादा खपाता है।

sections.title: Why a battery cannot deliver unlimited power

board_events.text: Why a battery cannot deliver unlimited power
A real battery has internal resistance $r$, so it cannot dump unlimited power into a load however small you make the load.
Make the load too small and the current is large but the load voltage is tiny. Make it too large and the voltage is high but the current is tiny.
The product therefore peaks somewhere in between, at the maximum power transfer condition.
That peak occurs when the load resistance exactly matches the internal resistance of the source.
At the match the load and the internal resistance dissipate equally, so the efficiency is only fifty percent.
Maximum power transfer is therefore deliberately inefficient, which is why power distribution lines run nowhere near this condition.
The result assumes a fixed source electromotive force and internal resistance, with only the load allowed to vary.

segments.text: There is a beautiful optimisation hiding at the end of this subtopic, and it carries a caveat that examiners set traps around.
A real battery has internal resistance, so it cannot dump unlimited power into a load however small you make that load.
Think through both extremes before any algebra. Make the load too small and the current is large but the load voltage is tiny. Make it too large and the voltage is high but the current is tiny.
Since power is the product of the two, and each extreme kills one factor, the product must peak somewhere in between. That peak is the maximum power transfer condition.
The result is remarkably clean. The peak occurs when the load resistance exactly matches the internal resistance of the source.

<whisper>Now the caveat worth a mark.</whisper> At that match, the load and the internal resistance dissipate equally, so exactly half the power is wasted inside the source and the efficiency is only fifty percent.

Maximum power transfer is therefore deliberately inefficient. It is the right goal for signal matching, and completely the wrong goal for power distribution, which is why transmission lines run nowhere near this condition.
One assumption to remember: the result holds for a fixed source electromotive force and a fixed internal resistance, with only the load allowed to vary.
Is subtopic के आख़िर में एक ख़ूबसूरत optimisation छिपी है, और उसके साथ एक चेतावनी आती है जिसके आसपास examiners जाल बिछाते हैं।

sections.title: Power, energy, Joule's law and the commercial unit

board_events.text: Power, energy, Joule's law and the commercial unit
SI unit: the watt, one joule per second, with dimensional formula $M L^{2} T^{-3}$.
Electrical energy is measured in joule, with dimensional formula $M L^{2} T^{-2}$.
This is Joule's law of heating, giving the heat produced in a resistor over a time $t$.

segments.text: Here is the first formula block, covering power, energy, and the two units you need to keep straight.
Power is the rate of energy conversion, and it appears in the three equivalent forms we discussed a moment ago.
Its S I unit is the watt, which is one joule per second, and its dimensional formula is M, L squared, T to the minus three.
Multiplying power by time gives the electrical energy, or equivalently the work done, and each of the three power forms carries a matching energy form.
Electrical energy is measured in joule, with dimensional formula M, L squared, T to the minus two. Note that power and energy differ by exactly one power of time.
The heat produced in a resistor over a time t is current squared times resistance times time.
<curious>That relation carries a name worth remembering.</curious> It is Joule's law of heating, and the current squared dependence is the key practical fact.

Finally the commercial unit. One kilowatt hour is one thousand watts multiplied by three thousand six hundred seconds, which is three point six times ten to the six joule. This is the unit your electricity bill actually counts.

Power energy बदलने की rate है, और वो उन्हीं तीन barabar रूपों में आती है जिनकी बात अभी हुई।

Electrical energy joule में मापी जाती है, dimensional formula M, L squared, T to the minus two के साथ। ध्यान दीजिए power और energy में ठीक time की एक power का फ़र्क़ है।
Kisi resistor में t समय में पैदा हुई heat है current squared into resistance into time।

sections.title: Appliance ratings and maximum power transfer

board_events.text: Appliance ratings and maximum power transfer
An appliance marked sixty watt at two hundred forty volt tells you its resistance, but only at its rated voltage.
A real filament rises sharply in resistance as it heats, so its cold resistance is far below its operating value.
At the matched condition the efficiency is exactly fifty percent, since load and source dissipate equally.
Symbols: $V$ potential difference in volt, $I$ current in ampere, $R$ and $r$ resistance in ohm, $E$ electromotive force in volt.

segments.text: The second formula block covers the two results that generate most of the numerical questions in this subtopic.
An appliance marked with a wattage and a voltage tells you its resistance directly: rated voltage squared, divided by rated power.
<whisper>But read the condition carefully.</whisper> A bulb marked sixty watt at two hundred forty volt has that resistance only at two hundred forty volt, not at every voltage.

The reason is physical. A real filament rises sharply in resistance as it heats, so its cold resistance is far below its operating value, and treating the rated resistance as fixed is a standard trap.
Now maximum power transfer. For a source of electromotive force E and internal resistance r feeding a variable load, the power delivered to the load is E squared R over the square of R plus r.
That expression is maximised when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, and the maximum value is E squared over four r.

At that matched condition the load and the source dissipate equally, so the efficiency is exactly fifty percent. Maximum power and maximum efficiency are different conditions, and examiners test the difference deliberately.
For the symbols: V is potential difference in volt, I is current in ampere, R and r are resistances in ohm, and E is the electromotive force in volt.
Doosra formula हिस्सा उन दो नतीजों को cover करता है जो इस subtopic के ज़्यादातर numerical सवाल पैदा करते हैं।
Kisi appliance पर लिखी wattage और voltage उसकी resistance सीधे बता देती है: rated voltage का square, rated power से divide।

<curious>Ab maximum power transfer।</curious> E electromotive force और r internal resistance वाले source के लिए जो एक बदलने वाले load को चला रहा है, load को मिलने वाली power है E squared R over R plus r का square।
Wo expression तब सबसे ज़्यादा होती है जब load की resistance internal resistance के बराबर हो, और अधिकतम value है E squared over four r।
Us मेल वाली हालत में load और source बराबर खपत करते हैं, इसलिए efficiency ठीक पचास percent होती है। Maximum power और maximum efficiency अलग अलग हालतें हैं, और examiners ये फ़र्क़ जान बूझकर पूछते हैं।

sections.title: Derivation: the power formula and Joule's law

board_events.text: Derivation: the power formula and Joule's law
Consider a resistor $R$ carrying a steady current $I$, driven by a potential difference $V$ across it.
Why this becomes heat: in a pure resistor the work done on the charges is not stored. It is handed to the lattice through collisions.
The $I^2$ dependence is the key practical fact: doubling the current quadruples the heating, which is why thick cables are used for heavy loads.

segments.text: This derivation is short, but the middle step, where work turns into heat, is the one worth stating explicitly in an answer.
Consider a resistor R carrying a steady current I, driven by a potential difference V across its ends.
Moving a small charge d q through that potential drop requires work equal to the drop times the charge, and the charge itself is the current times a small time interval.
Substituting and dividing through by the time interval gives the power directly as voltage times current.

<curious>Now say why this becomes heat</curious>, because that is the physical content. In a pure resistor the work done on the charges is not stored anywhere. It is handed to the lattice through collisions and emerges as thermal energy.
Applying Ohm's law to substitute for the voltage, or for the current, gives the other two forms of the power expression.
Multiplying by the elapsed time gives the heat produced, which is Joule's law of heating.

The current squared dependence is the key practical fact, and it is worth spelling out. Doubling the current quadruples the heating, which is exactly why thick low-current-density cables are used for heavy loads.
Ye derivation छोटी है, लेकिन बीच का वो step जहाँ काम heat में बदलता है, उसे answer में साफ़ लिखना ज़रूरी है।
Ek resistor R लीजिए जिसमें steady current I बह रहा है, और जिसके सिरों पर V potential difference लगा है।
Ek छोटे charge d q को उस potential drop के आर पार ले जाने में drop into charge जितना काम लगता है, और वो charge ख़ुद current into एक छोटा time interval है।
Rakh कर time interval से divide करने पर power सीधे voltage into current मिल जाती है।

Ab कहिए कि ये heat क्यों बनती है, क्योंकि यही physical सार है। Pure resistor में charges पर किया गया काम कहीं जमा नहीं होता। वो collisions के ज़रिए lattice को दे दिया जाता है और thermal energy बनकर निकलता है।
Voltage या current के लिए Ohm's law रखने पर power की expression के बाक़ी दो रूप मिल जाते हैं।
<curious>Beeta हुआ time गुणा कीजिए</curious> तो पैदा हुई heat मिलती है, जो Joule का law of heating है।

Current के square वाली निर्भरता सबसे काम की व्यावहारिक बात है, और इसे खोलकर कहना चाहिए। Current दोगुना कीजिए तो heating चार गुनी हो जाती है, और ठीक इसीलिए भारी loads के लिए मोटी, कम current density वाली cables लगाई जाती हैं।

board_events.text: Derivation: the maximum power transfer theorem
Consider a source of electromotive force $E$ and internal resistance $r$ connected to a variable load $R$.
To maximise the load power with respect to $R$, differentiate and set the derivative to zero.

board_events.text: Maximum power transfer is deliberately inefficient. Power lines instead run far from this condition, at high efficiency.

segments.text: This is the derivation J E E reaches for, and it is a straightforward maximisation once the power expression is set up correctly.
Consider a source of electromotive force E and internal resistance r, connected to a load R that we are free to vary.
The current around the loop is E over R plus r, so the power delivered to the load is that current squared times R, giving E squared R over the square of R plus r.
To maximise this with respect to the load resistance, differentiate the expression and set the derivative equal to zero.
Apply the quotient rule and simplify. A factor of R plus r cancels from top and bottom, and the numerator collapses neatly to r minus R.
Setting that to zero gives the condition immediately: the load resistance must equal the internal resistance.
<curious>Sketch the curve to see why this makes sense.</curious> The power rises from zero, peaks sharply at the match point, then falls away gradually, approaching zero again for very large loads.
Substituting the matched value gives a maximum power of E squared over four r, which is the headline result of the whole derivation.

And at that point the load and the internal resistance dissipate equally, so the efficiency is only fifty percent. Maximum power transfer is deliberately inefficient, which is why power lines run far from this condition.
Ye वो derivation है जिसे J E E उठाता है, और power की expression ठीक से बन जाने के बाद ये एक सीधा maximisation है।
Ek source लीजिए जिसका electromotive force E और internal resistance r है, और जो एक ऐसे load R से जुड़ा है जिसे हम बदल सकते हैं।
<curious>Loop में current है E over R plus r</curious>, इसलिए load को मिलने वाली power है उस current का square into R, यानी E squared R over R plus r का square।
Ise load resistance के हिसाब से सबसे ज़्यादा करने के लिए expression को differentiate कीजिए और derivative को zero रखिए।
Quotient rule लगाइए और simplify कीजिए। R plus r का एक factor ऊपर नीचे से कट जाता है, और numerator सिमटकर साफ़ साफ़ r minus R रह जाता है।
Use zero रखने पर शर्त तुरंत मिल जाती है: load की resistance internal resistance के बराबर होनी चाहिए।
Curve बनाकर देखिए कि ये सही क्यों लगता है। Power zero से चढ़ती है, मेल वाले point पर तेज़ चोटी बनाती है, फिर धीरे धीरे गिरती है और बहुत बड़े loads के लिए फिर zero की तरफ़ जाती है।
Mel वाली value रखने पर अधिकतम power मिलती है E squared over four r, जो पूरी derivation का मुख्य नतीजा है।

sections.title: Worked example: resistance and current of a rated bulb

board_events.text: Worked example, C B S E board level: a rated bulb
An electric bulb is rated sixty watt at two hundred forty volt. Find its resistance at the rated voltage, and the current it draws.
Cross-check with the third form: $I^2R$ should return the rated power.
The check closes, so both answers are consistent. This resistance applies at two hundred forty volt only, not when the filament is cold.

segments.text: The first worked example for this subtopic is at C B S E board level, and it exercises two of the three power forms on the same appliance.
An electric bulb is rated sixty watt at two hundred forty volt. You are asked for its resistance at the rated voltage, and for the current it draws.
For the resistance, start from the form that contains resistance and voltage but not current, since those are the two quantities you have been given.
Rearranging and substituting gives two hundred forty squared, which is fifty seven thousand six hundred, divided by sixty. That works out to nine hundred sixty ohm.
For the current, use the simplest form of all. Power equals voltage times current, so the current is sixty divided by two hundred forty, which is a quarter of an ampere.
<curious>Now cross-check using the third form</curious>, which we have not used yet. Current squared times resistance should return the rated power.
A quarter squared is zero point zero six two five, and multiplying by nine hundred sixty gives exactly sixty watt. The check closes.

One caution to carry forward. That nine hundred sixty ohm applies at two hundred forty volt only. When the filament is cold its resistance is far lower, which is why bulbs draw a surge of current at switch-on.
Is subtopic का पहला worked example C B S E board level का है, और ये एक ही appliance पर power के तीन में से दो रूपों का अभ्यास कराता है।

Rearrange करके रखने पर मिलता है दो सौ चालीस का square, यानी सत्तावन हज़ार छह सौ, साठ से divide। ये निकलता है नौ सौ साठ ohm।
Current के लिए सबसे सीधा रूप इस्तेमाल कीजिए। Power equals voltage into current, इसलिए current है साठ बटा दो सौ चालीस, यानी एक चौथाई ampere।
Ab तीसरे रूप से cross-check कीजिए, जो हमने अभी तक इस्तेमाल नहीं किया। Current squared into resistance वापस rated power देना चाहिए।
Ek चौथाई का square है zero point zero six two five, और नौ सौ साठ से गुणा करने पर ठीक साठ watt आता है। जाँच बंद हो गई।
Ek चेतावनी आगे के लिए। वो नौ सौ साठ ohm सिर्फ़ दो सौ चालीस volt पर लागू है। Filament ठंडा हो तो उसकी resistance कहीं कम होती है, और इसीलिए switch on करते ही bulbs current का एक झटका खींचते हैं।
