segments.text: The third worked example is at J E E Main level and needs the weighted formula, because the two cells are no longer identical.

Cell one has electromotive force four volt and internal resistance one ohm. Cell two has electromotive force two volt and internal resistance one ohm. Together they drive an external resistance of two point five ohm.
Draw the pair sharing the same two nodes before calculating, because the picture makes the next physical remark obvious.
Apply the weighted formula for the equivalent electromotive force. Four times one plus two times one is six, divided by the sum of the internal resistances, which is two, giving three volt.
The equivalent internal resistance is the ordinary parallel combination, one times one over two, which is half an ohm.
Now the pair is a single cell again. Three volt across two point five plus zero point five, which is three ohm, gives exactly one ampere.

<curious>Look at where the equivalent electromotive force landed.</curious> Three volt sits between the two cell values, and exactly midway, which happened only because the two internal resistances are equal.
Physically, the stronger four volt cell drives some current backwards through the weaker two volt cell, effectively charging it a little. That is why the pair behaves like neither cell on its own.
Teesra worked example J E E Main level का है और इसमें weighted formula चाहिए, क्योंकि दोनों cells अब barabar नहीं हैं।

Calculate करने से पहले दोनों को एक ही दो nodes साझा करते हुए बनाइए, क्योंकि तस्वीर अगली physical बात साफ़ कर देती है।
Equivalent electromotive force के लिए weighted formula लगाइए। चार into एक plus दो into एक है छह, internal resistances के जोड़ यानी दो से divide, जिससे मिलता है तीन volt।

Physically, ताक़तवर चार volt वाला cell कमज़ोर दो volt वाले में से कुछ current उल्टा चलाता है, यानी उसे थोड़ा charge कर देता है। इसीलिए जोड़ी किसी भी अकेले cell जैसी नहीं बर्ताव करती।

segments.text: The final worked example is at J E E Advanced level, and it is the optimisation we derived, now with numbers.
You have twenty four identical cells, each of electromotive force one point five volt and internal resistance zero point five ohm.
You must arrange them as m rows of n series cells to deliver the maximum possible current into an external resistance of three ohm.
Picture the array before starting. You are choosing the shape of a rectangle holding twenty four cells, and only certain shapes are allowed.
<curious>Write the matching condition first.</curious> Maximum current needs m R equal to n r, so m times three equals n times zero point five, which gives the ratio n over m as six.
Now bring in the constraint that all twenty four cells must be used. Substituting n equals six m into m n equals twenty four gives six m squared equals twenty four, so m is two and n is twelve.
So the answer to the arrangement question is two rows of twelve cells each. Now compute what that arrangement actually delivers.

The equivalent electromotive force is twelve times one point five, which is eighteen volt, and the equivalent internal resistance is three ohm, equal to the external resistance as required. Eighteen volt across six ohm gives three amperes.
Aakhri worked example J E E Advanced level का है, और ये वही optimisation है जो हमने derive किया था, अब numbers के साथ।
Aapke पास चौबीस barabar cells हैं, हर एक का electromotive force एक point पाँच volt और internal resistance zero point पाँच ohm।
Aapko इन्हें m rows और हर row में n series cells की तरह सजाना है ताकि तीन ohm की external resistance में सबसे ज़्यादा current जाए।
Shuru करने से पहले array की कल्पना कीजिए। आप चौबीस cells रखने वाले आयत की शक्ल चुन रहे हैं, और सिर्फ़ कुछ ही शक्लें मुमकिन हैं।
Pehle matching की शर्त लिखिए। Maximum current के लिए m R बराबर n r चाहिए, इसलिए m into तीन बराबर n into zero point पाँच, जिससे n over m का ratio छह मिलता है।
<curious>Ab वो शर्त लाइए</curious> कि चौबीसों cells इस्तेमाल होने चाहिए। n बराबर छह m को m n बराबर चौबीस में रखने पर मिलता है छह m squared बराबर चौबीस, यानी m है दो और n है बारह।
To arrangement वाले सवाल का जवाब है दो rows, हर में बारह cells। अब निकालिए कि वो arrangement असल में देता क्या है।

Equivalent electromotive force है बारह into एक point पाँच, यानी अठारह volt, और equivalent internal resistance है तीन ohm, external resistance के बराबर जैसा ज़रूरी था। छह ohm पर अठारह volt देता है तीन ampere।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for combining cells

board_events.text: Pitfalls that cost marks, and the pro-tips that save time
Adding electromotive forces in parallel. Identical cells in parallel give $E$, not $nE$. Only series stacks voltages.
Forgetting that a reversed cell counts double. Flipping one cell changes the net series electromotive force by $2E$, not by $E$.
Using $r/n$ for cells that are not identical. That shortcut needs identical cells; unequal ones need the weighted formula.
Choosing the wrong grouping for the load. Series for large $R$, parallel for small $R$, matched mixed grouping for maximum current.
Reduce any grouping to a single equivalent cell first, and then this one clean formula handles every case you will meet.
For mixed-grouping optimisation, jump straight to $mR = nr$ together with $mn = N$, and solve the two simultaneously.

segments.text: Let us close this subtopic with the four errors that reliably cost marks and the two shortcuts that save real time.
The first is adding electromotive forces in parallel. Identical cells in parallel give you E, not n times E, because every cell spans the same two nodes. Only series stacks voltages.
The second is forgetting that a reversed cell counts double. Flipping one cell changes the net series electromotive force by two E, because it moves from plus E to minus E.

The third is using r over n for cells that are not identical. That shortcut needs identical cells, and unequal ones need the weighted formula for both the electromotive force and the internal resistance.
The fourth is choosing the wrong grouping for the load. Series for a large external resistance, parallel for a small one, and matched mixed grouping when you want maximum current.
<excited>Now the shortcuts.</excited> Reduce any grouping to a single equivalent cell first, with its own electromotive force and internal resistance.
Then one clean formula, current equals equivalent electromotive force over the total resistance, handles every case you will ever meet, however the cells were wired.
And for mixed-grouping optimisation, do not grind through the algebra. Jump straight to m R equals n r together with m n equals the total number of cells, and solve those two simultaneously.
Is subtopic को उन चार ग़लतियों के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो पक्के तौर पर marks काटती हैं, और उन दो shortcuts के साथ जो सचमुच time बचाते हैं।
Pehli है parallel में electromotive forces जोड़ देना। Barabar cells parallel में E देते हैं, n into E नहीं, क्योंकि हर cell उन्हीं दो nodes के बीच है। Voltage सिर्फ़ series जोड़ता है।
Doosri है ये भूलना कि उल्टा cell दुगना गिनता है। एक cell पलटने से net series electromotive force दो E से बदलता है, क्योंकि वो plus E से minus E पर चला जाता है।
Teesri है उन cells पर r over n लगाना जो barabar नहीं हैं। वो shortcut barabar cells माँगता है, और अलग अलग cells के लिए electromotive force तथा internal resistance दोनों के लिए weighted formula चाहिए।
<curious>Chauthi है load के लिए ग़लत grouping चुनना।</curious> बड़ी external resistance के लिए series, छोटी के लिए parallel, और maximum current चाहिए तो matched mixed grouping।
Ab shortcuts। किसी भी grouping को पहले एक अकेले equivalent cell में समेटिए, अपने electromotive force और internal resistance के साथ।
Phir एक साफ़ formula, current बराबर equivalent electromotive force over कुल resistance, हर उस मामले को सँभाल लेता है जो आपको कभी मिलेगा, cells चाहे कैसे भी जुड़े हों।
Aur mixed-grouping optimisation में algebra में मत उलझिए। सीधे m R बराबर n r पर जाइए, साथ में m n बराबर कुल cells, और इन दोनों को एक साथ हल कीजिए।

sections.title: When series and parallel run out: the junction rule

board_events.text: When series and parallel run out
Series and parallel rules are wonderful, until the circuit refuses to be either one.
Meet two batteries pushing against each other, or a bridge where nothing is cleanly in series or parallel, and the simple tricks collapse.
Kirchhoff's two rules are completely general, and both are everyday conservation laws wearing circuit clothing.

board_events.text: The junction rule: a wire junction is a meeting point of wires, not a storage tank, so charge cannot pile up there.
If three wires bring in five, three and two amperes, the wires leaving must carry ten amperes in total, split however the resistances dictate.

segments.text: This is one of the most heavily examined subtopics in the whole chapter, and it exists because the tools we have built so far are not enough.
The series and parallel rules are wonderful, right up until the circuit refuses to be either one.
The moment you meet two batteries pushing against each other, or a bridge where no two resistors are cleanly in series or parallel, those simple tricks collapse entirely.
What you need is a completely general toolkit, and the beautiful thing is that both of Kirchhoff's rules are just everyday conservation laws wearing circuit clothing.

Take the junction rule first. Picture a busy local train pulling into a station. The number of people stepping onto the platform must equal the number stepping into the train and out through the exits.

<curious>Nobody evaporates and nobody materialises.</curious> A wire junction is exactly like that: it is a meeting point of wires, not a storage tank, so in the steady state charge cannot pile up there.
So whatever charge flows in per second must flow out per second, which is the junction rule written in currents.
Make it concrete. If three wires bring in five, three and two amperes, the wires leaving must carry ten amperes in total, split however the resistances happen to dictate.
Ye पूरे chapter के सबसे ज़्यादा पूछे जाने वाले subtopics में से एक है, और ये इसलिए है क्योंकि अब तक बनाए गए औज़ार काफ़ी नहीं हैं।
Series और parallel के नियम बहुत अच्छे हैं, ठीक उस वक़्त तक जब तक circuit इन दोनों में से कोई एक होने से मना न कर दे।
Jaise ही दो batteries एक दूसरे के ख़िलाफ़ धकेलने लगें, या ऐसा bridge आए जहाँ कोई दो resistors साफ़ साफ़ series या parallel न हों, वो सारे आसान तरीक़े ढह जाते हैं।
Aapko एक पूरी तरह general toolkit चाहिए, और ख़ूबसूरती ये है कि Kirchhoff के दोनों नियम बस रोज़ के conservation laws हैं, circuit के कपड़े पहने हुए।
<curious>Pehle junction rule लीजिए।</curious> सोचिए एक भीड़ भरी local train station पर रुकती है। Platform पर उतरने वालों की संख्या train में चढ़ने और बाहर निकलने वालों की संख्या के बराबर होनी चाहिए।
Na कोई ग़ायब होता है, न कोई पैदा। Wire का junction बिलकुल वैसा ही है: वो wires के मिलने की जगह है, कोई tanki नहीं, इसलिए steady state में वहाँ charge जमा नहीं हो सकता।
To per second जितना charge अंदर आता है उतना ही बाहर जाना चाहिए, और यही junction rule है, currents में लिखा हुआ।
Ise ठोस बनाइए। अगर तीन wires पाँच, तीन और दो ampere ला रही हैं, तो जाने वाली wires को कुल दस ampere ले जाना होगा, resistances जैसे भी बाँटें।

sections.title: The loop rule, and why potential behaves like altitude

board_events.text: The loop rule, and why potential behaves like altitude
Imagine walking on hilly trails. You climb some ridges, descend into some valleys, and eventually return to exactly where you started.
No matter how complicated the path, your net change in altitude is zero, because you are back where you began.
Electric potential behaves precisely like altitude: it has a single definite value at every point in the circuit.
This is conservation of energy. Each coulomb gains exactly as much energy from the cells as it loses in the resistors over one full lap.
Treat the whole circuit as a contour map. Cells are escalators lifting charge to higher potential; resistors are slopes down which charge slides.
With just these two rules you can crack any network, however tangled, without ever needing a series or parallel simplification.

segments.text: The second rule is the one that does the heavy lifting in problems, and it becomes obvious once you find the right analogy.
Imagine going for a walk on hilly trails. You set off, climb some ridges, descend into some valleys, wander around, and eventually return to exactly the spot you started from.
No matter how complicated your path was, your net change in altitude is exactly zero, because you are back where you began. That is not a coincidence, it is what returning means.
Electric potential behaves precisely like altitude. It has a single definite value at every point in the circuit, so trace any closed loop and the potential changes must sum to zero.
Written for a circuit, that becomes the sum of the electromotive forces equals the sum of the I R terms around the loop.
<curious>And this one is conservation of energy.</curious> Each coulomb of charge gains exactly as much energy from the cells as it surrenders to the resistors over one full lap.
Hold the contour map picture. Cells are escalators that lift charge to a higher potential. Resistors are slopes down which charge slides, dissipating energy as heat along the way.

With just these two rules, one for traffic at every crossroad and one for altitude on every round trip, you can crack any network however tangled, without ever needing a series or parallel simplification.
Doosra नियम वो है जो problems में असली बोझ उठाता है, और सही उपमा मिलते ही ये साफ़ हो जाता है।
Kalpana कीजिए कि आप पहाड़ी रास्तों पर टहलने निकले हैं। चलते हैं, कुछ चोटियाँ चढ़ते हैं, कुछ घाटियों में उतरते हैं, घूमते हैं, और आख़िर में ठीक उसी जगह लौट आते हैं जहाँ से शुरू किया था।
Raasta चाहे कितना भी उलझा हो, ऊँचाई में आपका net बदलाव बिलकुल zero है, क्योंकि आप वहीं वापस हैं जहाँ से चले थे। ये संयोग नहीं, लौटने का मतलब ही यही है।

<curious>Electric potential बिलकुल ऊँचाई की तरह बर्ताव करता है।</curious> Circuit के हर point पर इसकी एक ही निश्चित value होती है, इसलिए किसी भी closed loop पर चलिए और potential के बदलावों का जोड़ zero होना ही चाहिए।
Circuit के लिए लिखने पर ये बन जाता है electromotive forces का जोड़ बराबर loop के I R terms का जोड़।
Aur ये वाला energy conservation है। हर coulomb charge cells से ठीक उतनी ही energy लेता है जितनी वो एक पूरे चक्कर में resistors को दे देता है।
Contour map वाली तस्वीर पकड़िए। Cells escalators हैं जो charge को ऊँचे potential तक उठाते हैं। Resistors ढलानें हैं जिन पर charge फिसलता है, रास्ते भर heat के रूप में energy खोते हुए।
Sirf इन दो नियमों से, एक हर चौराहे की traffic के लिए और एक हर चक्कर की ऊँचाई के लिए, आप कोई भी network तोड़ सकते हैं चाहे वो कितना भी उलझा हो, बिना कभी series या parallel simplification की ज़रूरत के।

sections.title: Where Kirchhoff's rules need care

board_events.text: Where the rules need care
The junction rule as stated holds in the steady state, when currents are constant and no charge accumulates anywhere.
During the transient charging of a capacitor, charge genuinely does build up on the plates, so that branch needs separate treatment.
In the steady state, no direct current flows through a fully charged capacitor at all.
The loop rule in the form electromotive forces equal $IR$ terms assumes the only potential changes come from cells and resistors.
For alternating current or transient circuits you must add capacitor and inductor terms to the loop equation.
Both rules also need consistent sign bookkeeping. Get the signs right and the algebra does the rest by itself.
Sign chaos is the single biggest source of lost marks in this subtopic, which is why the conventions get a section of their own.

segments.text: Before we formalise anything, it is worth being precise about when these rules hold exactly, because two of the exceptions turn up in later chapters.
The junction rule as we have stated it holds in the steady state, meaning when the currents are constant and no charge is accumulating anywhere in the circuit.
During the transient charging of a capacitor, that condition genuinely fails. Charge really does build up on the plates, so that branch needs separate treatment rather than a naive junction equation.
In the steady state itself the capacitor causes no trouble, because no direct current flows through a fully charged capacitor at all. It is only the transient that needs care.
The loop rule in the form we will use, electromotive forces equal I R terms, assumes the only potential changes around the loop come from cells and resistors.

For alternating current or for transient circuits, that assumption breaks and you must add capacitor and inductor terms to the loop equation. Those come in later chapters, but the structure of the rule stays the same.
<whisper>Both rules also need consistent sign bookkeeping.</whisper> This sounds like a small administrative point and it is not. Get the signs right and the algebra does the rest by itself.
Sign chaos is the single biggest source of lost marks in this entire subtopic, which is exactly why the conventions get a section of their own rather than a passing mention.
Kuch भी औपचारिक करने से पहले ये तय कर लेना ज़रूरी है कि ये नियम ठीक ठीक कब लागू होते हैं, क्योंकि इनमें से दो अपवाद आगे के chapters में आते हैं।
Junction rule जैसा हमने कहा है वो steady state में लागू होता है, यानी जब currents स्थिर हों और circuit में कहीं charge जमा न हो रहा हो।
Capacitor के charge होने के transient के दौरान वो शर्त सचमुच टूट जाती है। Plates पर charge वाक़ई जमा होता है, इसलिए उस branch को सीधे junction equation की जगह अलग तरह से देखना पड़ता है।
<curious>Steady state में capacitor कोई परेशानी नहीं करता</curious>, क्योंकि पूरी तरह charge हो चुके capacitor से direct current बहता ही नहीं। सिर्फ़ transient को ध्यान चाहिए।
Loop rule जिस रूप में हम इस्तेमाल करेंगे, यानी electromotive forces बराबर I R terms, वो मानता है कि loop में potential के बदलाव सिर्फ़ cells और resistors से आते हैं।

Alternating current या transient circuits के लिए वो assumption टूटती है और आपको loop equation में capacitor तथा inductor के terms जोड़ने पड़ते हैं। वो आगे के chapters में आएँगे, लेकिन नियम का ढाँचा वही रहता है।
Dono नियमों को लगातार sign का हिसाब भी चाहिए। ये सुनने में छोटी सी प्रशासनिक बात लगती है और है नहीं। Sign सही कर लीजिए और बाक़ी algebra अपने आप हो जाती है।
Sign की गड़बड़ी इस पूरे subtopic में marks जाने की सबसे बड़ी वजह है, और ठीक इसीलिए conventions को यूँ ही ज़िक्र नहीं, अपना पूरा section मिलता है।

sections.title: The two rules, stated formally

board_events.text: The two rules, stated formally
Based on conservation of charge, with no accumulation at a node in the steady state.
Based on conservation of energy, and on the fact that electric potential is single-valued at every point.
Taking currents toward the junction as positive and away as negative turns the first statement into a plain algebraic sum equal to zero.
For $b$ branches and $n$ nodes, that total exactly matches the $b$ unknown branch currents, so count them before you start.

segments.text: Here are the two rules stated formally, together with the equation count that tells you how much work a problem will actually be.
The junction rule says the currents at a node sum to zero, or equivalently that what flows in equals what flows out.
It rests on conservation of charge, with no accumulation at a node in the steady state, and that is the justification you should write if asked.
The loop rule says the potential changes around any closed loop sum to zero, which rearranges to the sum of the electromotive forces equalling the sum of the I R terms.
It rests on conservation of energy, and on the fact that electric potential has a single definite value at every point in the circuit.

A small technical note on the first rule. Taking currents toward the junction as positive and away from it as negative turns the statement into a plain algebraic sum equal to zero, which is easier to automate.

<curious>Now the practical question: how many equations do you need?</curious> For a network with b branches and n nodes, you get n minus one independent junction equations and b minus n plus one independent loop equations.
Add those together and you get exactly b equations, which matches the b unknown branch currents. Count them before you start, and you will never write too few or waste time on a redundant loop.
Ye रहे दोनों नियम औपचारिक रूप में, साथ में equation की गिनती जो बता देती है कि problem में असल में कितना काम है।
Junction rule कहता है कि node पर currents का जोड़ zero होता है, या बराबरी में, जो अंदर आता है वही बाहर जाता है।
Ye charge conservation पर टिका है, steady state में node पर कुछ जमा न होने के साथ, और पूछे जाने पर यही justification लिखना चाहिए।
Loop rule कहता है कि किसी भी closed loop में potential के बदलावों का जोड़ zero होता है, जो rearrange होकर बनता है electromotive forces का जोड़ बराबर I R terms का जोड़।
Ye energy conservation पर टिका है, और इस बात पर कि circuit के हर point पर electric potential की एक ही निश्चित value होती है।

<curious>Pehle नियम पर एक छोटी तकनीकी बात।</curious> Junction की तरफ़ आते currents को positive और दूर जाते को negative लेने से बयान एक सीधा algebraic जोड़ बराबर zero बन जाता है, जिसे automate करना आसान है।
Ab व्यावहारिक सवाल: कितने equations चाहिए? b branches और n nodes वाले network के लिए आपको n minus one स्वतंत्र junction equations मिलते हैं और b minus n plus one स्वतंत्र loop equations।
Inhe जोड़िए तो ठीक b equations बनते हैं, जो b अनजान branch currents से मेल खाते हैं। शुरू करने से पहले इन्हें गिन लीजिए, और आप न कभी कम equations लिखेंगे न किसी बेकार loop पर time लगाएँगे।

sections.title: Sign conventions, where the marks actually go

board_events.text: Sign conventions, where the marks actually go
Pick a traversal direction for the loop first, and then apply four rules consistently all the way round.
Crossing a resistor along the assumed current gives minus $IR$, because you move from higher to lower potential.
Crossing a resistor against the assumed current gives plus $IR$, because you are climbing back up.
Crossing a source from its negative to its positive terminal gives plus $E$.
Crossing a source from its positive to its negative terminal gives minus $E$.
The source sign depends only on which terminal you enter first. It never depends on the direction of the current.
A negative current in your answer is not a mistake. It means the assumed direction was backwards, so keep the magnitude and flip the arrow.

segments.text: This section is short on formulas and long on discipline, and it is where the marks in this subtopic are genuinely won or lost.
Pick a traversal direction for the loop first, clockwise or anticlockwise, it does not matter which. Then apply four rules consistently all the way round without changing your mind.
First rule. Crossing a resistor along the assumed current direction gives minus I R, because you are moving from higher to lower potential across it.
Second rule. Crossing a resistor against the assumed current gives plus I R, because now you are climbing back up the slope.
Third rule. Crossing a source from its negative terminal to its positive terminal gives plus E, because the source lifts you.
Fourth rule. Crossing a source from positive to negative gives minus E, because you are going down through the escalator.

<whisper>Now the point that catches most students.</whisper> The source sign depends only on which terminal you enter first. It never depends on the direction of the current, and attaching the electromotive force sign to the current is the classic error.

One more thing worth settling now. A negative current in your answer is not a mistake. It simply means the direction you assumed was backwards, so keep the magnitude, flip the arrow, and move on without re-solving anything.
Is section में formulas कम और अनुशासन ज़्यादा है, और इसी जगह इस subtopic के marks सचमुच जीते या हारे जाते हैं।
Pehle loop के लिए एक traversal direction चुनिए, clockwise या anticlockwise, कोई फ़र्क़ नहीं पड़ता। फिर चारों नियम पूरे चक्कर में लगातार लगाइए, बीच में इरादा बदले बिना।
Pehla नियम। Assumed current की दिशा में resistor पार करने पर minus I R आता है, क्योंकि आप उस पर ज़्यादा से कम potential की तरफ़ जा रहे हैं।
Doosra नियम। Assumed current के ख़िलाफ़ resistor पार करने पर plus I R आता है, क्योंकि अब आप ढलान पर वापस चढ़ रहे हैं।
<curious>Teesra नियम।</curious> Source को उसके negative terminal से positive terminal की तरफ़ पार करने पर plus E आता है, क्योंकि source आपको ऊपर उठाता है।
Chautha नियम। Source को positive से negative की तरफ़ पार करने पर minus E आता है, क्योंकि आप escalator से नीचे जा रहे हैं।

Ab वो बात जो ज़्यादातर students को पकड़ती है। Source का sign सिर्फ़ इस पर निर्भर है कि आप कौन सा terminal पहले छूते हैं। ये कभी current की दिशा पर निर्भर नहीं करता, और electromotive force के sign को current से जोड़ देना ही classic ग़लती है।
Ek और बात अभी तय कर लीजिए। Answer में negative current कोई ग़लती नहीं है। इसका बस मतलब है कि आपकी मानी हुई दिशा उल्टी थी, इसलिए magnitude रखिए, arrow पलटिए, और बिना कुछ दोबारा हल किए आगे बढ़िए।

sections.title: Derivation: proving both of Kirchhoff's rules

board_events.text: Derivation: proving both rules
For the junction rule, consider any junction in the steady state. Charge is conserved and cannot accumulate at a point.
A junction has no capacity to store charge. That is the physical fact the whole rule rests on.
It is the steady-state assumption of no pile-up that turns a statement about charge into a statement about current.
For the loop rule, the electrostatic field inside the circuit is conservative, so electric potential has a unique value at each point.
Physically: each coulomb is handed exactly as much energy by the cells as it surrenders to the resistors per lap.

segments.text: Both proofs are short, and in each one it is worth identifying which single physical fact is doing the work.
For the junction rule, consider any junction where several wires meet, in the steady state. Charge is conserved and cannot accumulate at a point.
State the reason explicitly: a junction has no capacity to store charge. It is not a capacitor, it is simply a place where wires meet, and that physical fact is what the whole rule rests on.
So in a small time interval, the charge flowing in equals the charge flowing out. Dividing through by that interval converts it into a statement about currents.

<curious>Notice which assumption did the real work.</curious> It is the steady-state condition of no pile-up that turns a statement about charge into a statement about current. Remove that and the rule fails.
For the loop rule, the electrostatic field inside the circuit is conservative, so electric potential has a unique definite value at each point.

Start at any point in a closed loop, traverse the entire loop adding the potential change across each element, and return to the start. Since you arrive back at the same point with the same potential, the net change must vanish.

Split those changes into energy gained from sources and energy lost across resistors, and the rule takes its working form. Physically: each coulomb is handed exactly as much energy by the cells as it surrenders to the resistors per lap.
Dono प्रमाण छोटे हैं, और हर एक में ये पहचानना ज़रूरी है कि कौन सा एक physical तथ्य असली काम कर रहा है।
Junction rule के लिए steady state में कोई भी ऐसा junction लीजिए जहाँ कई wires मिलती हैं। Charge conserve होता है और किसी एक point पर जमा नहीं हो सकता।
Vajah साफ़ कहिए: junction में charge रखने की कोई क्षमता ही नहीं। वो capacitor नहीं है, बस wires के मिलने की जगह है, और यही physical तथ्य पूरे नियम की नींव है।
To एक छोटे time interval में अंदर आता charge बाहर जाते charge के बराबर है। उस interval से divide करने पर ये currents की बात बन जाती है।
Dhyan दीजिए किस assumption ने असली काम किया। Steady state की वो शर्त कि कुछ जमा नहीं होता, वही charge की बात को current की बात में बदलती है। उसे हटा दीजिए और नियम टूट जाता है।
<curious>Loop rule के लिए</curious>, circuit के अंदर का electrostatic field conservative होता है, इसलिए electric potential की हर point पर एक ही निश्चित value होती है।

Closed loop में कहीं से भी शुरू कीजिए, पूरे loop पर चलते हुए हर element का potential बदलाव जोड़िए, और शुरुआत पर लौट आइए। चूँकि आप उसी point पर उसी potential के साथ लौटते हैं, net बदलाव ग़ायब होना ही चाहिए।

Un बदलावों को sources से मिली energy और resistors में खोई energy में बाँटिए, और नियम अपना काम का रूप ले लेता है। Physically: हर coulomb को cells ठीक उतनी energy देते हैं जितनी वो एक चक्कर में resistors को दे देता है।

board_events.text: The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows zero deflection, meaning $I_g = 0$.
At balance no current diverts into the galvanometer, so the same $I_1$ flows through $P$ and $Q$, and the same $I_2$ through $R$ and $S$.

board_events.latex: -I_1 P - I_g G + I_2 R = 0 \xrightarrow{\ I_g = 0\ } I_1 P = I_2 R
-I_1 Q + I_2 S + I_g G = 0 \xrightarrow{\ I_g = 0\ } I_1 Q = I_2 S

segments.text: This is the derivation C B S E asks for almost every year, and it is four steps once the currents at balance are correctly identified.
Four resistances P, Q, R and S are arranged in a diamond. A cell drives current across one diagonal, and a sensitive galvanometer bridges the other diagonal.
Label the corners before writing anything: A on the left, C on the right, B at the top and D at the bottom, with P and Q on the upper path and R and S on the lower.
The bridge is called balanced when the galvanometer shows zero deflection, meaning the current through it is zero. That is the condition we impose.
Step one is about the currents. With no current diverting into the galvanometer at B, the same current flows through P and Q. Likewise the same second current flows through R and S.
Step two: apply the loop rule to the upper-left triangle, and setting the galvanometer current to zero collapses it to a clean relation between the first pair.
Step three: apply the loop rule to the lower-right triangle in the same way, which gives the matching relation for the second pair.
<curious>Step four is where the magic happens.</curious> Divide one relation by the other, and the unknown branch currents cancel completely, leaving P over Q equals R over S.

sections.title: Why the bridge is a null method

board_events.text: Why the bridge is a null method
The balance condition contains only the four resistances. The battery electromotive force has dropped out entirely.
So has the galvanometer resistance. Neither appears anywhere in the condition.
This is why the bridge is called a null method: it compares resistances without needing to know the source voltage at all.
That makes it far more accurate than reading a meter on a deflecting scale, where the reading depends on the meter's own calibration.
At balance the two midpoints B and D sit at exactly equal potential, which is the same statement in a different language.
Every instrument in the next subtopic, the meter bridge and the potentiometer alike, is built on this one idea.

segments.text: The balance condition itself is easy to remember. What deserves attention is what is missing from it, because that absence is the whole reason the bridge matters.
The condition is P over Q equals R over S, equivalently the cross products P S and Q R being equal.
Now look at what does not appear. The battery electromotive force has dropped out entirely. It cancelled during the division, and it plays no part in the answer.
Neither does the galvanometer resistance appear. The instrument you use to detect balance does not affect where the balance point is.

<curious>This is why the bridge is called a null method.</curious> It compares resistances without needing to know the source voltage at all, so an unstable or unknown battery does not corrupt the measurement.
That makes it far more accurate than reading a meter on a deflecting scale, where the reading depends on the meter's own calibration, its zero error, and the supply voltage all at once.
There is a second way to say the same thing. At balance the two midpoints of the bridge sit at exactly equal potential, which is why no current flows between them.
Hold onto this idea, because every instrument in the next subtopic is built on it. The meter bridge and the potentiometer are both null methods, and both inherit this accuracy for the same reason.
Balance की शर्त ख़ुद याद रखना आसान है। ध्यान उस चीज़ पर देना चाहिए जो इसमें से ग़ायब है, क्योंकि वही ग़ैरहाज़िरी पूरी वजह है कि bridge मायने रखता है।
Shart है P over Q बराबर R over S, या बराबरी में cross products P S और Q R का बराबर होना।
Ab देखिए क्या नहीं आया। Battery का electromotive force पूरी तरह निकल गया। वो भाग करते समय कट गया, और answer में उसकी कोई भूमिका नहीं।
Galvanometer की resistance भी नहीं आई। जिस उपकरण से आप balance पकड़ते हैं वो balance point कहाँ है इस पर असर नहीं डालता।
Isiliye bridge को null method कहते हैं। ये resistances की तुलना करता है बिना source voltage जाने, इसलिए कोई अस्थिर या अनजान battery measurement को ख़राब नहीं करती।
<curious>Isse ये deflecting scale पर meter पढ़ने से कहीं ज़्यादा सटीक हो जाता है</curious>, जहाँ reading meter की अपनी calibration, उसकी zero error, और supply voltage तीनों पर एक साथ निर्भर करती है।
Ek ही बात कहने का दूसरा तरीक़ा भी है। Balance पर bridge के दोनों midpoints बिलकुल barabar potential पर बैठते हैं, इसीलिए उनके बीच कोई current नहीं बहता।
Is विचार को पकड़े रखिए, क्योंकि अगले subtopic का हर उपकरण इसी पर बना है। Meter bridge और potentiometer दोनों null methods हैं, और दोनों को यही सटीकता इसी वजह से मिलती है।

board_events.text: Let $I_1$ rise through the left branch and $I_2$ through the right. By the junction rule the middle resistor carries $I_1 + I_2$.
The minus sign means the four volt cell is actually being charged by the stronger eight volt cell.

segments.text: The first worked example is at C B S E board level, and it is the standard two-loop problem that every board paper contains in some form.
The left branch has an eight volt cell in series with two ohm. The right branch has a four volt cell with two ohm. A four ohm resistor bridges the two nodes.
Draw it and assign currents before writing any equation. That order matters, because the equations depend on what you assumed.
Let the first current rise through the left branch and the second rise through the right branch. By the junction rule, the middle resistor then carries their sum flowing downward.
Now write the loop rule for the left loop, which contains the eight volt cell, its two ohm, and the shared four ohm resistor.
Do the same for the right loop, containing the four volt cell, its two ohm, and the same shared resistor.
Solving the pair simultaneously gives one point six amperes in the first branch and minus zero point four amperes in the second, so the shared resistor carries one point two amperes.

<curious>Do not panic at that minus sign.</curious> It tells you the real direction is opposite to what you assumed, and physically it means the four volt cell is actually being charged by the stronger eight volt cell.
Pehla worked example C B S E board level का है, और ये वही standard two-loop problem है जो हर board के paper में किसी न किसी रूप में होती है।
Baayin branch में आठ volt का cell दो ohm के series में है। Daayin branch में चार volt का cell दो ohm के साथ। Ek चार ohm का resistor दोनों nodes को जोड़ता है।
Koi equation लिखने से पहले इसे बनाइए और currents तय कीजिए। ये क्रम मायने रखता है, क्योंकि equations इसी पर निर्भर हैं कि आपने क्या माना।
Maan लीजिए पहला current बाईं branch में ऊपर चढ़ता है और दूसरा दाईं branch में। Junction rule से बीच वाला resistor उनका जोड़ नीचे की तरफ़ ले जाता है।
<curious>Ab बाएँ loop के लिए loop rule लिखिए</curious>, जिसमें आठ volt का cell, उसका दो ohm, और साझा चार ohm का resistor है।
Wahi दाएँ loop के लिए कीजिए, जिसमें चार volt का cell, उसका दो ohm, और वही साझा resistor है।
Dono को एक साथ हल करने पर पहली branch में एक point छह ampere और दूसरी में minus zero point चार ampere मिलते हैं, इसलिए साझा resistor एक point दो ampere ले जाता है।
Us minus sign से घबराइए मत। वो बता रहा है कि असली दिशा आपकी मानी हुई से उल्टी है, और physically इसका मतलब है कि चार volt वाला cell असल में ताक़तवर आठ volt वाले से charge हो रहा है।

board_events.text: The ratios are equal, so the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer branch carries no current at all. Erase it.

segments.text: The second worked example is a N E E T speed trap, and it is entirely a test of whether you check before you calculate.
A bridge has P equal to ten ohm, Q twenty, R fifteen and S thirty, with a galvanometer across the bridge diagonal and a six volt battery across the supply diagonal. Find the equivalent resistance.

<chuckle>Here is where the minutes go.</chuckle> Students dive into Kirchhoff with five resistors and three unknown currents, or worse, they try to fold the galvanometer arm into a series-parallel reduction.
The fast move is to always check balance first. Compute the two ratios: ten over twenty is one half, and fifteen over thirty is also one half.
They are equal, so the bridge is balanced, the galvanometer current is zero, and that branch carries no current whatsoever.
So erase it. A branch carrying no current can be removed without changing anything, and what remains is a network you can reduce in one line.
What remains is P plus Q in series, which is thirty ohm, in parallel with R plus S in series, which is forty five ohm.

Product over sum gives one thousand three hundred fifty over seventy five, which is eighteen ohm. And notice the six volt value never entered the answer at all, because equivalent resistance never depends on the supply.
Doosra worked example N E E T का speed trap है, और ये पूरी तरह इस बात की जाँच है कि आप calculate करने से पहले check करते हैं या नहीं।
Ek bridge में P है दस ohm, Q बीस, R पंद्रह और S तीस, bridge के diagonal पर galvanometer और supply के diagonal पर छह volt की battery। Equivalent resistance निकालिए।

Ye रही वो जगह जहाँ मिनट जाते हैं। Students पाँच resistors और तीन अनजान currents के साथ Kirchhoff में कूद पड़ते हैं, या उससे भी बुरा, galvanometer वाली arm को series-parallel reduction में घुसाने की कोशिश करते हैं।
<curious>Tez चाल है हमेशा पहले balance जाँचना।</curious> दोनों ratios निकालिए: दस बटा बीस है आधा, और पंद्रह बटा तीस भी आधा।
Ye barabar हैं, इसलिए bridge balanced है, galvanometer का current zero है, और उस branch में कोई current है ही नहीं।
To उसे मिटा दीजिए। जिस branch में current नहीं बहता उसे हटाने से कुछ नहीं बदलता, और जो बचता है वो एक line में reduce हो जाता है।
Jo बचता है वो है P plus Q series में, यानी तीस ohm, जो R plus S series में यानी पैंतालीस ohm के parallel में है।
Product over sum देता है तेरह सौ पचास बटा पचहत्तर, यानी अठारह ohm। और ध्यान दीजिए छह volt की value answer में आई ही नहीं, क्योंकि equivalent resistance supply पर कभी निर्भर नहीं करती।

sections.title: Worked example: Kirchhoff with a power balance check

board_events.text: Worked example, J E E Main: Kirchhoff with a power check
An eight volt cell with one ohm and a seven volt cell with one ohm drive current through a common two ohm resistor between nodes A and B.
Now verify by energy. The power delivered by the sources must equal the power dissipated in the resistors.

segments.text: The third worked example is at J E E Main level, and its real lesson is the check at the end rather than the solution itself.
An eight volt cell with one ohm and a seven volt cell with one ohm drive current through a common two ohm resistor between nodes A and B.
Set it up exactly as before. Currents rise in the two cell branches, and the middle resistor carries their sum, which gives the first loop equation.
The right loop gives the second equation, and the two come out unusually clean with small integer coefficients.
Solving them by adding and subtracting gives two amperes in the first branch, one ampere in the second, and three amperes through the shared resistor.

<curious>Now the part worth learning.</curious> Verify by energy conservation. The power delivered by the sources must equal the power dissipated in the resistors, and if it does not, you have a sign or arithmetic error hiding.
The sources deliver eight times two plus seven times one, which is twenty three watt in total.

The resistors dissipate current squared times resistance in each: four watt in the first, one watt in the second, and eighteen watt in the shared two ohm. That also totals twenty three watt. The perfect match is the loop rule showing up as a number.
Teesra worked example J E E Main level का है, और इसका असली सबक़ solution नहीं बल्कि आख़िर की जाँच है।
Ek आठ volt का cell एक ohm के साथ और एक सात volt का cell एक ohm के साथ, nodes A और B के बीच के साझा दो ohm resistor से current चला रहे हैं।
<curious>Ise बिलकुल पहले की तरह सजाइए।</curious> दोनों cell branches में currents ऊपर चढ़ते हैं, और बीच वाला resistor उनका जोड़ ले जाता है, जिससे पहला loop equation मिलता है।
Daayan loop दूसरा equation देता है, और दोनों असामान्य रूप से साफ़ आते हैं, छोटे पूर्णांक coefficients के साथ।
Inhe जोड़कर और घटाकर हल करने पर पहली branch में दो ampere, दूसरी में एक ampere, और साझा resistor में तीन ampere मिलते हैं।
Ab वो हिस्सा जो सीखने लायक़ है। Energy conservation से जाँचिए। Sources से मिली power resistors में खपी power के बराबर होनी चाहिए, और अगर नहीं है तो कहीं sign या arithmetic की ग़लती छिपी है।
Sources देते हैं आठ into दो plus सात into एक, यानी कुल तेइस watt।

Resistors में current squared into resistance खपती है: पहले में चार watt, दूसरे में एक watt, और साझा दो ohm में अठारह watt। इनका जोड़ भी तेइस watt है। ये पूरा मेल loop rule का number बनकर सामने आना है।

sections.title: Worked example: an unbalanced bridge

board_events.text: Worked example, J E E Advanced: an unbalanced bridge
Arms are $AB = R$, $BC = 2R$, $AD = 2R$, $DC = R$, with a bridge arm $BD = R$. Find the equivalent resistance between A and C.
Check balance first: $R/2R$ is one half but $2R/R$ is two, so the bridge is unbalanced and the bridge arm does carry current.
Let $i_1$ enter AB, $i_2$ enter AD, and $i_g$ flow from B to D. Then BC carries $i_1 - i_g$ and DC carries $i_2 + i_g$.

segments.text: The final worked example for this subtopic is at J E E Advanced level, and it is the case where the shortcut deliberately fails.
The arms are A B equal to R, B C two R, A D two R, and D C equal to R, with a bridge arm B D equal to R. Find the equivalent resistance between A and C.
Check balance first, as always. R over two R is one half, but two R over R is two. The ratios differ, so the bridge is unbalanced and its arm carries current.
Now assign currents carefully. The first enters A B, the second enters A D, and a bridge current flows from B to D. The junction rule at B and D then fixes the remaining two arms.
Write the loop rule for the first triangle, A to B to D and back to A, which gives the bridge current in terms of the other two.
Write it for the second triangle, B to C to D and back to B, which gives a second independent relation.
Substituting the first into the second lets you express everything in terms of a single branch current, and the total entering current works out as five thirds of it.

<curious>Finish with the potential difference.</curious> Going A to B to C gives seven thirds i one R, and dividing by the total current gives one point four R. The other path gives the identical value, as the loop rule guarantees.
Is subtopic का आख़िरी worked example J E E Advanced level का है, और ये वो मामला है जहाँ shortcut जान बूझकर नाकाम रहता है।
Arms हैं A B बराबर R, B C बराबर दो R, A D बराबर दो R, और D C बराबर R, और bridge arm B D बराबर R। A और C के बीच equivalent resistance निकालिए।
Pehle balance जाँचिए, जैसा हमेशा करना चाहिए। R बटा दो R है आधा, लेकिन दो R बटा R है दो। Ratios अलग हैं, इसलिए bridge unbalanced है और bridge arm में सचमुच current बहता है।
Ab currents ध्यान से तय कीजिए। पहला current A B में जाए, दूसरा A D में, और एक bridge current B से D की तरफ़ बहे। B और D पर junction rule लगाने से बाक़ी दो arms तय हो जाती हैं।
<curious>Pehle triangle के लिए loop rule लिखिए</curious>, A से B से D और वापस A, जिससे bridge current बाक़ी दोनों के रूप में मिल जाता है।
Doosre triangle के लिए लिखिए, B से C से D और वापस B, जिससे दूसरा स्वतंत्र relation मिलता है।
Pehle को दूसरे में रखने पर सब कुछ एक ही branch current के रूप में आ जाता है, और अंदर आता कुल current उसका पाँच बटा तीन निकलता है।

Potential difference निकालकर ख़त्म कीजिए। A से B से C जाने पर मिलता है सात बटा तीन i one R, और कुल current से divide करने पर equivalent resistance one point four R आती है। दूसरे रास्ते से निकालने पर बिलकुल वही value मिलती है, जैसा loop rule guarantee करता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for Kirchhoff's laws

board_events.text: Pitfalls that cost marks, and the pro-tips that save time
Sign chaos in the loop rule is the number one error, with no close competition.
Resistor sign depends on whether you move with or against the current. Source sign depends only on which terminal you enter first.
Panicking over a negative current. It simply means your assumed direction was backwards. Keep the magnitude, flip the arrow, never re-solve.
Brute-forcing a balanced bridge. A two-second ratio check would have collapsed the whole problem.
Using a loop that is not independent, so its equation is just a combination of the others and tells you nothing new.
Count your independent equations before you start, then finish with the power check: source power must equal total dissipated power.

segments.text: Let us close this subtopic with the four errors that cost marks and the two habits that catch nearly all of them.
Sign chaos in the loop rule is the number one error here, with no close competition at all.

So fix the two rules firmly and separately. The resistor sign depends on whether you move with or against the assumed current. The source sign depends only on which terminal you enter first, never on the current.
The second is panicking over a negative current. It is not a mistake. It simply means your assumed direction was backwards, so keep the magnitude, flip the arrow, and never re-solve the whole system.
The third is brute-forcing a balanced bridge. Launching into five-resistor Kirchhoff wastes minutes that a two-second ratio check would have saved entirely.
The fourth is using a loop that is not independent, so its equation is just a combination of the ones you already have and tells you nothing new.

<excited>That is where the counting rule earns its keep.</excited> Independent loops equal branches minus nodes plus one, so count your equations before you start and you will know exactly how many loops to write.

And finish every Kirchhoff problem with the power check. Total power from the sources must equal the total dissipated in the resistors. If they do not match, a sign or arithmetic slip is hiding somewhere in your currents.
Is subtopic को उन चार ग़लतियों के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो marks काटती हैं, और उन दो आदतों के साथ जो लगभग सब पकड़ लेती हैं।
Loop rule में sign की गड़बड़ी यहाँ की नंबर एक ग़लती है, और कोई इसके आसपास भी नहीं।

To दोनों नियम अलग अलग और पक्के कर लीजिए। Resistor का sign इस पर है कि आप assumed current के साथ जा रहे हैं या ख़िलाफ़। Source का sign सिर्फ़ इस पर कि आप कौन सा terminal पहले छूते हैं, current पर कभी नहीं।
Doosri है negative current देखकर घबराना। वो ग़लती नहीं है। उसका बस मतलब है कि आपकी मानी हुई दिशा उल्टी थी, इसलिए magnitude रखिए, arrow पलटिए, और पूरा system दोबारा कभी मत हल कीजिए।
Teesri है balanced bridge पर ज़बरदस्ती करना। पाँच resistor वाले Kirchhoff में कूदना उन मिनटों को बर्बाद करता है जो दो second का ratio check पूरी तरह बचा लेता।
<curious>Chauthi है ऐसा loop इस्तेमाल करना जो स्वतंत्र नहीं है</curious>, जिसका equation पहले वालों का ही जोड़ घटाव है और कुछ नया बताता ही नहीं।
Wahin गिनती वाला नियम अपनी क़ीमत वसूल करता है। Independent loops बराबर branches minus nodes plus one, इसलिए शुरू करने से पहले equations गिन लीजिए और आपको ठीक ठीक पता होगा कि कितने loops लिखने हैं।

Aur हर Kirchhoff problem को power check से ख़त्म कीजिए। Sources से मिली कुल power resistors में खपी कुल power के बराबर होनी चाहिए। अगर मेल न खाएँ तो आपके currents में कहीं sign या arithmetic की चूक छिपी है।

sections.title: Measure by balancing, not by deflecting

board_events.text: Measure by balancing, not by deflecting
How do you measure a resistance you cannot see inside, or the true voltage of a cell without disturbing it?
Every meter you clip on steals a little current, and that theft changes the very quantity you are trying to read.
The idea behind every instrument here is to arrange the circuit so that at the moment of measurement, no current flows through the detector at all.
A measurement made at zero current is a measurement that does not disturb what it measures. This is the null method.
The Wheatstone bridge is the parent idea: a see-saw for potentials, where two ladders of resistors are compared at their midpoints.
Imagine two identical staircases side by side. Lay a plank between two people standing on them, and if it stays level, they are at equal height.
The bridge weighs an unknown resistance against known ones exactly as a balance scale weighs an unknown mass against standard weights.

segments.text: The final subtopic turns everything we have built into instruments, and it opens with a genuine measurement problem.
How do you measure a resistance you cannot see inside, or the true voltage of a cell without disturbing it?
You could clip on an ohmmeter or a voltmeter, but every such meter steals a little current from the circuit, and that theft changes the very quantity you are trying to read.
The clever idea behind every instrument in this subtopic is to sidestep the problem entirely. Arrange the circuit so that at the moment of measurement, no current flows through the detector at all.
<curious>Say that back to yourself, because it is the whole subtopic.</curious> A measurement made at zero current is a measurement that does not disturb what it measures. That is the null method.
The Wheatstone bridge is the parent idea. Think of it as a see-saw for potentials: a battery drives current down two parallel ladders of resistors, and a galvanometer bridges their midpoints.
Imagine two identical staircases side by side, and you want to know whether two people standing on them are at the same height. Lay a level plank between them, and if it stays horizontal, they match.

You never needed to know how tall the staircases were or how the people climbed. The bridge weighs an unknown resistance against known ones exactly as a balance scale weighs an unknown mass against standard weights.
Aakhri subtopic अब तक बनाई गई हर चीज़ को उपकरणों में बदल देता है, और ये एक असली measurement की समस्या से शुरू होता है।
<curious>Aap ऐसी resistance कैसे मापेंगे जिसके अंदर आप देख नहीं सकते</curious>, या cell का असली voltage बिना उसे छेड़े कैसे निकालेंगे?
Aap कोई ohmmeter या voltmeter लगा सकते हैं, लेकिन हर ऐसा meter circuit से थोड़ा current चुरा लेता है, और वही चोरी उस चीज़ को बदल देती है जिसे आप मापना चाहते हैं।
Is subtopic के हर उपकरण के पीछे एक होशियार सोच है जो समस्या को पूरी तरह किनारे कर देती है। Circuit को ऐसे सजाइए कि measurement के पल detector में current बहे ही नहीं।
Ise ख़ुद को दोहराइए, क्योंकि यही पूरा subtopic है। Zero current पर की गई measurement वो है जो मापी जा रही चीज़ को छेड़ती नहीं। यही null method है।
Wheatstone bridge मूल सोच है। इसे potentials का see-saw समझिए: एक battery दो parallel resistor ladders में current चलाती है, और एक galvanometer उनके midpoints को जोड़ता है।
Do एक जैसी सीढ़ियाँ साथ साथ सोचिए, और आपको जानना है कि उन पर खड़े दो लोग एक ही ऊँचाई पर हैं या नहीं। बीच में एक सीधा पटरा रखिए, और अगर वो क्षैतिज रहे तो दोनों बराबर हैं।

Aapko कभी ये जानने की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ी कि सीढ़ियाँ कितनी ऊँची थीं या लोग कैसे चढ़े। Bridge अनजान resistance को जानी हुई resistances के सामने ठीक वैसे तौलता है जैसे तराज़ू अनजान द्रव्यमान को मानक बाटों के सामने तौलता है।

sections.title: The meter bridge, and the potentiometer's ramp

board_events.text: The meter bridge, and the potentiometer's ramp
The meter bridge is the Wheatstone bridge made practical and cheap: two of its resistor arms are replaced by a single uniform one-metre wire.
A sliding contact, the jockey, lets you tune the ratio continuously until the galvanometer nulls. Slide, find zero, read the length.
The potentiometer takes the null idea to its most elegant extreme. A steady current through a long uniform wire creates a perfectly even potential ramp.

board_events.text: So much potential drop per centimetre, the same everywhere along the wire.
To measure an electromotive force, tap the ramp at the exact point where it pushes back equally hard against the cell, so that no current flows.
At that balance point the cell is not being loaded at all, so what you read is its true electromotive force.
Not the diminished terminal voltage that a voltmeter would report, but the electromotive force itself.

segments.text: Two instruments descend from the bridge, and each makes the null idea more practical than the last.
The meter bridge is simply the Wheatstone bridge made practical and cheap. Two of its resistor arms are replaced by a single uniform one-metre wire.

A sliding contact called the jockey then lets you tune the ratio continuously instead of swapping resistors. Slide it along, listen for the galvanometer to read zero, and read off the length. That is the whole measurement.
The potentiometer takes the null idea to its most elegant extreme. A steady current through a long uniform wire creates a perfectly even potential ramp along its length.
Look at the two loops. The primary loop, with a driver cell and a rheostat, sets up that ramp. The secondary loop holds the cell under test and the galvanometer that detects balance.
The ramp is the key. There is so much potential drop per centimetre, and crucially the same amount everywhere along the wire, which is what makes length a reliable measure of potential.

<curious>Now here is the measurement.</curious> To find an electromotive force, tap the ramp at the exact point where it pushes back equally hard against the cell, so that no current flows in the secondary loop.
At that balance point the cell is not being loaded at all, because no current is flowing out of it.
So what you read is its true electromotive force, not the diminished terminal voltage that a voltmeter would have reported.
Bridge से दो उपकरण निकलते हैं, और हर एक null वाली सोच को पिछले से ज़्यादा व्यावहारिक बनाता है।
Meter bridge बस Wheatstone bridge का व्यावहारिक और सस्ता रूप है। इसके दो resistor arms की जगह एक uniform एक metre का तार लगा दिया जाता है।
Phir jockey नाम का एक सरकता contact आपको resistors बदलने की जगह ratio लगातार tune करने देता है। उसे सरकाइए, galvanometer के zero होने का इंतज़ार कीजिए, और लंबाई पढ़ लीजिए। यही पूरी measurement है।
Potentiometer null वाली सोच को उसकी सबसे ख़ूबसूरत हद तक ले जाता है। एक लंबे uniform तार में steady current उसकी पूरी लंबाई पर एक बिलकुल बराबर potential ramp बना देता है।
<curious>Dono loops देखिए।</curious> Primary loop, जिसमें driver cell और rheostat हैं, वो ramp बनाता है। Secondary loop में test वाला cell और balance पकड़ने वाला galvanometer होते हैं।
Ramp ही असली बात है। Per centimetre इतना potential गिरता है, और सबसे ज़रूरी बात, तार की हर जगह उतना ही, और यही लंबाई को potential का भरोसेमंद माप बनाता है।
Ab ये रही measurement। Electromotive force निकालने के लिए ramp को ठीक उस point पर छूइए जहाँ वो cell को उतनी ही ज़ोर से वापस धकेले, ताकि secondary loop में current बहे ही नहीं।
Us balance point पर cell पर कोई load है ही नहीं, क्योंकि उसमें से कोई current बाहर नहीं जा रहा।
Isliye आप जो पढ़ते हैं वो उसका असली electromotive force है, वो घटा हुआ terminal voltage नहीं जो voltmeter बताता।

sections.title: What these instruments assume

board_events.text: What these instruments assume
The bridge balance condition holds only in the steady state, with all four arms purely resistive.
The meter-bridge relation assumes a perfectly uniform wire of constant cross-section along its whole length.
Non-uniformity and contact resistances at the ends cause end errors, which need a correction in careful work.
The potentiometer's linearity requires both a uniform wire and a constant primary current.
If the driver cell runs down partway through the experiment, the calibration drifts and every reading after that is wrong.
A potentiometer can only balance an electromotive force smaller than the total potential drop across its wire.
The driver must be the stronger source, or there is simply no null point anywhere on the wire to find.

segments.text: Before the formulas, these instruments come with real experimental caveats, and two of them are standard exam questions in their own right.
The bridge balance condition holds only in the steady state, and only with all four arms purely resistive. Introduce a capacitor or an inductor and the condition no longer applies.
The meter-bridge relation assumes a perfectly uniform wire of constant cross-section along its whole length. That is what allows resistance to be replaced by length.
In a real apparatus that assumption is imperfect. Non-uniformity in the wire and contact resistances at the ends produce what are called end errors, which need a correction in careful work.
The potentiometer's beautiful linearity requires two things at once: a uniform wire, and a constant primary current flowing through it.

<whisper>The second is the one that bites in the lab.</whisper> If the driver cell runs down partway through the experiment, the potential gradient drifts, and every reading taken after that point is wrong.
There is one more limitation that decides whether the experiment works at all. A potentiometer can only balance an electromotive force smaller than the total potential drop across its wire.
So the driver must be the stronger source. If the cell under test exceeds the total drop, the galvanometer never nulls and there is simply no balance point anywhere on the wire to find.
Formulas से पहले, इन उपकरणों के साथ असली प्रायोगिक चेतावनियाँ आती हैं, और उनमें से दो अपने आप में standard exam के सवाल हैं।
<curious>Bridge की balance की शर्त सिर्फ़ steady state में लागू होती है</curious>, और तभी जब चारों arms पूरी तरह resistive हों। Ek capacitor या inductor डालिए और शर्त लागू नहीं रहती।
Meter-bridge वाला relation मानता है कि तार पूरी लंबाई में बिलकुल uniform है और उसका cross-section स्थिर है। यही चीज़ resistance की जगह लंबाई रखने देती है।
Asli उपकरण में वो assumption अधूरी होती है। तार में non-uniformity और सिरों पर contact resistances मिलकर वो पैदा करती हैं जिन्हें end errors कहते हैं, और सावधान काम में उनका सुधार करना पड़ता है।
Potentiometer की ख़ूबसूरत linearity को दो चीज़ें एक साथ चाहिए: uniform तार, और उसमें बहता स्थिर primary current।
Doosri वाली ही lab में काटती है। अगर driver cell experiment के बीच में ही ख़त्म होने लगे, तो potential gradient खिसक जाता है, और उस point के बाद ली गई हर reading ग़लत है।
Ek और limitation है जो तय करती है कि experiment चलेगा भी या नहीं। Potentiometer सिर्फ़ उस electromotive force को balance कर सकता है जो उसके तार पर के कुल potential drop से छोटी हो।
To driver को ज़्यादा ताक़तवर source होना चाहिए। अगर test वाला cell कुल drop से बड़ा हो, तो galvanometer कभी null नहीं होगा और तार पर कहीं कोई balance point मिलेगा ही नहीं।

sections.title: Balance condition and the meter bridge relation

board_events.text: Balance condition and the meter bridge relation
This is the Wheatstone condition we derived under Kirchhoff's laws, and every instrument here inherits it.
Known resistance $R$ in one gap, unknown $X$ in the other, with balance length $l$ in centimetres measured from the end on the $R$ side.
Read $l$ from the wrong end and the digits invert your answer silently, so fix the convention before you start.
Bridge sensitivity is greatest when the null sits near the middle of the wire, around fifty centimetres.
So choose the known resistance to be comparable to the unknown, which centres the balance point where a small jockey movement gives the largest kick.

segments.text: Here is the first formula block, carrying the balance condition and the meter bridge relation that follows from it.
The Wheatstone condition is the one we derived under Kirchhoff's laws: the ratio of the first pair equals the ratio of the second, and the galvanometer current is zero.
Every instrument in this subtopic inherits that condition, which is why deriving it once was worth the effort.
For the meter bridge, with a known resistance in one gap and the unknown in the other, the two wire arms are proportional to their lengths, giving the relation shown.
Be precise about that length. It is measured in centimetres from the end on the side of the known resistance, on a wire one hundred centimetres long.

<whisper>And here is the silent error.</whisper> Read the length from the wrong end and your answer inverts without any warning sign, so fix the convention before you start rather than halfway through.
One practical point that appears as a one-mark question. Bridge sensitivity is greatest when the null sits near the middle of the wire, around fifty centimetres.

So in the lab you deliberately choose the known resistance to be comparable to the unknown, which centres the balance point. There a small jockey movement produces the largest galvanometer kick, and the reading is sharpest.
Ye पहला formula हिस्सा है, जिसमें balance की शर्त और उससे निकलने वाला meter bridge का relation है।
<curious>Wheatstone की शर्त वही है जो हमने Kirchhoff के नियमों में derive की थी</curious>: पहली जोड़ी का ratio बराबर दूसरी जोड़ी का ratio, और galvanometer का current zero।
Is subtopic का हर उपकरण उसी शर्त को विरासत में लेता है, इसीलिए उसे एक बार derive करना मेहनत के लायक़ था।
Meter bridge के लिए, एक gap में known resistance और दूसरे में unknown हो, तो तार के दोनों arms अपनी लंबाइयों के अनुपात में होते हैं, जिससे दिखाया गया relation मिलता है।
Us लंबाई के बारे में सटीक रहिए। ये centimetre में उस सिरे से नापी जाती है जिस तरफ़ known resistance है, और तार सौ centimetre लंबा है।
Aur ये रही चुपचाप होने वाली ग़लती। लंबाई ग़लत सिरे से पढ़िए और आपका answer बिना किसी चेतावनी के उलट जाता है, इसलिए convention बीच में नहीं, शुरू करने से पहले तय कीजिए।
Ek व्यावहारिक बात जो एक mark के सवाल की तरह आती है। Bridge की sensitivity तब सबसे ज़्यादा होती है जब null तार के बीच के पास हो, लगभग पचास centimetre पर।

Isliye lab में आप जान बूझकर known resistance को unknown के क़रीब चुनते हैं, जिससे balance point बीच में आ जाता है। वहाँ jockey की ज़रा सी हरकत सबसे बड़ा galvanometer का झटका देती है, और reading सबसे तीखी होती है।

sections.title: Potential gradient and the ratio results

board_events.text: Potential gradient and the ratio results
The potential gradient is the drop per unit length. Its S I unit is volt per metre, with the same dimensions as electric field.
Comparing two electromotive forces reduces to a pure ratio of their two balance lengths, and the gradient cancels completely.
Here $l_1$ is the balance length for the cell alone and $l_2$ the shorter length once a shunt resistance $R$ is connected across it.
In every ratio question the gradient cancels, so never compute $k$ unless the question asks for an absolute voltage.

board_events.latex: E_1 + E_2 = kl_s, \qquad E_1 - E_2 = kl_d \implies \frac{E_1}{E_2} = \frac{l_s + l_d}{l_s - l_d}

segments.text: The second formula block covers the potentiometer, and one observation about it will save you more time than anything else in this subtopic.
The potential gradient is the total drop across the wire divided by its length, and the drop across any length from the start is simply the gradient times that length.
Its S I unit is volt per metre, which carries the same dimensions as electric field, and that is not a coincidence since both are potential per unit distance.
Comparing two electromotive forces then reduces to a pure ratio of their two balance lengths.
Notice what happened there. The gradient cancelled completely, so you never needed to know the primary current or the wire resistance at all.
The internal resistance result works the same way, needing only two lengths and one known shunt resistance.

<whisper>Here l one is the balance length for the cell alone</whisper>, drawing no current, and l two is the shorter length once a shunt resistance is connected across the cell and it starts delivering current.
So the rule to carry into the exam is this: in every ratio question the gradient cancels. Never compute k unless an absolute voltage is asked for.
The sum-and-difference result on the board is the same principle applied twice, once with the cells aiding and once with them opposing.
Doosra formula हिस्सा potentiometer को cover करता है, और इसके बारे में एक बात इस subtopic की किसी भी और चीज़ से ज़्यादा time बचाएगी।
Potential gradient तार पर का कुल drop divided by उसकी लंबाई है, और शुरू से किसी भी लंबाई तक का drop बस gradient into वो लंबाई है।
Iska S I unit volt per metre है, जिसके dimensions electric field जैसे ही हैं, और ये संयोग नहीं क्योंकि दोनों ही per unit दूरी potential हैं।
Do electromotive forces की तुलना फिर सिर्फ़ उनकी दो balance lengths के ratio पर सिमट जाती है।
<curious>Dhyan दीजिए वहाँ हुआ क्या।</curious> Gradient पूरी तरह कट गया, इसलिए आपको primary current या तार की resistance जानने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ी।
Internal resistance वाला नतीजा भी वैसे ही काम करता है, जिसमें सिर्फ़ दो लंबाइयाँ और एक known shunt resistance चाहिए।
Yahan l one वो balance length है जब cell अकेला हो और कोई current न खींच रहा हो, और l two वो छोटी लंबाई है जब cell के आर पार shunt resistance जुड़ जाए और वो current देने लगे।
To exam में ले जाने वाला नियम ये है: हर ratio वाले सवाल में gradient कट जाता है। k तब तक मत निकालिए जब तक कोई absolute voltage न माँगा जाए।
Board पर लिखा sum-and-difference वाला नतीजा वही सिद्धांत दो बार लगाया हुआ है, एक बार cells साथ देते हुए और एक बार विरोध करते हुए।

board_events.text: Because the wire is uniform, its resistance is proportional to length. Let $\sigma$ be the resistance per unit length.

segments.text: This derivation is short, and its punchline is a cancellation that explains why the instrument is cheap to build.
A meter bridge is a Wheatstone bridge in which two of the arms are a single uniform wire, one hundred centimetres long.
A known resistance sits in the left gap and the unknown in the right. A galvanometer connects the junction between them to a jockey resting on the wire, and you slide until it reads zero.
Now the key physical fact. Because the wire is uniform, its resistance is proportional to length, so let sigma be the resistance per unit length of the wire.
The arm from the left end to the jockey is then sigma times l, and the arm from the jockey to the right end is sigma times one hundred minus l.
These two play exactly the roles of the lower pair of arms in the Wheatstone diamond, with the known and unknown resistances sitting above them.
<curious>Now apply the balance condition and watch what happens.</curious> The sigma appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels completely.

That cancellation is the whole point. It is why the wire only needs to be uniform, and not of any particular resistivity, which makes the instrument cheap and robust. Rearranging gives the unknown directly from the known and the length.
Ye derivation छोटी है, और इसका असली मोड़ एक कटाव है जो समझाता है कि ये उपकरण बनाने में सस्ता क्यों है।
Meter bridge एक Wheatstone bridge है जिसमें दो arms की जगह एक uniform तार है, सौ centimetre लंबा।
Baayen gap में known resistance बैठती है और दाएँ में unknown। Ek galvanometer उनके बीच के junction को तार पर टिके jockey से जोड़ता है, और आप तब तक सरकाते हैं जब तक वो zero न पढ़े।
Ab असली physical तथ्य। तार uniform है, इसलिए उसकी resistance लंबाई के अनुपात में है, तो मान लीजिए sigma तार की per unit length resistance है।
<curious>Baayen सिरे से jockey तक की arm तब sigma into l है</curious>, और jockey से दाएँ सिरे तक की arm sigma into सौ minus l।
Ye दोनों ठीक वही भूमिका निभाती हैं जो Wheatstone diamond में नीचे की जोड़ी की है, और known तथा unknown resistances उनके ऊपर बैठी हैं।
Ab balance की शर्त लगाइए और देखिए क्या होता है। Sigma numerator और denominator दोनों में आता है और पूरी तरह कट जाता है।
Wahi कटाव पूरी बात है। इसीलिए तार को सिर्फ़ uniform होना चाहिए, किसी ख़ास resistivity का नहीं, और यही उपकरण को सस्ता और मज़बूत बनाता है। Rearrange करने पर unknown सीधे known और लंबाई से मिल जाती है।

sections.title: Derivation: the potentiometer principle

board_events.text: Derivation: the potentiometer principle
A steady current $I$ flows through a uniform wire of length $L$ and total resistance $R_{\text{wire}}$.
The potential drops uniformly along it, because equal lengths carry equal resistance and the same current.

board_events.latex: V_l = I \times (\text{resistance of length } l) = I\sigma l

board_events.text: Since $k$ is fixed by a uniform wire and a constant current, $V_l$ is strictly proportional to $l$.
This proportionality is the entire principle of the instrument: length becomes a precise proxy for potential difference.
A voltmeter of finite resistance draws current and reads $E - Ir$. The potentiometer at balance draws none, so it behaves as an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance.

segments.text: This derivation is two lines of algebra, but it is worth dwelling on because everything the potentiometer does rests on it.
A steady current flows through a uniform wire of length L and total resistance R wire.
Say why the drop is uniform, because that is the physical content. Equal lengths of the wire carry equal resistance and the same current, so equal lengths must drop equal potential.
The drop across any length l measured from the start is therefore the current times the resistance of that length, which is I sigma l.
Rewriting sigma in terms of the whole wire gives the drop as a constant times the length, where that constant is the potential gradient k.
Plotted out, potential against length is a straight line through the origin, and the slope of that line is exactly the potential gradient.
<curious>Since k is fixed by a uniform wire and a constant current</curious>, the potential is strictly proportional to the length, with no correction term anywhere.
That proportionality is the entire principle: length becomes a precise proxy for potential difference.
And this is why the instrument beats a voltmeter. A voltmeter of finite resistance draws current and reads E minus I r, while the potentiometer at balance draws none at all.
Ye derivation दो lines की algebra है, लेकिन इस पर ठहरना ज़रूरी है क्योंकि potentiometer जो कुछ करता है वो सब इसी पर टिका है।
Ek steady current L लंबाई और R wire कुल resistance वाले uniform तार से बहता है।
Drop uniform क्यों है ये कहिए, क्योंकि यही physical सार है। तार की barabar लंबाइयों में barabar resistance है और वही current है, इसलिए barabar लंबाइयों में barabar potential गिरना ही चाहिए।
Shuru से नापी गई किसी भी लंबाई l पर drop इसलिए current into उस लंबाई की resistance है, यानी I sigma l।
<curious>Sigma को पूरे तार के रूप में दोबारा लिखने पर</curious> drop बन जाता है एक स्थिरांक into लंबाई, और वो स्थिरांक ही potential gradient k है।
Plot कीजिए तो potential versus length एक सीधी line है जो origin से गुज़रती है, और उस line का slope बिलकुल potential gradient है।
Kyunki k uniform तार और स्थिर current से तय है, potential लंबाई के ठीक अनुपात में है, कहीं कोई सुधार का term नहीं।
Wahi अनुपात पूरा सिद्धांत है: लंबाई potential difference का सटीक प्रतिनिधि बन जाती है।
Aur इसीलिए ये उपकरण voltmeter से बेहतर है। Finite resistance वाला voltmeter current खींचता है और E minus I r पढ़ता है, जबकि potentiometer balance पर बिलकुल current नहीं खींचता।

sections.title: Derivation: comparing EMFs and measuring internal resistance

board_events.text: Derivation: comparing EMFs and measuring internal resistance
Balance each cell in turn against the ramp and note its balancing length. Each electromotive force equals the gradient times its own length.
At the null point no current is drawn from the cell, so the balanced potential equals its true electromotive force with no internal drop.
For internal resistance, first balance the cell alone with the shunt key open, giving $E = kl_1$.
